lessons.title: What a Final Year Project or Thesis Is
lessons.content:
Imagine you have been learning to cook for four years. You learned to cut vegetables, boil rice, fry fish and bake a cake, one skill at a time, each with a teacher standing next to you. Now your family says: next month is Eid, and you are in charge of the whole lunch for twenty guests. You decide the menu, buy the ingredients, plan the timing, cook everything and serve it. Nobody tells you each step. That big, self-run job is exactly what a final year project or thesis is for a computer science student. All the small skills you learned in separate courses now have to work together on one real piece of work that you own.

What it is: A final year project or thesis is a long piece of independent work, usually done in the last year of a BSc, where a student (or a small team) picks a problem, studies what is already known about it, designs a solution or an experiment, carries it out, evaluates the result honestly, writes it up as a book-length report and defends it in front of a board of teachers. It is done under the guidance of a supervisor, a teacher who advises you but does not do the work for you. It usually counts as one of the largest courses in the whole degree, so the marks matter, but the skills matter even more.

Why universities make you do it: Exams test whether you can answer questions someone else wrote. Real work, whether in a company or in research, is different: nobody gives you the question. You have to find the right problem, decide how to attack it, manage months of time, recover when things break, and explain what you did to people who were not there. The final year project is the first place in the degree where you practise all of that together. It is also the one piece of your degree that is truly yours, so it becomes the thing you talk about in job interviews and in applications for higher studies.

Project and thesis, the two flavours: Most departments allow two broad kinds of final year work, and the names are often used loosely. A project mainly builds something useful: an app, a web system, a device, a tool. Its main question is 'Does this system solve the problem well for its users?' A thesis mainly answers a research question with evidence: 'Does method A detect fake Bangla news more accurately than method B on the same data?' Its main output is new knowledge, backed by experiments. In practice the two overlap. A good project still compares options and measures performance, and many theses build software to run their experiments. Some departments call everything a thesis; others let you choose 'project' or 'thesis' when you register. Check your own department's handbook for what each option requires.

Other shapes you may see: Some universities offer an industry attachment or internship-based project, where you work on a real problem inside a company and write a report about it. Some allow a hardware project, such as an IoT soil-moisture monitor or a line-following robot, which needs parts, soldering and lab time. Some interdisciplinary theses mix computing with agriculture, health, finance or language. The steps you will learn in this course apply to all of them: choose a problem, understand the background, plan, build or experiment, evaluate, write and defend.

The typical shape in Bangladesh: Details differ between universities, so treat this as a common pattern rather than a rule. The final year work is often spread across two or three terms or semesters. Students form a group of one to four, or work alone, and are assigned a supervisor from the department's faculty. There is usually a proposal or topic approval early on, one or more progress presentations in the middle, a final report or thesis book near the end, and a final defence or viva in front of a board. Marks are often split between the supervisor's assessment, the board's assessment of the presentation and report, and sometimes continuous progress marks. Credit hours, page limits, formatting and the exact marking split come from your department, so read the official guidelines in your first week and keep a copy.

What you hand in: Across the whole journey you will usually produce several deliverables. First, a topic title and a short proposal. Second, progress reports or presentations showing what you have done so far. Third, the actual work: source code, a working system or prototype, datasets, trained models, experiment logs or hardware. Fourth, the thesis book, a formal document of roughly 40 to 100 pages in many departments, describing everything. Fifth, the final presentation with a demo or results, and the defence where you answer questions. Some departments also ask for a poster, a CD or online repository link, or a similarity (plagiarism) report.

How it is judged: Examiners ask a small set of questions, even if the marking sheet uses different words. Is the problem clear and worth solving? Did the student understand what others have already done? Is the method sound and appropriate for the problem? Was the work actually done, and is it of decent quality? Are the results measured fairly and reported honestly, including weaknesses? Is the report clear and properly referenced? Can the student explain and defend every decision? Notice that 'did you invent something world-changing' is not on the list. A small problem solved carefully and explained clearly almost always scores better than a giant idea done badly.

What counts as a contribution: For a project, the contribution might be a working system that solves a real local need, a careful design, or an honest evaluation with users. For a thesis, it might be a new dataset (for example, 3,000 labelled photos of local rice leaf diseases), a new or modified method, a fair comparison of existing methods on a new kind of data, or a replication that checks whether a published result really holds. At BSc level nobody expects a revolution. They expect a clear, honest, well-executed step.

The journey map: Here is the whole route you will follow in this course. Months 0 to 1: choose a topic and a supervisor, form a team, read the department rules. Months 1 to 3: search and read the literature, write the problem statement and research questions, write and defend the proposal, plan the work and the risks. Months 3 to 8: collect data or set up the system, build, run experiments, evaluate, keep notes and code safe. Months 6 to 10: analyse results and write the thesis book chapter by chapter, getting feedback. Final month: polish, check similarity, submit, rehearse and defend. The months overlap on purpose; writing starts early and reading never fully stops. If your department runs the work over two semesters instead of a full year, squeeze each phase proportionally, but keep the order. The most common reason students panic in the last month is that they treated these phases as strictly one after another, so all the writing landed at the end. A useful habit is to ask at the end of every month: which phase am I mainly in, and what is the one deliverable that proves I finished the last one? If you cannot name that deliverable, the phase is not really finished.

A running example: Throughout this course we will follow two invented student works so the steps feel concrete. The first is a thesis by Nusrat and Rafi: 'Can a phone camera and a small neural network tell fresh mangoes from rotten ones well enough for a Rajshahi market seller?' The second is a project by Tanvir: a campus bus tracker that shows students where the university bus is on a map and how long until it reaches their stop. One is research-flavoured, one is build-flavoured, and together they cover almost every situation you will meet.

Real-life example 1, the mango thesis at a glance: Nusrat and Rafi notice that sellers at a fruit market in Rajshahi sort mangoes by eye and lose money when rotten ones spread mould to good ones. They read papers on fruit quality detection and find many used foreign datasets of apples and oranges, but very few used South Asian mango varieties photographed with cheap phones. Their gap is local data and low-cost hardware. They collect and label photos, train a small model, compare it with a simple baseline, test it in the market, write the thesis and defend it. Every lesson ahead will zoom into one of these steps.

Real-life example 2, the bus tracker project at a glance: Tanvir sees students waiting twenty minutes in the rain for the campus bus without knowing whether it has left. He interviews ten students and two drivers, writes requirements, builds a simple Android app for drivers that sends GPS location every few seconds, a server that stores it, and a student app that shows the bus on a map with an estimated arrival time. He measures how accurate the arrival estimates are and runs a short usability survey. The contribution is not new science; it is a well-engineered, tested, documented system that solves a real problem.

What this course is and is not: You have already learned how to write in Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8): clear sentences, figures and tables, report structure, proposals, citing, avoiding plagiarism and giving presentations. We will only recap those skills when needed and point you back. This course is about running the work itself: making decisions, managing time and risk, doing research and engineering properly, and getting through the board. Deeper research theory comes later in Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7), and professional project management in Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11).

Common misunderstandings: Many students think the thesis is mainly about the final book, so they leave writing and thinking for the last month. Others think it must be completely original, so they reject good small ideas. Some think the supervisor will tell them exactly what to do each week, and wait. Others believe a fancy technology (blockchain, a giant AI model) makes a project good. In reality, examiners reward a clear problem, sound method, honest results and real understanding. Technology choice only matters if it fits the problem.

What exams and boards often ask about this topic: In proposal or defence sessions you may be asked 'Is this a project or a thesis, and why?', 'What exactly is your contribution?', 'What problem does your work solve and for whom?' and 'How will you know if you succeeded?'. Being able to answer those four questions in one or two sentences each, from the very first month, is the best sign that your work is on track.

Recap: A final year project or thesis is a long, supervised, independent piece of work where you choose a problem, study the background, plan, build or experiment, evaluate honestly, write it up and defend it. Projects lean towards building useful systems; theses lean towards answering research questions with evidence; both share the same steps. Rules differ by department, so read your handbook early. Next lesson: the mindset, skills and time budget that make this long journey manageable.
key_points: A final year project or thesis is a long, supervised, independent piece of work that you own from problem to defence.
A project mainly builds a useful system; a thesis mainly answers a research question with evidence; they overlap a lot.
Typical deliverables: proposal, progress reports, the actual work (code, data, system), the thesis book, and the presentation and defence.
Examiners judge a clear problem, awareness of existing work, a sound method, real work done, honest evaluation, clear writing and your understanding.
A BSc contribution can be a useful system, a new local dataset, a fair comparison or a careful replication; nobody expects a revolution.
Credit hours, page limits and marking splits differ by department, so read the official guidelines in the first week.
Writing starts early and reading never fully stops; the phases of the journey overlap on purpose.
lessons.tip: From week one, keep a single document where you can answer four questions in one sentence each: what problem, for whom, what is my contribution, and how will I know I succeeded. Update it every month.
lessons.task: Find your department's final year project or thesis guidelines (handbook, notice board or website). Write down: duration, team size limit, deliverables and deadlines, and how marks are split. If something is missing, write it as a question to ask your coordinator.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a final year project and a thesis?
options: A project is done alone and a thesis is done in a team
A project mainly builds a useful system; a thesis mainly answers a research question with evidence
A project has no report and a thesis has no code
There is no difference at all
quiz.explain: Both share the same steps, but projects lean towards building systems and theses towards answering research questions.

quiz.q: Which of these is usually NOT something examiners judge?
options: Whether the idea is a world-changing invention
Whether the student can defend decisions
quiz.explain: A small, clear, well-executed contribution is what is expected at BSc level.

quiz.q: Which is a valid BSc-level contribution?
options: Copying a paper's results into your book
Using the most famous technology regardless of the problem
A new labelled dataset of local rice leaf diseases with a fair comparison of methods
quiz.explain: New local data plus a fair comparison is a real, honest contribution.

quiz.q: Why should you read your department's guidelines in the first week?
options: Because credits, page limits, deadlines and marking split differ between departments
Because every university uses identical rules
Because the supervisor will write the thesis
Because the guidelines contain your topic
quiz.explain: Rules vary, and missing a formatting rule or deadline can cost marks.

quiz.q: Which order best matches the overall journey?
options: Write the book, then choose a topic, then read papers
Build first, then choose a problem
Choose topic and supervisor, read literature and propose, build or experiment, evaluate, write, defend
quiz.explain: This is the standard flow, with phases overlapping, especially writing.

lessons.title: Mindset, Skills and Time
lessons.content:
Think about two ways of getting fit. In the first, you join a class where a trainer counts every push-up for you, three times a week, with a test at the end of the month. In the second, you decide to run a half marathon in ten months, alone. Nobody checks on you on rainy mornings. Nobody tells you that this week you should rest. The second way needs a completely different mindset: you plan, you track, you adjust, and you keep going when motivation drops. Your regular courses are the trainer's class. The final year project is the half marathon. This lesson is about the mindset, the skills and the time budget that get you to the finish line.

From courses to self-driven work: In a normal course the teacher sets the syllabus, the pace, the assignments and the deadlines. You react. In a final year project, almost all of that becomes your job. You decide what to read, what to build first, which experiment to run next and when a piece is good enough. The supervisor sets the direction and checks quality, but the weekly steering wheel is in your hands. Students who wait for instructions lose the first two or three months, and those months are very hard to win back.

The owner mindset: Owning a project means you treat its problems as yours to solve. If the dataset is messy, you clean it or find another. If the library does not install, you search the error, read the docs, try a different version, and only then ask for help with a clear description of what you tried. If your teammate is stuck, you ask how to help. Owners do not say 'the supervisor didn't tell us' or 'the internet was slow this week'. They say 'this blocked us, here is what we did about it, and here is what we need'. Boards notice this attitude immediately in the defence.

What you already know: You are not starting from nothing. Programming courses taught you to build. Data Structures and Algorithms (deep-cse-2-2, deep-cse-3-1) taught you to choose efficient solutions. Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) taught requirements, design and documentation. Software Testing (deep-cse-5-8) taught you how to check quality. Probability and Statistics (deep-cse-2-6) gives you the tools for fair evaluation. Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1), Networks, Databases and others give domain skills. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8) taught you how to write and present. The final year project is where you glue them together, and it is completely normal to go back to old notes.

New skills you will grow: Some skills appear for the first time. Finding and reading research papers. Turning a vague interest into a precise question. Estimating how long unknown work will take. Managing risk. Running fair experiments. Writing a long document that stays consistent across 60 pages. Defending your work in front of experts. You do not need to have these on day one; the following lessons teach each one. What you need on day one is willingness to be a beginner again.

The time budget, worked: Let us estimate the total effort. Suppose your department spreads the work over about 40 teaching weeks and expects around 10 hours per week from each student. That is 40 x 10 = 400 hours per person. A reasonable split looks like this: reading and planning 15 percent, which is 60 hours; building and experimenting 45 percent, 180 hours; writing 20 percent, 80 hours; meetings, presentations and admin 10 percent, 40 hours; and a 10 percent buffer for surprises, 40 hours. Check: 60 + 180 + 80 + 40 + 40 = 400. The numbers for your department will differ, so recompute them with your own weeks and expectations. The point is that 400 hours sounds like a lot, but divided over 40 weeks it is only 10 hours a week, and missing a few weeks makes the remaining weeks very heavy.

What happens if you start late: Say you lose the first 10 weeks to waiting and indecision. The same 400 hours now have to fit into 30 weeks: 400 / 30 is about 13.3 hours per week, a third more every week, and usually during the busiest exam period. Lose 20 weeks and it becomes 20 hours per week, which is almost a part-time job on top of your other courses. This simple division is the strongest argument for starting in week one, even if only with small steps.

The weekly rhythm: Big projects are finished by small, regular steps. A good rhythm has three parts. First, a fixed time slot: for example, Sunday and Tuesday evenings plus Friday morning, protected like a class. Second, a weekly goal written as a deliverable: 'cleaned 500 images and wrote the cleaning script', not 'worked on data'. Third, a short weekly review: what did I finish, what blocked me, what is next week's goal. If you are a team, do the review together in fifteen minutes. These three habits beat occasional all-night sessions every time.

Balancing with other courses and life: In the final year you also have other courses, maybe tuition jobs, internship hunting, and family duties. Look at your term calendar and mark exam weeks and assignment peaks. Plan lighter project goals for those weeks and heavier ones for quieter weeks. Do not try to do everything in the semester break unless you have truly planned it; breaks often disappear into weddings, travel and rest. If you are applying for jobs or higher studies, remember the project is your best story, so investing in it also helps those applications.

The motivation curve: Almost every long project follows a similar emotional curve. At the start you are excited; everything seems possible. A few months in, you hit the valley: the data is messier than expected, the model performs worse than the papers, the app crashes, and the end is far away. Many students think this valley means they chose the wrong topic. Usually it does not; it is simply the middle of every real project. What gets you through is breaking the next step into something tiny you can finish today, showing even small progress to your supervisor, and remembering why the problem matters to real people.

Keeping a project diary: A project diary or lab notebook is a simple dated log. Every work session, write a few lines: date, what you did, what you found, what failed, what you will try next, and links to files or commits. It can be a Google Doc, a Markdown file in your repository or a paper notebook. It sounds boring, but it saves you many times: when you forget which settings gave the best result, when you write the methodology chapter months later, when the supervisor asks why you dropped an idea, and when a teammate needs to continue your work. Treat it as notes to your future self, who will have forgotten almost everything.

Asking for help well: Owning the project does not mean never asking for help. It means asking well. A good request says what you are trying to do, what you tried, what happened, and what you think the options are. 'The model does not work' wastes everyone's time. 'Training accuracy reaches 98 percent but validation stays at 60 percent after 20 epochs; I suspect overfitting; I tried dropout 0.3 and it moved to 63 percent; should I collect more data or try data augmentation first?' gets a useful answer in two minutes, from a supervisor, a senior or an online forum.

Deep work sessions: Research and engineering need long stretches of focus. Reading one dense paper or debugging a training script can take ninety minutes before you even understand what is going on. If your phone buzzes every three minutes, you restart from zero each time. So protect at least two blocks of 90 to 120 minutes per week: phone on silent and in another room, one clear task written on paper, all needed files open before you start. Short tasks, like renaming files or formatting references, can fill the small gaps between classes. Matching the type of task to the type of time slot is one of the simplest productivity tricks there is.

Health and burnout: A final year project is a marathon, so treat your body like a runner would. Regular sleep matters more than one extra night of coding, because tired brains write buggy code and miss obvious mistakes in results. Eat properly, move a little every day, and keep at least one evening per week completely free. If you notice that you dread opening the project, feel constantly guilty, or cannot sleep because of it, talk to your supervisor, a friend or your university's counselling service. Shrinking the scope a little is always better than breaking down near the deadline.

Real-life example 1, Rafi's slow start: In the mango thesis, Rafi waited for the supervisor to send a reading list. Three weeks passed. Nusrat instead searched Google Scholar for 'mango quality detection deep learning', read five abstracts, and brought a one-page note to the next meeting with three possible directions. The supervisor picked one and gave specific advice in ten minutes. Rafi learned the lesson: bring something, even something rough, and the supervisor can react to it. Afterwards they agreed on fixed work slots: Saturday afternoons together at the library and two solo evenings each.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir's exam-season plan: Tanvir looked at his calendar and saw that midterms filled weeks 7 and 8 and finals filled weeks 15 and 16. He planned only small tasks in those weeks, like writing documentation and fixing small bugs, and put the hard tasks, like the arrival-time algorithm and server deployment, in weeks 4 to 6 and 9 to 13. When a bus driver's phone broke in week 10, he still had buffer to borrow another phone and recollect GPS data. Planning around the calendar turned a crisis into a small delay.

Common mistakes: Waiting for perfect clarity before starting. Working in random bursts instead of a steady rhythm. Measuring effort in hours instead of finished deliverables. Hiding from the supervisor when progress is slow, which makes things worse. Not keeping notes, then being unable to reproduce the best result. Assuming the semester break will magically fix everything. Treating the motivation valley as proof of failure.

What boards and supervisors look for here: Supervisors often judge consistency: did you meet regularly, did you show progress, did you respond to feedback. In progress presentations, boards ask 'what have you done since last time?' and 'what is your plan to finish?'. A clear weekly log and a realistic time plan make those questions easy.

Recap: The final year project needs an owner mindset: you steer, the supervisor guides. Combine old course skills with new research skills. Budget your hours explicitly (for example 40 weeks x 10 hours = 400 hours) and see how a late start pushes the weekly load up. Keep a weekly rhythm with deliverable-style goals, plan around exam weeks, expect the motivation valley, keep a project diary and ask for help with specific details. Next lesson: how to find and choose a good topic.
key_points: The final year project is self-driven: you steer week by week, the supervisor guides direction and quality.
An owner mindset means treating every blocker as yours to solve, then asking for help with clear details.
Budget hours explicitly, for example 40 weeks x 10 hours = 400 hours, split across reading, building, writing, meetings and buffer.
Starting late raises the weekly load sharply: 400 hours over 30 weeks is about 13.3 hours per week, over 20 weeks it is 20.
Keep a weekly rhythm: fixed slots, a deliverable-style goal and a short weekly review.
Plan lighter tasks for exam weeks and expect a motivation valley in the middle of the project.
A dated project diary saves you when writing the methodology, reproducing results or handing work to a teammate.
lessons.tip: Write your weekly goal as something someone else could check: a file, a script, a table, a page. If nobody could check it, it is an activity, not a goal.
lessons.task: Compute your own time budget: count the weeks you have until the final submission, choose realistic hours per week, and split the total into reading, building, writing, meetings and buffer. Then block your fixed weekly project slots in your phone calendar.

quiz.q: If you have 400 hours of work and only 25 weeks left, how many hours per week do you need?
quiz.explain: 400 / 25 = 16 hours per week.

quiz.q: Which weekly goal is written as a checkable deliverable?
options: Label 500 images and commit the labelling script
quiz.explain: A deliverable can be checked by someone else.

quiz.q: What is the 'motivation valley' in a long project?
options: A normal middle phase where problems pile up and the end feels far away
Proof that you chose the wrong topic
quiz.explain: Almost every long project hits this phase; small steps and visible progress get you through.

quiz.q: Which help request is the most useful?
options: Validation accuracy stays at 60 percent while training reaches 98 percent; I tried dropout 0.3; should I try augmentation or more data?
Can you send me a better topic?
quiz.explain: It states the goal, what was tried, what happened and the options.

quiz.q: Why keep a dated project diary?
options: To reproduce results, write the methodology later and hand over work
quiz.explain: Notes to your future self save time in writing, reproducing and handover.

lessons.title: Finding and Choosing a Topic
lessons.content:
Picking a final year topic is a bit like choosing which house to rent for a whole year. A house can look beautiful in photos, but if it is too far from your university, too expensive, or has no water supply, you will regret it every single day. A good house is one you like, can afford, can reach, and that has what you need. A topic works the same way. You will live with it for many months, so it must be interesting enough to keep you going, small enough to finish, and supplied with the data, tools and guidance you need. This lesson shows where ideas come from, how to narrow them, and how to choose between them with a simple, honest scoring method.

What a topic is, and what it is not: A topic is not just an area like 'machine learning' or 'blockchain'. Those are fields, as large as countries. A topic is a specific problem inside a field, in a specific setting, that you can work on with specific methods. 'Machine learning for agriculture' is still too broad. 'Detecting rotten mangoes from phone photos for small market sellers' is a topic. By the end of this lesson you should be able to write your topic as one clear sentence and, ideally, as one question.

Why topic choice matters so much: The topic decides almost everything that follows: which papers you read, which skills you need, whether data exists, how long the work takes and how interesting your defence will be. A strong student with a poorly chosen topic often ends up with weaker results than an average student with a well-chosen one. Fixing a bad topic in month five is painful, because you lose much of the work. Spending two or three focused weeks on choosing is one of the best investments in the whole project.

Source 1, problems around you: Look at daily life in Bangladesh with an engineer's eye. Long queues at hospitals and passport offices. Traffic and unpredictable buses. Farmers who cannot identify crop diseases. Shops that keep accounts in paper khatas. Floods, waterlogging and air pollution. Bangla text and speech that most software handles poorly. Every frustration you notice is a possible problem. Write them down in a notebook for a week; you will be surprised how many you collect.

Source 2, your supervisor and department: Many teachers publish a list of topics they want to supervise, often linked to their own research. These topics come with a big advantage: the supervisor already knows the literature, may have data or equipment, and is genuinely interested. Ask seniors which teachers supervise what, and look at the titles of recent theses in your department library or repository, which shows the scale that is realistic.

Source 3, papers and their future work: Research papers usually end with limitations and future work. These sections are gold mines. If a paper on Bangla sentiment analysis says 'our dataset contained only product reviews; testing on social media comments is future work', that sentence is practically a topic. Survey papers, which summarise an entire area, also list open challenges. You will learn to search papers properly in lesson 06; for now, skim a few recent ones in an area you like.

Source 4, data, competitions and industry: Sometimes the idea starts from an available resource. A public dataset (for example, Bangla handwritten digits or local road images) can suggest a question. A competition on Kaggle or a national hackathon can provide both data and a clear task. Companies and NGOs sometimes have real problems and data they are willing to share for a student project, such as predicting demand at a pharmacy chain or classifying customer complaints. Industry links can also help your job search later.

The funnel, from area to question: Narrow in steps. Area: computer vision. Domain: agriculture. Problem: fruit quality at markets. Specific task: classify mangoes as fresh or rotten from photos. Setting and constraint: photos from a cheap Android phone under market lighting, model small enough to run on that phone. Question: 'Can a small CNN on a low-cost phone classify local mangoes as fresh or rotten with at least 90 percent accuracy?' Each step removes ambiguity. If you cannot write the last line, keep narrowing.

The criteria for a good topic: Use the same six questions for every candidate. Interest: will you still care in month eight? Size: can it be done in the time and team size you have? Data and resources: do the data, hardware and software already exist or can you realistically collect or buy them? Skills: do you have, or can you learn quickly, the needed skills? Supervisor fit: does a teacher in your department know this area and want to supervise it? Value: does it help someone or add knowledge, even in a small way? Some departments also value novelty, meaning it should not exactly copy an existing thesis.

The weighted scoring matrix, worked: Suppose Nusrat and Rafi have three candidates. A: rotten mango detection from phone photos. B: fake Bangla news detection. C: a blockchain-based land registry. They choose weights that reflect what matters most to them: interest 0.20, size 0.25, data 0.25, skills 0.10, supervisor fit 0.10, value 0.10. The weights add up to 1. Then they score each topic from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). Topic A scores 4, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4. Weighted total: 0.20 x 4 + 0.25 x 4 + 0.25 x 3 + 0.10 x 4 + 0.10 x 5 + 0.10 x 4 = 0.8 + 1.0 + 0.75 + 0.4 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 3.85. Topic B scores 5, 3, 4, 3, 3, 4, which gives 1.0 + 0.75 + 1.0 + 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 3.75. Topic C scores 3, 2, 1, 2, 2, 5, which gives 0.6 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.5 = 2.25.

Reading the matrix honestly: Topic C is clearly out: high value, but there is no access to real land records, the scope is huge and no supervisor works on it. A and B are very close, 3.85 against 3.75. A tiny change in one score would flip them. This is important: the matrix does not decide for you; it shows you where the real trade-off lies. Here it is data and supervisor fit (A) against interest and existing data (B). Nusrat and Rafi take both to their preferred supervisor, who works in computer vision, and choose A. The matrix made the conversation short and focused.

The feasibility check: Before committing, do a two-week mini test. Find at least five closely related papers. Confirm that the data exists or collect a tiny sample, for example 50 mango photos. Run the simplest possible version, such as a pretrained model on those 50 photos, or a hello-world version of the app with one screen and one API call. Estimate the hours using the budget from lesson 02. If any step reveals a wall, such as data you cannot get or hardware that costs too much, it is far cheaper to discover it now.

Red flags: Be careful with topics that sound impressive but hide trouble. Too big: 'an AI doctor for all diseases'. No data: 'predict earthquakes in Dhaka', when the needed sensor data does not exist publicly. Hardware you cannot get: imported sensors with months of customs delay. Hype words without a problem: 'blockchain plus metaverse for education'. Topics that need private data from hospitals or banks, unless permission is already arranged. Topics that are a copy of a tutorial with nothing added. And topics nobody in your department can supervise.

Project-style topics: For build-style projects the same logic applies, but the question becomes 'which real users, which problem, which measurable improvement?'. A campus bus tracker, a clinic appointment system for a small town, a Bangla voice assistant for checking train schedules, or a stock app for a small pharmacy are all fine if you can reach real users, collect requirements, build it and evaluate it. A project does not need novel science, but it does need real users and evidence that the system works for them.

How new does it need to be: Students often worry that someone has already done their idea. Usually someone has done something similar, and that is fine. Novelty at BSc level can be small: a new setting (Bangla instead of English, local mango varieties instead of apples), a new constraint (runs offline on a cheap phone), a new comparison (testing five known methods fairly on the same local data), or a new combination of known parts that solves a real need. What is not acceptable is repeating an existing thesis or tutorial and presenting it as your own. Your job in the literature review is to show exactly what is different about your work.

Can you change the topic later: Small adjustments are normal and healthy; the question gets sharper as you read and experiment. A complete change is expensive but sometimes right, for example when the promised data never arrives. If you must change, do it early, explain the reason to your supervisor in writing, check whether your department needs a formal approval for a new title, and reuse whatever you can from the old reading and code.

Real-life example 1, Tanvir's funnel: Tanvir starts with 'something with maps'. His notebook from the week shows four complaints about campus buses. He narrows: domain, university transport; problem, students do not know when the bus will arrive; users, about 2,000 students using four buses; constraint, drivers have basic Android phones; measurable goal, arrival estimates within 2 minutes for most trips. He checks feasibility: the transport office agrees to let drivers run a test app, and a free map SDK is available. His scoring matrix puts the bus tracker well above his other idea, a generic chat app.

Real-life example 2, a rescue from a too-big topic: A team first proposed 'a complete Bangla speech recognition system'. Their supervisor pointed out that big companies spend years and huge datasets on this. In the feasibility check they found a public Bangla speech dataset but realised training a full system was impossible on their laptops. They narrowed to 'recognising 20 spoken Bangla commands for a farmers' helpline menu', using a small model. It was finished on time, worked on a cheap phone and got good marks.

Common mistakes and what boards ask: Choosing by trend instead of fit. Choosing by what a friend's team did last year. Writing a topic as a field ('IoT') rather than a problem. Skipping the feasibility test. Ignoring data access until month four. Boards commonly ask: 'Why this topic?', 'Why is it important in our context?', 'Is the scope realistic for your time?' and 'Where does your data come from?'. Your scoring matrix and feasibility notes give you ready answers.

Recap: Ideas come from problems around you, supervisors' lists, papers' future work, datasets, competitions and industry. Narrow from area to domain to problem to specific task to a one-line question. Judge candidates on interest, size, data, skills, supervisor fit and value, with a weighted matrix that shows trade-offs rather than deciding blindly. Do a short feasibility check and watch for red flags. Next lesson: choosing a supervisor and working well with them.
key_points: A topic is a specific problem in a specific setting, not a whole field like 'machine learning'.
Idea sources: everyday problems, supervisors' lists, papers' limitations and future work, datasets, competitions and industry partners.
Narrow in steps: area, domain, problem, specific task, setting and constraints, then one clear question.
Judge topics on interest, size, data and resources, skills, supervisor fit and value.
A weighted scoring matrix (weights summing to 1, scores 1 to 5) shows trade-offs; close totals mean you must discuss, not just pick the higher number.
Run a two-week feasibility check: related papers, a small data sample, the simplest working version and an hour estimate.
Red flags: too big, no data, unobtainable hardware, hype without a problem, private data without permission, no supervisor.
lessons.tip: Write each candidate topic as one question with a measurable target. If you cannot, the topic is still a field, not a problem.
lessons.task: List three candidate topics. Choose weights for interest, size, data, skills, supervisor fit and value that add up to 1, score each topic from 1 to 5, and compute the weighted totals. Then write one sentence about the real trade-off between your top two.

quiz.q: Which of these is a topic rather than a field?
options: Detecting rotten mangoes from low-cost phone photos for market sellers
quiz.explain: A topic is a specific problem in a setting; the others are whole fields.

quiz.q: Weights are 0.5 for data and 0.5 for interest. A topic scores 4 for data and 2 for interest. What is its weighted total?
Two topics score 3.85 and 3.75 in a weighted matrix. What should you do?
options: Pick the one your friends chose
Treat it as a near tie, identify the real trade-off and discuss with the supervisor
quiz.explain: A small difference can flip with one score; the matrix shows the trade-off, it does not decide alone.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag in a proposed topic?
options: It needs private hospital data with no permission arranged
It has a clear measurable target
A supervisor in the department works in the area
quiz.explain: Data you cannot legally or practically access will stop the work.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the two-week feasibility check?
options: To finish the whole thesis early
To discover walls like missing data or costly hardware before committing
quiz.explain: Finding problems early is much cheaper than finding them in month five.

lessons.title: Choosing and Working with a Supervisor
lessons.content:
Imagine you are learning to drive on Dhaka roads. Your instructor sits beside you. They do not hold the steering wheel, and they will not drive for you, but they spot the rickshaw coming from the left before you do, tell you when you are about to take a wrong turn, and stop you from doing something dangerous. A thesis supervisor is that instructor. You drive the project; the supervisor watches the road with years more experience. This lesson is about choosing a supervisor who fits your work and building a working relationship that gets the most out of their limited time.

What a supervisor does: A supervisor is a faculty member officially responsible for guiding your final year work. Their usual roles are: helping you shape and approve the topic, pointing you to key literature and methods, checking that your approach is sound, giving feedback on drafts, warning you about risks, judging your progress and often giving part of your marks, and representing your work in front of the board. What they usually do not do: choose every step for you, write your code or chapters, fix your bugs, or chase you for meetings. Knowing this boundary avoids a lot of frustration on both sides.

How allocation usually works: Departments use different systems, so check yours. Common patterns in Bangladesh include: students submit a ranked list of preferred supervisors and topics and the department matches them; teachers post topics and students apply; students approach teachers directly and get a signature on a form; or the department assigns supervisors based on area and load. Each teacher can usually take only a limited number of groups, so popular supervisors fill up fast. Know your deadlines and have a first and second choice ready.

Finding a good fit: The best supervisor for you is someone whose area matches your topic and whose working style suits you. To judge area, look at their recent publications on Google Scholar or the department website, theses they supervised in the past few years, and courses they teach. To judge style, ask seniors politely: how often do they meet, how quickly do they reply, how detailed is their feedback, do they expect publications? A famous professor with twenty groups may have less time than a younger teacher with three groups who is actively publishing in your area. Neither is automatically better; it depends on how much guidance you need.

The first contact email: Teachers receive many vague requests, so a clear first email stands out. A good structure is: a specific subject line, a one-line introduction, why you are contacting this teacher, your topic idea in two or three sentences, evidence you have done some homework, and a clear ask. For example: 'Subject: Request to discuss a final year thesis on mango quality detection. Dear Sir, I am Nusrat Jahan, a final year CSE student (ID 1903041). I read your 2022 paper on fruit disease classification and would like to work in a related area. Our idea is to classify local mangoes as fresh or rotten from low-cost phone photos for market sellers. We have shortlisted five related papers and collected 50 sample photos. Could we meet for 15 minutes this week to discuss whether you would supervise this? Thank you. Nusrat Jahan, Rafi Ahmed.' Short, specific and respectful.

The first meeting: Bring a one-page summary: the problem, the candidate question, three to five key papers, your skills, any data you have, and two or three possible directions. Ask the supervisor about their expectations: meeting frequency, preferred communication channel, how they like drafts submitted, and whether they expect a paper. Before you leave, agree on the next step and the date of the next meeting. Send a short email the same day summarising what was agreed. That summary becomes the first entry in your meeting record.

How much supervisor time you really have, worked: Suppose you meet for 30 minutes every two weeks across 40 weeks. That is 40 / 2 = 20 meetings, and 20 x 30 = 600 minutes, which is only 10 hours in the entire project. Even with extra email feedback, the supervisor's total attention is maybe 15 to 20 hours, while you spend 400 hours or more. Every meeting minute is valuable. Coming unprepared and spending 20 of 30 minutes describing what you might do wastes a large share of your total guidance.

Preparing for each meeting: Send a short agenda one day before. It should list what you did since the last meeting, results or problems with a figure or table if possible, specific questions or decisions you need, and your proposed next steps. For example: '1. Finished labelling 1,200 images. 2. Baseline accuracy 78 percent (table attached). 3. Question: should we merge the semi-rotten class into rotten? 4. Next: try a pretrained MobileNet.' With this, the supervisor can think ahead and the meeting becomes about decisions, not reporting.

Meeting minutes: During or right after the meeting, write minutes: date, who attended, decisions made, feedback received, action items with an owner and a deadline. Send them to the supervisor and teammates and store them in a shared folder. Minutes protect everyone. If later someone asks 'why did you drop the semi-rotten class?', you can point to the decision and its reason. They also make writing the methodology chapter easier, because your design decisions are already recorded with dates.

Receiving feedback: Supervisors are busy, so feedback can feel short or blunt: 'this section is unclear', 'where is the baseline?', 'too many claims'. Do not take it personally; it is about the work, not you. Read all comments before reacting. If something is unclear, ask a specific question. For each comment, either make the change or write a short, respectful reason why not. Keeping a feedback table (comment, action, status) helps you track rounds and shows the supervisor that every point was considered.

Communication habits: Use the channel your supervisor prefers, often official email, sometimes a messaging group. Keep messages short with a clear subject. Do not send ten messages in an evening; collect them. Respect their time: avoid late-night messages unless they invited them, and give reasonable time for draft feedback, often a week or two for a chapter. If a deadline is close, say so clearly and early. Thank them for feedback; a little courtesy keeps the relationship warm through a long project.

Monthly progress notes: Besides meetings, a one-page progress note at the end of each month is a powerful habit. It has four short parts: planned this month, actually done, problems and how they were handled, and plan for next month. Compare planned with done honestly; if you planned five tasks and finished three, say so and explain why. Over a year you build a set of about ten notes that show steady work, help the supervisor fill in any evaluation form, and give you a ready timeline for the thesis book. Many departments ask for formal progress reports anyway; your monthly notes make those take minutes instead of days.

Authorship and credit: If your work turns into a paper, discuss authorship openly and early. A common practice is that the students who did the work are first authors and the supervisor, who shaped and guided it, is also an author, but norms vary by field and university. Do not submit a paper based on your thesis without telling your supervisor, and do not add or remove names silently. Equally, the supervisor should not present your work as theirs without credit. Clear, early conversations prevent most of these disputes, and a written note of the agreement helps.

Co-supervisors and external help: Some projects have a co-supervisor, for example a teacher with machine learning skills and another with domain knowledge, or a supervisor from industry. Clarify early who is the main supervisor for administrative matters and how to handle conflicting advice; usually you bring both views to a joint discussion rather than picking one secretly. Experts outside the department, like an agriculture officer for crop diseases or a doctor for medical images, can be very valuable; acknowledge their help in the thesis.

What if the relationship goes wrong: Problems happen. The supervisor goes abroad for higher studies, falls ill, replies slowly, or you strongly disagree about direction. First, try direct, polite communication with specific requests: 'Could we fix a 20-minute meeting every second Sunday?' If the supervisor will be away for a long time, ask who will cover. If the problem persists, talk to your project coordinator or head of department through the proper channel, with your meeting records as evidence. Never simply disappear or stop working; your marks depend on progress whatever the cause.

Real-life example 1, a well-run supervision: Nusrat and Rafi send an agenda every second Saturday evening and meet on Monday. In month three they bring a confusion matrix showing the model confuses semi-rotten and rotten mangoes. The supervisor suggests asking a fruit wholesaler how sellers treat semi-rotten fruit. The wholesaler says such fruit is sold cheaply that same day, so it matters. They keep three classes. Their minutes record this decision and the reason, which later becomes a strong paragraph in the thesis and an easy answer in the defence.

Real-life example 2, recovering from silence: Tanvir's supervisor became very busy with an accreditation process and did not reply for three weeks. Tanvir did not stop. He sent one short email listing two decisions he had made on his own with reasons and asked for confirmation at the supervisor's convenience. He also asked the coordinator whether short weekly progress notes would be acceptable instead of meetings for that month. When the supervisor returned, everything was documented, and they approved the decisions in ten minutes.

Common mistakes: Choosing a supervisor only by popularity or by which teacher seems easy. Arriving at meetings with nothing to show. Hiding problems until the end. Treating feedback as an attack. Not writing minutes, then arguing later about what was agreed. Sending huge unfinished drafts and expecting detailed comments in two days. Going silent for a month and then asking for a signature.

What boards ask: Boards often ask the supervisor about your regularity and independence. In the defence, questions like 'Why did you make this decision?' are easier when your minutes show that decisions were discussed and justified. Some departments include supervisor evaluation forms that rate regular contact, initiative and response to feedback, so your behaviour across the year directly affects your marks.

Recap: The supervisor is your experienced driving instructor: they guide, warn and judge, but you drive. Learn how your department allocates supervisors, choose by area fit and working style, and make first contact with a short, specific email. Supervisor time is scarce (about 10 hours of meetings in a typical year), so send agendas, keep minutes, handle feedback with a table, communicate respectfully and escalate problems through proper channels. Next lesson: working well as a team.
key_points: A supervisor guides, warns, checks quality and often marks you, but does not do the work or choose every step.
Allocation systems differ; know your department's process and deadlines and have backup choices.
Choose by area fit (their papers and past theses) and working style (ask seniors), not just popularity.
A good first email has a specific subject, a short introduction, the idea, evidence of homework and a clear ask.
Supervisor time is scarce: 30-minute meetings every two weeks for 40 weeks is only 10 hours in total.
Send an agenda before each meeting and minutes after, with decisions and action items with owners and deadlines.
Handle feedback calmly with a comment-action-status table, and escalate persistent problems through proper channels.
lessons.tip: End every meeting by saying out loud: 'So the next step is X by date Y, and we meet again on Z.' Then put exactly that in the minutes.
lessons.task: Draft a first contact email to a teacher you might want as a supervisor, following the structure in this lesson. Then write a one-page meeting summary with your problem, candidate question, three key papers and two possible directions.

quiz.q: Which of these is usually NOT a supervisor's job?
quiz.explain: The supervisor guides and checks; the work is yours.

quiz.q: You meet 20 minutes every week for 30 weeks. How many hours of meetings is that?
quiz.explain: 30 x 20 = 600 minutes = 10 hours.

quiz.q: What should a meeting agenda sent one day before contain?
options: Work done, results or problems, specific questions and proposed next steps
quiz.explain: This lets the supervisor prepare so the meeting focuses on decisions.

quiz.q: Why write meeting minutes?
options: To impress the board with paperwork
To record decisions, reasons and action items for later reference and writing
quiz.explain: Minutes protect everyone and feed directly into the methodology chapter and defence answers.

quiz.q: Your supervisor has not replied for three weeks. What is the best first step?
options: Send one short, specific email with your decisions and questions, and keep working
quiz.explain: Keep progress documented and communicate clearly; escalate through proper channels only if needed.

lessons.title: Working as a Team
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket team. Eleven players, but only one bats at each end, one bowls, and the rest field in positions chosen for them. A team with eleven great batsmen and no bowler loses. A team where everyone runs after the same ball also loses. Good teams succeed because roles are clear, everyone knows what the others are doing, and they trust each other to do their part. Most final year projects in Bangladesh are done in teams of two to four students, and the same rules apply. This lesson covers how to choose teammates, split work, collaborate on code and writing, record contributions and handle the conflicts that almost every team meets at some point.

Why team projects exist: Departments allow or require teams for several reasons. Bigger problems become possible: a system with a mobile app, a server, a machine learning model and a user study is too much for one person in one year. Supervisors can guide more students. And teamwork itself is a skill employers care about: almost all real software is built by teams. But a team also adds costs: coordination, communication and the risk that one person's problems become everyone's problems.

Team size and communication, worked: Every pair of people in a team is a communication line that must be kept working. With n people there are n x (n - 1) / 2 pairs. Two people: 2 x 1 / 2 = 1 line. Three people: 3 x 2 / 2 = 3 lines. Four people: 4 x 3 / 2 = 6 lines. Five people: 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 lines. Going from three to four members doubles the lines that can break, while the work capacity grows only by a third. That is why final year teams are usually small, and why a team of four needs more structure (shared plans, meeting minutes, clear ownership) than a pair.

Solo or team: Working alone means full control, no coordination cost and clear individual credit, but all the work and all the risk sit on one person. A team gives more hands, more ideas and someone to share the low moments with, but needs coordination and fair division. Choose solo if your topic is narrow and research-style and you prefer to control everything. Choose a team if the project naturally has several parts or you know reliable partners. Check your department's rules; some fix the team size.

Choosing teammates: Friendship is a nice bonus, but it is not the main criterion. Look for three things. Reliability: do they submit assignments on time and reply to messages? Complementary skills: one is strong in machine learning, another in app development, another in writing and design. Compatible goals and schedules: if one wants a publication and the other just wants to pass, or one has a full-time job, frictions will appear. Before forming a team, work together on something small, like a weekend hackathon or a lab assignment, and see how it feels.

The team contract: In the first week, write a one-page team agreement and all sign it, even informally. It should say: the shared goal (for example, 'aim for an A and try to submit a paper'), roles and areas of ownership, the weekly meeting time, which tools and channels you use, expected response time for messages (say within 24 hours), how decisions are made (discussion, then majority, supervisor breaks ties), what happens if someone misses deadlines repeatedly, and how you will record contributions. It sounds formal for friends, but it turns future arguments into a simple 'what did we agree?'

Roles inside the team: Beyond technical areas, give each member a responsibility role. A coordinator who keeps the plan and sends meeting agendas. A repository keeper who manages Git, branches and backups. A writing editor who maintains the thesis template, references and consistency. A communication lead who handles the supervisor and outside contacts. Roles can rotate each term. Every member should still do real technical work; no one should be only the 'presentation person'.

Splitting work by component, not by chapter: A common mistake is to split by thesis chapter: 'you write the literature review, I write the methodology, she writes the results'. That leads to a book with three styles and members who do not understand each other's work. Split the work by component instead. In the mango thesis, Nusrat owns the data pipeline (collection, labelling, cleaning) and Rafi owns modelling (baselines, training, evaluation), and both write the chapters about their own parts and review each other's. In Tanvir's bus tracker, if he had teammates, one could own the driver app, one the server and arrival estimates, one the student app and usability testing. Each member should be able to explain the whole system in the defence.

Interfaces between parts: When work is split, agree on the interfaces early. For the mango thesis: the data owner delivers images in folders named by class, resized to 224 x 224 pixels, plus a CSV file listing image name, class, phone model and date; the model owner reads only that format. For the bus tracker: the driver app sends JSON with bus id, latitude, longitude and timestamp every 5 seconds to a defined API endpoint. With a clear interface, each person can work independently and test with fake data until the real part is ready.

Collaborating on code: Use Git with a shared remote repository (GitHub, GitLab or similar), never a shared folder of zip files named final_v3_really_final. A simple workflow works well: the main branch always runs; each task gets its own branch; when a task is done, open a pull request; a teammate reviews it briefly before merging. Code review takes ten minutes and catches bugs, spreads knowledge and keeps style consistent. Write clear commit messages ('Add stratified train/test split with seed 42') so the history explains itself. Lesson 17 covers tools and reproducibility in more detail.

Collaborating on writing: Use one shared document system: Overleaf for LaTeX, or a shared Google Doc or Word file on OneDrive. Agree on one template, one reference style and one glossary of terms from day one, so 'CNN', 'convolutional neural network' and 'ConvNet' are not mixed randomly. Each chapter has an owner, and another member reviews it. Before submission, one person (the writing editor) reads the whole book start to finish to smooth the voice.

The contribution log: Keep a simple shared table: date, member, task, hours, link to commit or document. Update it weekly. It takes two minutes and solves several problems at once: the supervisor can see who did what, you can fill in contribution statements that some departments require, and if a dispute arises, there is evidence rather than memory. Git history is also a contribution record, but it misses reading, data collection, meetings and writing, so the table is still needed.

How individual marks are often judged: Even in a team, many departments give individual marks. Common ways include the supervisor's observation across the year, individual questions in the defence, a contribution statement in the thesis, and sometimes peer evaluation. In the defence, board members often point to one member and ask about a part that person did not build. So everyone must understand the whole project, not just their piece. A good habit is a monthly session where each member explains their part to the others in ten minutes.

Handling free-riders: Sometimes one member stops contributing. First, check what is happening: illness, family problems, a job or simply being lost. Talk privately and kindly, and offer a smaller, clear task with a deadline. If nothing changes, raise it in a team meeting with reference to the team contract and the contribution log. If it still continues, inform the supervisor early, with facts, not anger. Supervisors can only act on what they know, and telling them in month three is much better than in the last week, when nothing can be fixed.

Resolving disagreements: Technical disagreements are normal and often useful: 'Should we use Flutter or native Android?', 'ResNet or MobileNet?'. Resolve them with evidence, not volume. Each side writes two or three reasons, you run a quick test if possible (for example, measure model size and accuracy for both on 200 images), then decide and record the decision with its reason in the minutes. Once decided, everyone supports it. Personal conflicts need a calmer approach: talk about specific behaviours ('the last three merges broke the main branch'), not character ('you are careless').

Working when you cannot meet: Team members may live far apart, commute from different parts of the city, or go home during breaks. Plan for that. Keep one shared task board (a simple Trello, GitHub Projects or even a shared spreadsheet) with columns To do, Doing and Done, so anyone can see the state of the project without asking. Hold the weekly meeting online if needed, with cameras on for the first few minutes and the agenda shared on screen. Write decisions in the shared minutes rather than only in a chat group, where they get buried under jokes and stickers. Agree on quiet hours so nobody feels they must answer at midnight. And during load-shedding or poor internet, the person with the stable connection should push everyone's latest work to the repository, so nothing exists only on one laptop.

Real-life example 1, a working pair: Nusrat and Rafi split by component, agree on the data format interface in week 3, and meet every Saturday. Rafi builds the training script on 100 dummy images while Nusrat is still labelling, so no one waits. When Rafi falls sick with dengue for two weeks in month five, Nusrat can continue running his experiments because his code is in Git with a README and the experiment log is up to date. A clear interface and shared documentation turned a crisis into a short delay.

Real-life example 2, rescuing a three-person team: In a three-member team building a clinic appointment system, one member stopped coming after month two. The other two waited, hoping he would return. In month six they finally told the supervisor, who checked the contribution log and saw almost nothing from him. The department let the two continue with a reduced scope and assessed the third separately. They succeeded, but their lesson was clear: raise the problem when it first appears, with evidence.

Common mistakes: Choosing teammates only because they are friends. No written agreement. Splitting by chapter. Not agreeing on interfaces. One person controls the only copy of the code. No contribution record. Avoiding difficult conversations until the final month. Members who cannot explain parts they did not build.

Recap: Teams make bigger projects possible but add coordination cost; communication lines grow as n x (n - 1) / 2. Choose teammates for reliability, complementary skills and compatible goals. Write a team contract, assign responsibility roles, split work by component with clear interfaces, collaborate with Git and a shared writing tool, keep a contribution log, and handle free-riders and conflicts early with evidence. Every member must understand the whole project. Next lesson: finding the literature.
key_points: Teams make bigger projects possible but add coordination; n people have n x (n - 1) / 2 communication lines (3 people: 3, 4 people: 6).
Choose teammates for reliability, complementary skills and compatible goals and schedules, not just friendship.
A one-page team contract covers goal, roles, meeting time, tools, response time, decision rules and missed-deadline handling.
Split work by component (data, model, app, server) with clearly agreed interfaces, not by thesis chapter.
Use Git with branches and short code reviews, and one shared writing tool with one template, reference style and glossary.
Keep a weekly contribution log; it supports individual marking and settles disputes with evidence.
Raise free-rider problems and conflicts early, kindly and with facts; every member must be able to explain the whole project.
lessons.tip: Once a month, have each teammate explain another member's part to the group in five minutes. If they cannot, you have found a defence weakness while there is still time to fix it.
lessons.task: Write a one-page team contract for your (real or imagined) final year team: goal, roles, meeting time, tools, response time, decision rule, what happens after two missed deadlines, and the format of your contribution log.

quiz.q: How many communication pairs are there in a team of 4?
quiz.explain: 4 x 3 / 2 = 6 pairs.

quiz.q: Why is splitting work by component better than by chapter?
options: Members own real technical parts, write about what they built and the book stays consistent after review
It means fewer people need to code
It avoids talking to each other
quiz.explain: Component ownership plus mutual review gives understanding and consistent writing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of agreeing on an interface early?
options: So each member can work and test independently with fake data until the real part is ready
quiz.explain: A clear data or API format decouples the parts of the work.

quiz.q: A teammate has contributed almost nothing for a month. What should you do first?
options: Talk privately and kindly, find out what is wrong and agree a small task with a deadline
quiz.explain: Start with a private, kind conversation; escalate with evidence only if needed.

quiz.q: Why do board members ask a member about a part they did not build?
options: To check that every member understands the whole project
Because only one member is graded
quiz.explain: Individual understanding of the whole system is commonly assessed.

lessons.title: Finding the Literature
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to open a tea stall near your university. Before buying a kettle, a smart person walks around: how many tea stalls are already there, what do they sell, how much do they charge, which one is always crowded and why, and what do customers complain about? Maybe nobody sells good lemon tea, or nobody is open after 9 pm. That walk is market research, and it tells you where your chance lies. In a thesis, the same walk is called searching the literature. Before you build anything, you find out what other people have already built, tried and measured on your problem. This lesson is about where to search, how to search well, and how to tell trustworthy sources from weak ones.

What 'the literature' means: In research, the literature is the body of published work on a topic: research papers, books, theses and some reports. It is the shared memory of a field. When your supervisor says 'check the literature', they mean: find out what is already known, which methods exist, which datasets people use, what results they got and what problems remain. Your thesis must show that you know this landscape, and your own contribution must be placed inside it.

Why search before building: There are four strong reasons. First, to avoid reinventing the wheel: someone may have solved your exact problem already, and you will look bad if the board knows it and you do not. Second, to learn methods and tricks: other people's papers tell you which models, tools and evaluation methods work, saving months of trial and error. Third, to find the gap, the space where your work adds something. Fourth, to find baselines and datasets you can compare against. Searching costs a few weeks; skipping it can cost the whole project.

Kinds of sources: Journal articles are published in academic journals after peer review, usually longer and more polished; they can take months or years to appear. Conference papers are published in conference proceedings after peer review; in computer science, top conferences are often as respected as journals and are faster. Preprints are papers posted publicly before or without peer review, mostly on arXiv; they are fast and useful but not yet checked by reviewers. Theses and dissertations, from your own department and others, show the realistic scope of student work. Books and textbooks give stable background. Grey literature includes technical reports, government statistics, company white papers and documentation; useful for context, like the number of mango farmers in Rajshahi, but not peer reviewed.

Where to search: Google Scholar is the easiest starting point: free, broad and good at finding papers by keyword, with 'Cited by' links. IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library cover most computing conferences and journals; your university may have access. Springer Link and ScienceDirect (Elsevier) host many journals. arXiv holds preprints, especially in machine learning. Semantic Scholar and similar tools give summaries and connections between papers. Your university library may subscribe to some databases; ask the librarian, who is often an underused expert. For Bangladesh-specific context, look at papers from local conferences and journals, government data portals and statistics bureau reports.

Building keywords: Start by listing the main concepts of your question and synonyms for each. For the mango thesis: concept 1, mango (also: fruit); concept 2, rotten (also: spoilage, decay, defect, quality, freshness); concept 3, method (deep learning, CNN, convolutional neural network, image classification, computer vision); concept 4, setting (smartphone, mobile, low-cost). Different authors use different words for the same idea, so your list of synonyms decides what you find.

Boolean search strings, worked: Most databases understand AND, OR, quotes and brackets. OR widens a concept with synonyms, AND combines concepts, quotes keep phrases together. A first string might be: (mango OR fruit) AND (rotten OR spoilage OR defect OR quality) AND ('deep learning' OR CNN OR 'image classification'). In Google Scholar you would use double quotes for phrases; the idea is the same. If you get 50,000 results, add a concept, such as AND (smartphone OR mobile), or limit the years to the last five or six. If you get 12 results, remove the narrowest concept or add synonyms. Write every string you try in your diary with the date and the number of results; this becomes part of your methodology if you do a systematic review (lesson 08).

Backward and forward snowballing: Keyword search finds the first good papers; snowballing finds the rest. Backward snowballing means reading the reference list of a good paper and picking relevant older papers. Forward snowballing means clicking 'Cited by' in Google Scholar to find newer papers that cite it. Suppose you start with 5 strong seed papers, each with about 30 references. That gives roughly 5 x 30 = 150 older candidates. Scanning titles, you might keep about 1 in 5, so around 30. Forward snowballing on the same 5 seeds might add another 20 recent ones. After removing duplicates you may have 40 to 50 papers to look at more closely. Two rounds of snowballing usually reveal the key papers in a small area.

Start with surveys: A survey or review paper summarises many papers in an area, compares methods, lists datasets and open problems. For a newcomer, one good recent survey is worth ten random papers. Search your keywords plus 'survey' or 'review'. Read the survey first, then use its references for backward snowballing. Be careful about the survey's date: in fast-moving areas like deep learning, a survey from six years ago misses a lot.

Judging quality: Not every published paper is reliable. Ask: Was it peer reviewed? Where was it published, and is the venue respected in the field? Who are the authors and do they work in this area? Is the method described clearly enough to repeat? Is the evaluation fair, with baselines and proper test data? Is it recent enough? Citation count helps but needs care: older papers naturally have more citations, and a new paper with few citations can still be excellent. A preprint on arXiv may be great, but treat its claims more cautiously until it is reviewed.

Predatory journals: Some so-called journals charge authors a fee and publish almost anything with no real review, often within days. Warning signs include aggressive spam emails inviting you to publish, promises of very fast acceptance, very broad scope ('journal of engineering, science and management'), fake impact factors, and editorial boards with unclear affiliations. Papers from such venues may be weak or wrong. Avoid citing them as strong evidence, and never publish your own thesis there. Ask your supervisor if unsure about a venue.

Getting access legally: Many papers are behind paywalls. Legal routes include: your university library's subscriptions; open access versions (often linked as [PDF] in Google Scholar); the authors' own websites or institutional repositories; arXiv versions; and simply emailing the author, who is usually happy to share. Some publishers offer free or reduced access programmes for lower-income countries through the institution. Avoid pirated copies; besides the legal issue, they can be outdated or modified versions.

Organising what you find: Use a reference manager from day one: Zotero (free), Mendeley or similar. Save each paper with its PDF, tag it (survey, dataset, baseline, method, Bangladesh), and add one-line notes. The manager also produces citations and reference lists automatically in IEEE or APA style later, which saves days during writing. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-22) covered citation styles; here, just make sure every paper you read is stored in one place.

How much is enough: There is no fixed number, but many BSc theses cite roughly 30 to 60 sources, and the core of the literature review rests on maybe 15 to 25 closely related papers. A good sign that you have searched enough: new searches keep returning papers you already have, and you can name the main approaches, datasets and best reported results in your area without looking. Searching never fully stops; set a monthly alert in Google Scholar for your main keywords so new papers come to you.

AI tools in searching: Chat-based AI assistants and AI-powered search tools can help you brainstorm keywords, explain an unfamiliar term or summarise an abstract you have already found. But they have a well-known weakness: they can produce references that look perfect, with real-sounding authors, titles and venues, yet do not exist, or they can describe a real paper's results wrongly. So never copy a citation from an AI answer into your thesis. Every source you cite must be one you have found in a real database, opened and at least partly read yourself. Use AI as a helper for thinking, not as a source. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-23) discussed honest disclosure of AI use; follow your department's policy.

Real-life example 1, Nusrat's search: Nusrat starts with the string about mango and rotten and deep learning and gets thousands of hits. She adds a time filter for the last six years and the word 'smartphone'. She finds two surveys on fruit quality detection using computer vision, reads both, and picks five seed papers. Backward and forward snowballing gives 42 candidates. Reading titles and abstracts, she keeps 22. She also discovers a public dataset of mango images from another South Asian country, which becomes a useful second test set, and a paper whose future work section says 'testing on low-cost phones under market lighting remains open'. That sentence becomes the heart of their gap.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir's search for a project: Even a build-style project needs literature. Tanvir searches for 'bus arrival time prediction GPS' and 'campus shuttle tracking system'. He finds papers comparing simple methods (average speed, historical averages per segment) with machine learning models, and a few student projects at other universities. He learns that historical segment averages already work well for short routes, which saves him from building a complex model. He also finds usability studies on transit apps, which give him a questionnaire to reuse.

Common mistakes: Searching only Google with no academic database. Using one keyword and giving up. Reading only very old or only very new papers. Trusting citation counts blindly. Citing predatory journals or random blogs as evidence. Downloading PDFs into a messy folder with no notes. Starting the search after the method is already fixed. Not recording search strings, then being unable to explain how papers were found.

What boards ask: 'What are the closest existing works to yours?', 'How is your work different from paper X?', 'Why didn't you compare with method Y?', 'How did you find your sources?' and sometimes 'Is this venue peer reviewed?'. A well-organised reference library and a short search log make these easy.

Recap: The literature is the published memory of your field. Search it before building, to avoid repeating work, learn methods, find the gap, and find baselines and datasets. Use Google Scholar plus databases like IEEE Xplore, ACM DL and arXiv; build keywords with synonyms and Boolean strings; snowball backward and forward from strong seed papers; start with surveys; judge quality and avoid predatory venues; access papers legally; and organise everything in a reference manager. Next lesson: reading papers efficiently.
key_points: The literature is the body of published work on a topic; you search it to avoid repetition, learn methods, find the gap and find baselines and datasets.
Source types: journals, conference papers, preprints (arXiv), theses, books and grey literature, each with different reliability.
Search Google Scholar plus databases such as IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, Springer, ScienceDirect and arXiv; ask the librarian.
Build keyword lists with synonyms and combine them with OR inside a concept and AND between concepts; log every string and result count.
