Snowball backward (reference lists) and forward ('Cited by') from 5 or so strong seed papers, starting with recent surveys.
Judge quality by peer review, venue, authors, method clarity, fair evaluation and date; avoid predatory journals.
Get papers legally and store everything in a reference manager like Zotero with tags and short notes.
lessons.tip: Keep a search log with date, database, exact search string and number of results. It takes seconds, and later it lets you explain and repeat your search in the thesis.
lessons.task: Write a Boolean search string for your own topic with at least three concepts and two synonyms each. Run it in Google Scholar, then narrow it until you get a few hundred results. Pick three promising papers and do one round of backward and forward snowballing.

quiz.q: What does OR do in a search string like (mango OR fruit)?
options: Narrows results to papers containing both words
Widens results to papers containing either word
quiz.explain: OR combines synonyms to widen a concept; AND combines concepts to narrow.

quiz.q: What is forward snowballing?
options: Finding newer papers that cite a good paper, for example via 'Cited by'
quiz.explain: Backward goes to older references; forward goes to newer citing papers.

quiz.q: Five seed papers each have about 30 references, and you keep about 1 in 5 after reading titles. Roughly how many do you keep?
quiz.explain: 5 x 30 = 150 candidates; one fifth of 150 is 30.

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign of a predatory journal?
options: Spam invitations promising acceptance within days for a fee
Being indexed by a major digital library of a professional society
quiz.explain: Very fast acceptance for a fee with aggressive spam suggests little or no real review.

quiz.q: Why start with a recent survey paper?
options: Surveys are always the newest research
It summarises methods, datasets and open problems and gives references to snowball from
Surveys never need to be cited
quiz.explain: A good survey maps the area quickly, but check its date.

lessons.title: Reading Papers Efficiently
lessons.content:
When you go shopping at a big market like New Market in Dhaka, you do not examine every item in every shop. You walk past most shops with a quick glance, step into a few that look promising, and only in one or two do you sit down, try things on and bargain seriously. Reading research papers works the same way. You will find forty or fifty papers, but you cannot read each one word by word; it would take months and you would remember little. Instead, you skim many, read some properly, and study a few deeply. This lesson teaches a simple layered method for reading papers, how to take notes that stay useful, and how to read results critically instead of just believing the numbers.

Why reading papers feels hard at first: Research papers are written for experts by experts. They are dense, full of terms you have not met, assume background knowledge, and squeeze months of work into eight or twelve pages. The first few papers you read may take hours and leave you confused. That is normal. Reading papers is a skill, and like any skill it gets faster with practice. After twenty or so papers in one area, you will notice the same terms, datasets and methods repeating, and reading speed often doubles or triples.

Quick anatomy recap: Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-21) covered paper structure, so just a reminder. A typical computing paper has a title, abstract, introduction (problem, motivation, contributions), related work, method or system design, experimental setup (datasets, baselines, metrics), results, discussion, conclusion with limitations and future work, and references. Knowing this map lets you jump directly to the part you need instead of reading from top to bottom.

The three-pass method: A well-known approach, described by S. Keshav in a short essay called 'How to Read a Paper', reads a paper in up to three passes, each deeper than the last. You stop after any pass if the paper is not useful enough. This saves enormous time, because most papers you find will only need the first pass.

First pass, the bird's-eye view (about 5 to 10 minutes): Read the title, abstract and introduction carefully. Read the section and subsection headings, glance at the figures and tables, and read the conclusion. Glance over the references and tick any you already know. After this pass you should be able to answer five questions: What kind of paper is it (new method, system, dataset, survey, comparison)? What context or related area does it belong to? Do its main assumptions seem valid? What are its main contributions? Is it clearly written? Then decide: is this paper relevant enough for a second pass?

Second pass, the content (up to about an hour): Read the whole paper, but skip heavy proofs and fine details. Pay special attention to the figures, diagrams and tables: are axes labelled, are error bars shown, are the results convincing? Mark unread references that seem important for later. Write a short summary in your own words. After the second pass you should be able to explain the main idea, the method and the evidence to a classmate. For most papers in your related work, this level is enough.

Third pass, deep understanding (several hours): Only for the handful of papers that are central to your work: your main baseline, the method you will build on, or the dataset paper you depend on. Here you try to virtually re-implement the paper in your head: what exactly are the inputs, steps and outputs, which choices did the authors make and why, what would you do differently? Note every hidden assumption and possible weakness. Keshav suggests beginners may need about four or five hours for this pass. Often this is where your own idea appears: 'they assumed bright lighting; what happens in a market at dusk?'.

The time budget, worked: Suppose you collect 40 candidate papers. First pass on all: 40 x 10 minutes = 400 minutes, about 6.7 hours. Second pass on the 20 most relevant: 20 x 1 hour = 20 hours. Third pass on the 4 central papers: 4 x 4 hours = 16 hours. Total: about 6.7 + 20 + 16 = 42.7 hours, roughly 43 hours. Reading all 40 deeply at 4 hours each would be 160 hours, nearly four times more, for little extra benefit. Spread over four to six weeks, 43 hours fits well into the 60 hours of reading and planning from the budget in lesson 02.

What to write while reading: Never read without writing. For each paper, record in your reference manager or a notes file: the full citation; a one-sentence summary; the problem it addresses; the method in two or three lines; the dataset (name, size, where from); the metrics and main results with numbers; strengths; limitations and assumptions; and how it relates to your work (baseline, competitor, inspiration, dataset source). Write in your own words, not copied sentences. This protects you from accidental plagiarism later, because your notes are already paraphrased, and it forces understanding.

The extraction matrix: Put the key fields of all your papers into one table, one row per paper and one column per field: Paper, Year, Problem, Method, Dataset, Size, Metric, Best result, Device or setting, Limitation. With 20 rows, patterns jump out that you would never see paper by paper. For the mango thesis, the matrix showed that 14 of 20 papers used images taken in controlled lab lighting, only 3 tested on a phone, and none used local Bangladeshi mango varieties. That column-wise view is exactly how the gap becomes visible; lesson 08 turns it into the literature review.

Reading result tables critically: Numbers in papers are claims, not facts, until you understand how they were produced. Ask: Is the test set separate from the training data? Is the dataset balanced? Is there a baseline? Are results averaged over several runs? Is the comparison fair, with the same data for all methods? Here is a classic trap, worked: a paper reports 97 percent accuracy for detecting a disease in a dataset where 95 percent of images are healthy. A dumb model that always says 'healthy' would already get 95 percent. So the real improvement is only 2 percentage points over doing nothing, and the paper should report precision and recall for the disease class. Lesson 18 explains these metrics in detail.

Critical questions for any paper: What problem exactly is solved, and for whom? What are the assumptions, and do they hold in your setting? Is the method described well enough to repeat? Are data and code available? What does the evaluation prove, and what does it not prove? Would the result still hold with different data, devices or users? What did the authors themselves list as limitations? Critical does not mean negative; it means careful. Many good papers have honest limitations that become your opportunity.

Understanding unfamiliar parts: When you hit a term or equation you do not understand, do not stop the whole paper. Mark it, finish the pass, then look it up in a textbook, a survey or a good tutorial. If a whole section is beyond you, ask whether you really need it for your work. If you do, ask a senior or your supervisor with a specific question: 'In section 3.2, why do they divide by the batch size here?'. Keeping a personal glossary of terms with one-line meanings speeds up every future paper.

Beyond the PDF: Many recent papers come with extra material: a supplementary file with more results, a public code repository, a dataset page, or a project website with demos. For papers in your third pass, check these. Running the authors' code on their own sample data is often the fastest way to understand what the paper really does, and it immediately tells you whether reproducing their baseline will be easy or painful. Read the repository's README and open issues too; other users often report bugs, missing files or results they could not reproduce, which is valuable information that never appears in the paper itself. Note the code's licence before reusing any of it, as lesson 13 explains.

Reading with a team: In a team, do not all read the same papers deeply. Split the second and third passes by topic, and hold a weekly 30-minute reading meeting where each person presents one paper in five minutes using the extraction fields. Everyone learns the whole landscape at a fraction of the time, and the shared matrix grows quickly. Rotate who presents the hardest paper so nobody stays only on easy ones.

Real-life example 1, Rafi learns to read: Rafi's first paper on mobile CNN models took him five hours and he still could not explain it. With the three-pass method, he first read only the abstract, introduction, figures and conclusion in ten minutes and wrote the five-question answers. In the second pass he focused on the architecture figure and the results table, and noted that the model had many times fewer parameters than the larger standard models it was compared with, while accuracy on the benchmark dropped only a little. That one line in his notes later justified choosing a small model for the phone.

Real-life example 2, catching a weak claim: Tanvir found a paper claiming 'arrival prediction error under 30 seconds'. In the second pass he noticed it was tested on a single 2 km route on three days with almost no traffic, and the error was measured only at the final stop. He noted this limitation, cited the paper fairly as an early result, and designed his own evaluation to measure error at every stop during peak and off-peak hours. In his defence, an examiner asked about this paper and was impressed that Tanvir had read it critically.

Common mistakes: Reading every paper fully from start to end. Reading without notes, then forgetting everything a week later. Copying sentences into notes, which later leaks into the thesis as plagiarism. Believing every number without checking the setup. Getting stuck on one hard equation and abandoning the paper. Reading only papers that agree with your idea. Not recording which paper a note came from.

What boards ask: 'What is the main limitation of your closest related work?', 'Did paper X use the same dataset as you?', 'Why are your numbers lower than the ones reported in paper Y?'. That last question is common; answering it needs a critical reading of Y's setup, such as different data, lighting or balanced classes.

Recap: Read in layers: a 5 to 10 minute first pass for every paper, a second pass of up to an hour for relevant ones, and a deep third pass for the few central ones. This cuts reading time for 40 papers from about 160 hours to about 43. Always write notes in your own words, build an extraction matrix across papers, read result tables critically (balanced data, baselines, fair comparison) and keep a glossary. Next lesson: turning these notes into a literature review that reveals your gap.
key_points: Papers are dense and written for experts; reading speed improves a lot after about 20 papers in one area.
Use three passes: a 5 to 10 minute bird's-eye view, a second pass of up to an hour for content, and a deep third pass only for central papers.
Layered reading of 40 papers takes about 43 hours instead of about 160 hours for reading all deeply.
Always write notes in your own words: citation, summary, problem, method, dataset, metrics and results, strengths, limitations, relation to your work.
An extraction matrix (one row per paper, one column per field) reveals patterns and gaps across the literature.
Read results critically: separate test data, class balance, baselines, repeated runs and fair comparison; 97 percent on a 95 percent majority class is a small gain.
Mark unfamiliar parts, finish the pass, then look them up; keep a personal glossary.
lessons.tip: After the first pass of any paper, write the five answers (type, context, assumptions, contributions, clarity) in two minutes. If you cannot, read the abstract and introduction again before going further.
lessons.task: Pick one paper from your topic. Do a timed first pass (10 minutes) and write the five answers. Then do a second pass and fill one row of an extraction matrix with the fields from this lesson. Finally, write one critical question about its evaluation.

quiz.q: What do you mainly read in the first pass of a paper?
options: Title, abstract, introduction, headings, figures and conclusion
quiz.explain: The first pass is a 5 to 10 minute overview to decide relevance.

quiz.q: 40 papers get a 10-minute first pass, 20 get a 1-hour second pass and 4 get a 4-hour third pass. About how many hours in total?
quiz.explain: About 6.7 + 20 + 16 = 42.7 hours.

quiz.q: A paper reports 97 percent accuracy on data where 95 percent of samples belong to one class. What is the best interpretation?
options: Always predicting the majority class already gives 95 percent, so the real gain is small and per-class metrics are needed
quiz.explain: With imbalance, compare against the majority baseline and check precision and recall.

quiz.q: Why should your reading notes be written in your own words?
options: It forces understanding and prevents copied sentences leaking into the thesis
quiz.explain: Paraphrased notes protect against accidental plagiarism.

quiz.q: What is an extraction matrix?
options: A table with one row per paper and columns such as method, dataset, metric, result and limitation
A matrix used inside a CNN
quiz.explain: Comparing fields across papers makes patterns and gaps visible.

lessons.title: Writing the Literature Review
lessons.content:
Imagine your cousin asks you which mobile phone to buy for about 20,000 taka. You could answer by describing ten phones one after another: 'Phone A has this camera and that battery, phone B has this screen...'. After the fourth phone your cousin is lost. A much better answer groups and compares: 'In this budget, phones fall into two groups: big-battery phones with weaker cameras, and good-camera phones with average batteries. Most of them struggle with gaming. If you want a good camera and long battery and gaming, nothing in this price range really does all three.' That last sentence is the gap. A literature review does exactly this for research: it organises what is known, compares it, and shows clearly what is still missing, which is where your work fits.

What a literature review is: A literature review is a section or chapter of your thesis that critically summarises and connects the existing work related to your problem. It is not a list of paper summaries. It is an argument with a destination: by the end, the reader should agree that a specific gap exists and that your work is a sensible way to address it. In many theses it is Chapter 2, sometimes called 'Background and Related Work'. Shorter versions also appear in your proposal and in any paper you publish.

Why it matters: The review proves to examiners that you know your field, so your contribution is real and not accidental repetition. It justifies your choices: why this method, this dataset, this metric, these baselines. It gives credit to others, which is basic academic honesty. And it helps you: writing the review forces you to see the landscape clearly, and many students only truly understand their own gap while writing this chapter.

Summary versus synthesis: A summary describes one source: 'Hasan et al. used a CNN on 2,000 apple images and got 94 percent accuracy.' Synthesis connects several sources to make a point: 'Most CNN-based fruit quality studies report accuracies above 90 percent, but nearly all of them used images taken under controlled lab lighting [3, 5, 8, 11]; the few that tested in field conditions reported drops of 10 to 15 points [7, 12].' The second sentence is far more valuable. It groups, compares and draws a conclusion that leads towards a gap. Aim for synthesis in most paragraphs, with individual summaries only for the few papers most central to your work.

The weak pattern to avoid: The most common weak review is the 'paper parade': one paragraph per paper, each starting with 'In [7], the authors proposed...'. It reads like a shopping list, hides patterns and never reaches a conclusion. If you see that pattern in your draft, it is a sign that you have not yet organised your extraction matrix (lesson 07) into themes.

Ways to organise: There are several common structures. Thematic: group by sub-topic or theme, such as 'image acquisition', 'classical machine learning approaches', 'deep learning approaches', 'deployment on mobile devices'. By approach or method family: classical methods, then CNNs, then lightweight mobile networks. Chronological: how the field developed over time, useful when there is a clear history but risky if it becomes a parade. By problem dimension: accuracy, speed, cost, data. Most good reviews are thematic or method-based, with a short historical note where needed. Pick the structure that makes your gap most visible.

The funnel shape: A strong review usually narrows like a funnel. Start broad: why the general problem matters and the main families of approaches. Then narrow to work closest to yours, compared in detail. End with a short summary paragraph that states the gap explicitly and links it to your research questions. For the mango thesis: food loss and fruit quality inspection in general, then computer vision for fruit quality, then deep learning for fruit defects, then mobile and low-cost deployments, then the specific gap.

The comparison table: Most computing reviews include a table comparing the closest 8 to 15 works on key dimensions: method, dataset (and its size and origin), conditions, metric and result, device, and limitation. Readers love these tables because they see the landscape at a glance. The table is a filtered version of your extraction matrix. Add a final row for your own work, so the board sees exactly where you differ. Use consistent units and mark missing information as 'not reported' instead of guessing.

Types of gaps: A gap is the specific thing your work adds. Common types are: a knowledge gap, a question nobody has answered yet; a method gap, an approach that has not been tried on this problem; a data or context gap, where existing work used different data, language, population or setting, such as no Bangla data or no local fruit varieties; a performance gap, where existing methods are too slow, too large, too costly or not accurate enough for a real need; and an evaluation gap, where previous work was tested only in the lab, on small data or without users. Most BSc theses fill a context, performance or evaluation gap, and that is perfectly respectable.

Stating the gap clearly: End your review with two or three sentences that name the gap, using evidence from the review. For example: 'In summary, deep learning methods achieve high accuracy for fruit quality classification under controlled conditions. However, we found no study that evaluates such methods on South Asian mango varieties photographed with low-cost smartphones under market lighting, and the few field evaluations report large accuracy drops. This thesis addresses this gap by building a local dataset and evaluating lightweight models on-device.' Clear, specific, honest, and directly connected to the work that follows.

Narrative versus systematic review: A narrative review is the usual kind in BSc theses: you search sensibly, select relevant work using judgement, and organise it to make an argument. A systematic review follows a strict, repeatable protocol: defined search strings and databases, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, documented screening and counts. Systematic reviews are expected in some research-heavy theses and are themselves publishable. Even in a narrative review, borrowing a little discipline (a recorded search log and stated selection criteria) makes your chapter more convincing.

PRISMA-style counts, worked: Systematic reviews often report a flow of numbers, popularised by the PRISMA guidelines. Suppose your database searches return 420 records and snowballing adds 35, giving 420 + 35 = 455. Removing 85 duplicates leaves 455 - 85 = 370. Screening titles and abstracts against your criteria excludes 310, leaving 370 - 310 = 60 for full-text reading. Of those, 32 are excluded with recorded reasons (for example, 18 not about fruit, 9 no quantitative evaluation, 5 not in English), leaving 60 - 32 = 28 included studies. Check that the reasons add up: 18 + 9 + 5 = 32. Presenting these numbers in a small flow diagram shows the board that your selection was careful and not cherry-picked.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria: Whether narrative or systematic, decide what counts as relevant and write it down. For example, include: peer-reviewed papers or well-known preprints from the last eight years, image-based fruit quality classification, quantitative evaluation. Exclude: non-image methods such as gas sensors, papers without accessible full text, duplicate versions of the same study. Clear criteria prevent the review from drifting and protect you from the accusation of choosing only papers that make your work look good.

Writing style for the review: Use your own words and cite every claim. Prefer reporting verbs that show your stance: 'X showed', 'X reported', 'X claimed', 'X argued' carry different strengths. Be fair and respectful even when pointing out weaknesses: 'the evaluation used a single lighting condition' rather than 'the authors were careless'. Mix paragraph-level synthesis with occasional detail on key papers. Keep tense consistent, usually past tense for specific studies and present tense for general knowledge. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-21, -22) covered citation styles and research writing in more detail.

Background versus related work: Many theses separate two things that students often mix. Background explains the concepts a reader needs to understand your work: what a convolutional neural network is, what transfer learning means, how GPS positions are reported. It is textbook knowledge, kept short and cited to good textbooks or tutorials. Related work discusses specific studies that tackled problems similar to yours and how they compare. If your 'literature review' spends ten pages explaining what machine learning is, it is mostly background, and the actual comparison with other work is too thin. Keep background to what is needed, and spend most of the chapter on related work.

How long and when to write: In many BSc theses the literature review is around 8 to 15 pages, but follow your department and supervisor. Write a first version early, right after the proposal stage, while the reading is fresh, then update it near the end with any new papers and to make sure it points precisely at what you actually did. A review written entirely at the end often does not match the final work, and examiners notice.

Real-life example 1, rebuilding Rafi's draft: Rafi's first draft had 18 paragraphs each describing one paper. Their supervisor wrote 'So what?' on the last page. Using their extraction matrix, Nusrat and Rafi regrouped the papers into four themes: lab-condition studies, field-condition studies, lightweight mobile models, and South Asian fruit datasets. Each theme got one synthesis paragraph with group citations and one or two highlighted papers, followed by a comparison table of 12 works and a three-sentence gap statement. The chapter became shorter and much stronger.

Real-life example 2, a review for a project: Tanvir's bus tracker review had three themes: existing commercial and open-source transit tracking apps (features and limitations for small campuses), arrival time estimation methods from simple averages to machine learning, and usability evaluation of transit apps. His gap was practical: existing solutions needed costly hardware on buses or city-scale data, while his campus needed a low-cost, phone-only system with simple, accurate estimates for short routes. The review directly justified using driver phones and segment-average estimation.

Common mistakes: The paper parade. No clear gap at the end. Reviewing only very old or only very recent work. Copying abstract sentences, which similarity checkers flag immediately. Citing papers you never opened. Ignoring work that contradicts your idea. Overly harsh or dismissive language. A review that does not connect to your research questions or that does not mention the baselines you later compare against.

What boards ask: 'What is the state of the art in your problem?', 'Which work is closest to yours, and how exactly do you differ?', 'Why did you not include method Z?', 'How did you select these papers?'. The comparison table, gap statement and selection criteria give you ready answers.

Recap: A literature review is an organised, critical argument that ends at a clear gap. Synthesise rather than summarise, avoid the paper parade, organise by theme or method in a funnel shape, include a comparison table with your own work as the last row, name the type of gap you fill, state it in a few sentences, and use clear inclusion criteria and, if systematic, PRISMA-style counts. Next lesson: turning the gap into a precise problem statement, research questions and objectives.
key_points: A literature review is an organised critical argument that ends by showing a specific gap your work fills.
Synthesis connects several sources to make a point; avoid the 'paper parade' of one paragraph per paper.
Organise by theme or method family in a funnel: broad context, closest work in detail, then the gap.
A comparison table of the closest 8 to 15 works, with your work as the last row, shows your difference at a glance.
Gap types: knowledge, method, data or context, performance and evaluation; BSc theses often fill context, performance or evaluation gaps.
Systematic reviews use a fixed protocol and report PRISMA-style counts, for example 455 found, 370 after duplicates, 60 full texts, 28 included.
Write clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, cite every claim in your own words, and update the review at the end to match your final work.
lessons.tip: Read only the first sentence of each paragraph in your review. If those sentences alone tell a story that ends at your gap, the structure is right; if they all start with 'In [x], the authors...', regroup.
lessons.task: Take your extraction matrix (or 6 to 8 papers you know) and group them into 2 or 3 themes. Write one synthesis paragraph for one theme using group citations, then write a three-sentence gap statement naming the gap type.

quiz.q: Which sentence is synthesis rather than summary?
options: Rahman et al. used SVM on 500 images.
In [7], the authors proposed a CNN.
Most studies reported over 90 percent accuracy under lab lighting [3, 5, 8], but field tests showed drops of 10 to 15 points [7, 12].
quiz.explain: Synthesis groups several sources and draws a conclusion.

quiz.q: Existing methods were tested only on English text, and you test them on Bangla. What type of gap is this?
options: Knowledge gap about a totally new question
quiz.explain: A new language, population or setting is a data or context gap.

quiz.q: 455 records found, 85 duplicates removed, 310 excluded at screening. How many go to full-text reading?
Why add your own work as the last row of the comparison table?
options: Because it is required in all universities
So readers see exactly how your work differs from the closest existing work
quiz.explain: It makes your contribution visible against the landscape.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with the 'paper parade' style?
options: It lists papers one by one, hides patterns and never reaches a clear gap
quiz.explain: A review must organise and compare, not just list.

lessons.title: Problem Statement, Research Questions and Objectives
lessons.content:
When you call a Pathao or Uber ride, the app does not ask 'where would you like to go, roughly?'. It needs an exact pickup point and an exact destination, or the driver wanders around and you both waste time and money. A thesis without a precise problem statement and research questions is like a ride with no destination: lots of driving, no arrival. This lesson shows how to turn the gap you found in the literature into a sharp problem statement, clear research questions, testable hypotheses where they fit, and objectives that tell you exactly when you have arrived.

Why precision matters: Every later decision depends on these few sentences. The research questions decide which data you need, which method fits, which metrics you report and what goes into the results chapter. Examiners also judge your whole thesis against them: 'Did you answer what you asked?'. A vague question like 'How can AI help farmers?' cannot be answered in a year, so students drift. A precise question like 'How accurately can a lightweight CNN running on a low-cost Android phone classify local mangoes into fresh, semi-rotten and rotten under market lighting?' tells you exactly what to do and what to measure.

What a problem statement is: A problem statement is a short paragraph, often 150 to 300 words, that explains the problem your work addresses and why it matters, ending with the gap. It is not a description of your solution. A useful formula has five parts: context (the situation), problem (what is wrong), evidence (numbers or sources showing the problem is real), consequence (what happens if it stays unsolved, and to whom), and gap (why existing solutions do not fix it). Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-20) showed how evidence strengthens a problem statement; here we connect it to research design.

A problem statement, worked: 'Mango is one of Bangladesh's most important fruits, and much of it is sold through small wholesale and retail markets (context). Sellers sort fruit by eye, and rotten fruit that is missed can spread decay to neighbouring fruit in the same crate (problem). Post-harvest losses of fruit in South Asia are widely reported to be substantial, and sellers we interviewed estimated losing several crates per week in peak season (evidence: cite a published loss study and your own interviews). These losses reduce the income of small sellers who cannot afford automated grading machines (consequence). Existing image-based quality systems mostly use lab lighting, imported fruit varieties and powerful computers, so they do not fit a seller with a low-cost phone in a crowded market (gap).' Notice that every sentence earns its place, and the evidence should be cited, not invented.

The aim: The aim is one sentence describing the overall purpose of your work. 'The aim of this thesis is to develop and evaluate a low-cost, phone-based system that classifies the freshness of local mangoes under market conditions.' It is broad enough to cover the whole thesis and narrow enough to be achieved. Think of it as the destination city.

Research questions: Research questions (RQs) are the precise questions your work will answer, usually two to four. They are the exact addresses inside the destination city. Common kinds are: descriptive ('What is the distribution of defect types in mangoes at Rajshahi markets?'), comparative ('Which of three lightweight CNNs gives the best accuracy-size trade-off on our dataset?'), relational or causal ('How does lighting condition affect classification accuracy?'), and design-oriented, common in projects ('How can a phone-only bus tracking system be designed to give arrival estimates within 2 minutes for a small campus?'). Good RQs are answerable with your data and time, specific, and clearly tied to the gap.

Testing your RQs: Ask four checks for each question. Can I answer it with data I can realistically collect? Will the answer be a clear statement, number or comparison, not just 'it depends'? Is the scope narrow enough for my time? Does answering it fill part of the gap I described? If any answer is no, rewrite. A bad RQ: 'Is deep learning good?'. A better one: 'Does fine-tuning MobileNet on 3,000 local mango images improve rotten-class recall compared with the same model trained only on a public foreign fruit dataset?'.

Hypotheses: In thesis-style work, especially experimental work, an RQ can be turned into a hypothesis, a testable prediction. The null hypothesis (H0) usually says there is no effect or no difference; the alternative hypothesis (H1) says there is. For example, H0: mean classification accuracy under dim market lighting equals accuracy under bright lighting. H1: accuracy under dim lighting is lower. Your experiments then gather evidence to see whether H0 can be rejected. You never 'prove' H1 absolutely; you show that the data are unlikely if H0 were true. Lesson 19 explains how significance testing does this. Build-style projects often do not need formal hypotheses; clear design questions and acceptance criteria work better.

Objectives: Objectives are the concrete steps you will complete to answer the RQs, usually three to six, written with action verbs: collect, build, implement, compare, evaluate, deploy. Technical Writing introduced the SMART checklist: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. For the mango thesis: O1, collect and label at least 3,000 mango images from at least two Rajshahi markets using three low-cost phone models by month 4. O2, train and compare three lightweight CNN models and one classical baseline by month 6. O3, deploy the best model in an offline Android app and measure on-device inference time by month 7. O4, evaluate the app with 5 sellers on 200 real mangoes in the market by month 8.

Aim, RQs and objectives together: The aim says where you are going; the RQs say what you must find out; the objectives say what you must do. Each RQ should be served by at least one objective, and each objective should serve at least one RQ. An objective that serves no question is wasted work; a question with no objective will never be answered.

The alignment check, worked: Build a small table with columns: Research question, Objective(s), Method, Data, Metric, Thesis chapter. For the mango thesis: RQ1 (which lightweight model gives the best accuracy-size trade-off?) uses O1 and O2, method controlled comparison, data local dataset with fixed splits, metrics macro F1 and model size in MB, chapter 5. RQ2 (how does lighting affect accuracy?) uses O1 and O2, method subgroup analysis, data images tagged bright or dim, metric F1 per lighting group, chapter 5. RQ3 (is the app practical for sellers?) uses O3 and O4, method field test plus questionnaire, data 200 mangoes and 5 sellers, metrics accuracy in the field, inference time and SUS score, chapter 6. If any row has an empty cell, something is missing.

Scope and delimitations: Scope states what your work covers; delimitations are the boundaries you choose on purpose. 'This thesis considers only three mango varieties common in Rajshahi, only external visual defects (not internal rot), and only Android phones.' Stating these early protects you: the board cannot fairly criticise you for not doing what you clearly placed outside the scope, as long as your reasons are sensible. Limitations, in contrast, are weaknesses you could not avoid, such as a small number of sellers in the field test; they are discussed in the results and conclusion chapters.

Assumptions: Write down what you assume to be true without testing: 'Sellers are willing to photograph each mango', 'Phone camera quality is similar across the three models used'. Assumptions are fine if they are reasonable and stated. Hidden assumptions are dangerous because examiners will find them for you.

The contributions list: Many theses list contributions near the end of the introduction as three to five bullet-like sentences. For example: a new labelled dataset of 3,000 local mango images under market conditions; a comparison of three lightweight CNNs and a classical baseline on this dataset; an offline Android app with on-device inference; a field evaluation with sellers. Each contribution should match an objective and be backed by results later. Do not list things you did not finish.

Project-style version: For a build-focused project, the same structure works with slightly different words. Problem statement: students wait without knowing bus arrival times. Aim: develop and evaluate a low-cost campus bus tracking system. Design questions: How can arrival time be estimated accurately using only driver phones? How usable is the student app? Objectives: gather requirements from 20 users, build driver and student apps and server, achieve median arrival error under 2 minutes on 50 test trips, reach a SUS score above 68 with at least 15 students. Acceptance criteria replace hypotheses.

The title follows the question: Once the RQs are clear, the thesis title becomes easy. A good title names the task, the method family and the setting, in about 10 to 15 words, without hype. 'Lightweight Deep Learning for Mango Freshness Classification on Low-Cost Smartphones under Market Conditions' tells the reader almost everything. 'A Novel AI Revolution in Agriculture' tells them nothing. Many departments register a working title early and allow small changes later; check whether a change needs formal approval.

Real-life example 1, from vague to sharp: Nusrat and Rafi's first draft question was 'Can AI detect bad mangoes?'. Their supervisor asked: which AI, which mangoes, which phone, how good is good, and compared with what? Their second version was 'Can a CNN detect rotten mangoes?'. Still vague. After the literature review and the alignment table, they arrived at three RQs on model trade-offs, lighting effect and practical usefulness, each with a metric and a chapter. Their proposal sailed through because the board could see exactly what would be delivered.

Real-life example 2, a scope that saved a project: Tanvir originally included 'support for city buses in Dhaka' in his scope. During the problem statement work he realised city bus data, routes and driver cooperation were impossible to get. He moved city buses to future work and stated the delimitation clearly: campus buses only, four routes. In the defence, an examiner asked about city buses, and Tanvir pointed to his delimitation and explained why, which the board accepted.

Common mistakes: A problem statement that describes the solution instead of the problem. Evidence that is invented or uncited. RQs that are too broad, unanswerable or yes/no with no measure. Objectives that are activities without measures ('study deep learning'). Mismatch between RQs and results chapter. No stated scope, so the board expects everything. Contributions that the work does not actually deliver.

What boards ask: 'What exactly is your research question?', 'How do your results answer RQ2?', 'Why did you limit the study to three varieties?', 'What is your hypothesis, and did your results support it?', 'Which of your listed contributions is the most important?'. With an alignment table you can answer all of these in one breath.

Recap: Turn your gap into a five-part problem statement (context, problem, evidence, consequence, gap), one aim, two to four precise research questions, hypotheses where the work is experimental, and three to six SMART objectives. Check alignment with a table linking every RQ to objectives, methods, data, metrics and chapters. State scope, delimitations and assumptions openly, and list contributions that your results will back up. Next lesson: putting all of this into the thesis proposal.
key_points: Precise research questions decide data, method, metrics and the results chapter; the whole thesis is judged against them.
A problem statement has five parts: context, problem, evidence, consequence and gap, and does not describe the solution.
The aim is one sentence for the overall purpose; research questions are 2 to 4 precise, answerable questions tied to the gap.
In experimental work, turn RQs into hypotheses: H0 says no effect or difference, H1 says there is one; you test whether H0 can be rejected.
Objectives are 3 to 6 SMART action steps; every objective must serve an RQ and every RQ must have objectives.
An alignment table links each RQ to objectives, method, data, metric and chapter; empty cells reveal missing work.
State scope, delimitations and assumptions early; list only contributions your results will actually support.
lessons.tip: Paste your RQs at the top of every chapter draft while writing. If a paragraph does not help answer one of them, it probably belongs in an appendix or nowhere.
lessons.task: Write a five-part problem statement for your topic (mark each part), one aim sentence, two research questions and three SMART objectives. Then draw the alignment table with columns RQ, objectives, method, data, metric and chapter, and fill every cell.

quiz.q: Which part is NOT in the five-part problem statement formula?
quiz.explain: The problem statement explains the problem and gap, not your solution.

quiz.q: Which is the best research question?
options: How accurately can a lightweight CNN on a low-cost phone classify local mangoes into three freshness classes under market lighting?
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable and answerable with realistic data.

quiz.q: What does a null hypothesis usually state?
options: There is no effect or no difference
The proposed method is always better
quiz.explain: H0 states no effect; experiments test whether the data make H0 unlikely.

quiz.q: In an alignment table, an objective serves no research question. What does that mean?
options: It is the most important objective
It must be moved to the abstract
It proves the thesis is novel
It is likely wasted work, or an RQ is missing
quiz.explain: Every objective should serve at least one RQ.

quiz.q: What is a delimitation?
options: A boundary of the study chosen on purpose, such as only three mango varieties
quiz.explain: Delimitations are deliberate scope choices; limitations are unavoidable weaknesses.

lessons.title: The Thesis Proposal
lessons.content:
Before a building goes up in Dhaka, the owner hires an architect to draw plans: how many floors, where the stairs go, what materials, how much it will cost and how long it will take. Those plans are checked and approved before a single brick is laid, because fixing a wrong foundation after the fifth floor is a disaster. A thesis proposal is the approved plan for your final year work. It tells your supervisor and the department what problem you will tackle, why, how, with what resources and on what timeline, and it lets them catch weak foundations early. This lesson shows what goes into a thesis proposal, how to write each part well, how proposal defences usually work, and what to do when the plan later changes.

What a thesis proposal is: A thesis or project proposal is a document, often around 5 to 15 pages depending on your department, written after you have chosen a topic, read the core literature and formed your research questions, but before the main work starts. Many departments also require a short proposal presentation, sometimes called a pre-defence or proposal defence, in front of a small board. Approval of the proposal usually allows you to continue; sometimes it comes with required changes.

Recap of general proposal skills: In Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-20) you learned that a proposal offers future work and asks for a decision, that solicited proposals must follow instructions exactly, that problem statements need evidence, that objectives should be SMART, and that budgets must add up. All of that applies here. This lesson focuses on what is special about a thesis proposal: it must show research thinking, not just a work plan.

Typical sections: Departments have their own templates, so always use yours. A common structure is: title page with names, IDs and supervisor; abstract or summary of about 150 to 250 words; introduction with background and motivation; problem statement; aim, research questions and objectives; literature review (a condensed version, ending with the gap); proposed methodology; preliminary work or results, if any; expected outcomes and contributions; timeline; resources and budget; risks and ethical considerations; and references. Projects may add requirements and a high-level system design.

The proposal abstract: Many board members read only the abstract before the presentation, so it must stand alone. In about 150 to 250 words, say: the problem and why it matters (one or two sentences), the gap (one sentence), the aim and research questions (one or two sentences), the planned method with data and evaluation (two or three sentences), and the expected contribution (one sentence). Write it last, after the other sections are stable, and check that every number in it matches the body. Unlike a final thesis abstract, it uses future tense ('we will collect', 'we will compare') because the work has not happened yet, except for any preliminary results, which are reported in past tense.

The introduction and problem: Open with the real-world context in two or three sentences, then narrow to the specific problem. Use the five-part problem statement from lesson 09: context, problem, evidence, consequence, gap. Keep it short; the proposal reader wants to reach your research questions within the first page or two.

Research questions and objectives: Present the aim, the RQs and the SMART objectives clearly, ideally as a numbered list so the board can refer to them: 'RQ2 seems too broad'. Including your alignment table from lesson 09, even in compact form, is a powerful way to show that everything fits together.

The condensed literature review: The proposal does not need your full review chapter. Two to four pages are usually enough: the main approaches, the closest works compared in a small table, and the gap stated explicitly. The board wants evidence that you know the field and that your idea is not already done.

Proposed methodology: This is the heart of a research proposal and the section boards question most. Describe: the overall research design (experimental comparison, design and evaluation of a system, survey and so on; lesson 11 covers the options); the data you will use and how you will obtain it, with numbers; the methods or system components; baselines for comparison; evaluation metrics and how they connect to the RQs; and any tools or hardware. Be specific enough that a reader could imagine you doing it. 'We will use deep learning' is not a methodology. 'We will fine-tune MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0, pretrained on ImageNet, on 3,000 labelled images split 70/15/15 by market and date, compared against a colour-histogram plus SVM baseline, using macro F1 as the primary metric' is.

Preliminary results: If you have done the feasibility check from lesson 03, include it. Even a small result, such as 'a pretrained model reached 74 percent accuracy on 150 pilot images without fine-tuning', shows that the plan is realistic and that you have started. It also shows the board your data pipeline works.

Expected outcomes and contributions: List what you expect to deliver: a dataset, a trained model, an app, a comparison, a field evaluation, possibly a paper. Phrase them honestly as expectations, not promises of particular numbers: 'we expect to determine which model offers the best accuracy-size trade-off' rather than 'we will achieve 99 percent accuracy'.

Timeline: Show the main phases and milestones by month or week, usually as a Gantt chart. Include writing, not just building, and leave buffer. Lesson 12 goes deeper into planning; at proposal stage a one-page chart with 8 to 12 tasks is usually enough.

Resources and budget, worked: List hardware, software, data, travel and other costs, and say who pays (self, department, grant). Suppose the mango team plans 6 market trips at 300 taka each, which is 6 x 300 = 1,800 taka; buying 50 kg of mangoes, including deliberately ripened and spoiled samples, at 120 taka per kg, which is 50 x 120 = 6,000 taka; and printing and binding at 1,500 taka. The subtotal is 1,800 + 6,000 + 1,500 = 9,300 taka. Adding a 10 percent contingency of 930 taka gives 10,230 taka. They use their own phones and free cloud notebooks, so compute costs zero, and they say so. A small, honest, correctly added budget builds trust.

Risks and ethics: List the main risks and your mitigations, for example 'mango season is short (May to August); we will collect most images in June and July and keep a public dataset as backup'. Mention ethical issues such as consent for interviews or photographing sellers, and data privacy. Lesson 13 covers risks and ethics in depth.

A worked mini proposal outline: Title: Lightweight Deep Learning for Mango Freshness Classification on Low-Cost Smartphones under Market Conditions. Problem: losses from missed rotten fruit at small markets; existing systems assume lab conditions. Aim: build and evaluate a phone-based classifier. RQs: model trade-off, lighting effect, practical usefulness. Method: local dataset of 3,000 images, three lightweight CNNs plus SVM baseline, macro F1, on-device timing, field test with 5 sellers. Preliminary result: pilot of 150 images. Timeline: 9 months with data by month 4, models by month 6, app by month 7, field test by month 8, writing throughout and final month for polishing. Budget: 10,230 taka. Risks: season, lighting, seller cooperation.

The proposal presentation: Typically 10 to 15 minutes plus questions. A clear slide plan: title and team (1 slide); problem and motivation with one strong number or photo (1 to 2); related work and gap (1 to 2, including the comparison table); RQs and objectives (1); methodology diagram (1 to 2); preliminary results (1); timeline (1); expected contributions (1). That is about 8 to 11 slides, matching roughly one slide per minute or a little more. Practise so you finish on time. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-24) covered presentation skills in general.

Common board questions at proposal stage: 'Has this already been done?', 'Why is this problem important here?', 'Is your dataset big enough and how will you label it?', 'What is your baseline?', 'How will you know if you succeeded?', 'Can you finish this in the time you have?', 'What if you cannot collect the data?'. Prepare a one-line answer for each, backed by your literature table, alignment table, timeline and risk list.

Why proposals get sent back: Common reasons include an unclear or too broad problem; no clear gap or evidence the idea already exists; methodology too vague ('we will use machine learning'); no baseline or evaluation plan; unrealistic scope for the time and team; data not available or not ethically obtainable; weak literature review; and ignoring the department's format. A returned proposal is not a failure; it is cheap feedback before expensive work.

When the plan changes later: Research rarely follows the plan exactly. Small changes, such as switching one model for another or adjusting dataset size, are normal; record them in your minutes with reasons. Bigger changes, such as a different research question or a new title, may need your supervisor's approval and sometimes a formal departmental change. In the final thesis, the methodology chapter describes what you actually did, and it is good practice to mention briefly how and why the plan evolved. Boards respect honest adaptation much more than pretending the original plan worked perfectly.

Real-life example 1, Nusrat and Rafi's proposal defence: They presented 10 slides in 11 minutes. The board asked whether 3,000 images were enough. They showed that the pilot reached 74 percent on 150 images without fine-tuning and cited two papers that fine-tuned similar models successfully on 2,000 to 4,000 images. Another examiner asked about the season risk; they showed the plan to collect in June and July with a public dataset backup. The proposal was approved with one change: add a fourth class for 'unripe' or explain why not. They chose to explain why not, with a scope note.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir's revised proposal: Tanvir's first proposal said 'use machine learning to predict bus arrival'. The board sent it back: no data existed yet, and no baseline was planned. His revised proposal described a simple segment-average method as the main approach, a plan to collect 4 weeks of GPS traces, a comparison against a naive distance-divided-by-average-speed baseline, and machine learning only as optional future work if time allowed. It was approved immediately.

Common mistakes: Writing the proposal in the last two days before the deadline. Copying the abstract and introduction from papers. Vague methodology. Promising specific high accuracies. A timeline with no writing time. A budget that does not add up. Ignoring the template. Not preparing for obvious questions.

Recap: A thesis proposal is the approved architectural plan for your work. Use your department's template; include problem, aim, RQs and objectives, a condensed literature review with a clear gap, a specific methodology with data, baselines and metrics, any preliminary results, expected outcomes, a timeline, an honest budget (add it up), and risks and ethics. Present it in about 8 to 11 slides, prepare for standard questions, treat sent-back proposals as cheap feedback, and record plan changes honestly. Next lesson: choosing the right research design and methodology.
key_points: A thesis proposal is the plan approved before the main work: problem, why, how, resources and timeline.
Typical sections: abstract, introduction, problem statement, aim and RQs, condensed literature review, methodology, preliminary results, outcomes, timeline, budget, risks and ethics, references.
The methodology must be specific: design, data and how it is obtained, methods, baselines and metrics linked to RQs.
Preliminary results from a feasibility pilot show the plan is realistic and the pipeline works.
Budgets list each line's calculation and must add up, for example 1,800 + 6,000 + 1,500 = 9,300 taka plus 10 percent contingency = 10,230.
A proposal presentation is often 10 to 15 minutes with about 8 to 11 slides; prepare answers to standard questions.
Sent-back proposals are cheap early feedback; later plan changes should be recorded and approved when large.
lessons.tip: Before submitting, give your proposal to a classmate and ask them to answer from it alone: what is the gap, what is RQ1, what is the baseline and what is the main metric. Every question they cannot answer marks a section to fix.
lessons.task: Write a one-page outline of your own proposal using the worked mini outline in this lesson as a model: title, problem, aim, RQs, method with data size, baseline and metric, preliminary result (or pilot plan), timeline in months, budget with each line calculated and a 10 percent contingency, and top three risks.

quiz.q: Which methodology statement is specific enough for a proposal?
options: We will try many things and see
We will fine-tune two pretrained lightweight CNNs on 3,000 labelled images with a 70/15/15 split, compare them with an SVM baseline and report macro F1
We will use the best method
quiz.explain: It names models, data, split, baseline and metric.

quiz.q: Lines of 2,000, 4,500 and 1,500 taka plus a 10 percent contingency give what total?
Why include preliminary results in a proposal?
options: To replace the final results chapter
To show the plan is realistic and the pipeline works
quiz.explain: Even a small pilot builds confidence in feasibility.

quiz.q: Which is a common reason proposals are sent back?
options: The methodology names baselines and metrics
The scope is unrealistic for the time and team
quiz.explain: Unrealistic scope is one of the most common reasons.

quiz.q: Your project switches from one CNN to another during the work. What should you do?
options: Record the change and reason in minutes and describe what you actually did in the methodology
Hide it and describe the original plan
Restart the proposal process from zero
quiz.explain: Small changes are normal; document them honestly.

lessons.title: Research Design and Methodology
lessons.content:
Suppose three friends want to know the best way to get from Mirpur to Motijheel in the morning. One times the metro, a bus and a CNG for two weeks and compares the minutes: that is an experiment. Another asks fifty office workers which route they use and why: that is a survey. The third follows one worker for a week, notes every decision and talks to her about her frustrations: that is a case study. All three are asking a reasonable question, but they use different methods, and each method can answer some questions well and others badly. Research design is choosing the method that can actually answer your question. This lesson introduces the main research designs used in computing theses and projects, how to choose between them, and the vocabulary you will need in your methodology chapter.

Method versus methodology: People mix these words. A method is a specific technique: training a CNN, running a questionnaire, measuring latency with a load-testing tool. Methodology is the overall reasoning about how you will answer your research questions: which design, which methods, which data, how you will analyse results and why this combination is valid. Your thesis has a methodology chapter, not just a list of methods, because the board wants to see the reasoning.

Why design matters: A wrong design can make perfect work useless. If your question is 'Does our new interface make students find the bus faster?', a survey asking 'Do you like the new interface?' cannot answer it; liking is not speed. You need a controlled comparison where you time users on both interfaces. Choosing the design that fits your RQ is the single most important methodological decision, and boards often ask 'Why this design?'.

Quantitative, qualitative and mixed: Quantitative research measures things with numbers and analyses them statistically: accuracy, error in minutes, response time, survey ratings. It is good for 'how much', 'how many', 'which is better' questions. Qualitative research collects rich, non-numerical data such as interview transcripts, observation notes and open-ended answers, and looks for themes and meanings. It is good for 'why' and 'how do people experience' questions. Mixed methods combine both, for example measuring app accuracy and also interviewing sellers about why they would or would not use it. Most computing theses are mainly quantitative with a small qualitative part.

Experimental design: In an experiment, you deliberately change one thing and measure the effect while keeping everything else the same. The thing you change is the independent variable (for example, which model you use, or lighting condition). The thing you measure is the dependent variable (accuracy, latency, task time). Everything you keep fixed is a controlled variable (same test images, same phone, same random seed). In machine learning theses, the typical experiment compares methods on the same data split with the same metric. In human studies, a true experiment randomly assigns participants to conditions, so differences are not caused by who chose which condition.

Quasi-experiments: Sometimes you cannot randomise. For example, you can deploy the bus tracker only on two of four routes because of driver availability, and compare waiting complaints on those routes with the others. This is a quasi-experiment. It is still useful, but you must discuss other explanations: maybe those two routes were already less crowded. Being honest about this is a sign of good methodology.

Design science: Many computing projects follow what is called design science research: you identify a problem, design and build an artifact (an app, algorithm, system, model or framework) to solve it, and then evaluate how well the artifact works. The contribution is the artifact plus evidence that it works and lessons about its design. Tanvir's bus tracker fits this perfectly: problem identification from interviews, artifact design and implementation, then evaluation of arrival accuracy and usability. Naming this design in your methodology shows the board that a project is research-informed engineering, not just coding.

Benchmarking and comparative evaluation: A very common thesis design in computing is comparing several existing methods on a dataset or workload, possibly including a modified method of your own. The key requirements are a fair setup (same data, same splits, same compute budget where possible), clear metrics and enough repetitions. Lesson 16 and lesson 19 cover how to run and analyse such comparisons properly.

Surveys: A survey collects answers from many people using a questionnaire, often online. It is suitable for measuring opinions, habits or self-reported experiences: 'How long do students usually wait for the campus bus?'. Good surveys use clear, neutral questions, avoid leading wording ('Don't you agree the old system is terrible?'), test the questionnaire on a few people first, and think about who responds. If only your friends on Facebook respond, your sample is biased.

How many survey responses, worked: A common formula estimates the sample size needed to measure a proportion: n = z^2 x p x (1 - p) / e^2, where z is 1.96 for 95 percent confidence, p is the expected proportion (0.5 if unknown, which gives the largest n), and e is the margin of error. For e = 0.05 (plus or minus 5 percentage points): n = 1.96^2 x 0.5 x 0.5 / 0.05^2 = 3.8416 x 0.25 / 0.0025 = 384.16, so about 385 responses. For a small population, such as 2,000 students using the campus bus, a finite population correction gives n = 384.16 / (1 + 383.16 / 2,000), about 322.4, so about 323 responses. If you can only get about 100 responses, the margin of error is roughly plus or minus 10 points, since 1.96^2 x 0.25 / 0.1^2 is about 96. This formula assumes a random sample; it does not fix a biased one.

Case studies and interviews: A case study examines one or a few real situations in depth, such as how one pharmacy manages stock, to understand context and requirements. Interviews, semi-structured with prepared questions but freedom to follow up, are the main tool. For requirement gathering in projects, 8 to 15 good interviews often reveal most of the important needs. Record with permission, take notes, and analyse by grouping repeated themes. Qualitative work needs care with consent and privacy (lesson 13).

Simulation: When real experiments are too costly, slow or dangerous, you can simulate. Network protocols, traffic flows, epidemics, queueing at a hospital counter or flood evacuation can be modelled in software and tested under many scenarios. The key question boards ask is validity: how do you know the simulation matches reality? Calibrate with real data where possible and test sensitivity to your assumptions. Simulation & Modeling (deep-cse-6-5) covered the techniques.

User studies and usability evaluation: When your work has users, evaluate with users. Task-based testing measures success rate, time on task and errors while users try realistic tasks. Standard questionnaires such as the System Usability Scale (SUS) give comparable scores (lesson 18 shows how to compute SUS). Even 5 to 8 users in a careful think-aloud test reveal many usability problems, though more are needed for reliable statistics. HCI (deep-cse-5-5) covered these methods in depth.

Replication studies: A replication repeats a published study to check whether its results hold, either exactly (same data and method) or conceptually (same method on new data, such as Bangla instead of English). Replications are undervalued but very useful, because many published results turn out to be hard to reproduce. For a BSc thesis, a careful replication of an important paper, followed by testing it on local data, is a respectable and achievable design. The key is to document every difference between your setup and the original, and to report honestly whether the original numbers were reached.

Choosing a design from the research question: Read the verb in your RQ. 'Which is better/how much does X affect Y' points to an experiment or benchmark. 'How can we build a system that...' points to design science with evaluation. 'What do users think/how common is...' points to a survey. 'Why do people.../what are the needs of...' points to interviews or a case study. 'What would happen if... at large scale' points to simulation. Many theses combine two designs: a benchmark for the model plus a small user study for the app.

Validity and reliability, first look: Validity asks whether you are measuring what you think you are measuring and whether your conclusion follows. Reliability asks whether you would get similar results if you repeated the study. A model tested once on a tiny, unrepresentative test set has low reliability. A survey asking about 'satisfaction' to measure 'speed' has low validity. Lesson 19 lists the classic threats to validity; here, just remember that every design has weaknesses, and good methodology names them and reduces them.

The methodology chapter preview: Your thesis methodology chapter usually contains: the research design and why it fits the RQs; data sources and collection procedures; materials, tools and setup; the methods or system design; the evaluation plan with metrics and baselines; analysis procedures; ethical considerations; and limitations of the design. It should be detailed enough that another student could repeat your work. Lessons 14 to 19 fill in each piece.

Real-life example 1, the mango thesis design: Nusrat and Rafi use mixed methods. RQ1 and RQ2 use a quantitative comparative experiment: independent variables are model type and lighting group, dependent variable is macro F1, controlled variables are the test set, image size and training budget. RQ3 uses a small field evaluation with 5 sellers, combining accuracy on 200 real mangoes with short interviews about trust and usefulness. Their methodology chapter explains why each design matches each RQ.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir chooses design science: Tanvir frames his project as design science: problem identification through 12 interviews and a survey of 150 students (he notes that 150 gives a margin of error of about plus or minus 8 points, so results are indicative), artifact design and implementation, then evaluation in two parts: a quantitative comparison of arrival-time error against a naive baseline on 50 trips, and a usability test with 15 students using SUS. The board praised the clarity of the design.

Common mistakes: Choosing a design because a friend used it. Using a satisfaction survey to answer a performance question. No control or baseline in an experiment. Changing several things at once and not knowing which caused the effect. Tiny, biased samples presented as representative. Calling a project 'research' with no evaluation at all. A methodology chapter that is just a list of tools.

Recap: Methodology is the reasoning that connects your research questions to your methods. Quantitative designs measure, qualitative designs explore meanings, mixed methods combine both. Experiments change an independent variable, measure a dependent variable and control the rest; design science builds and evaluates an artifact; benchmarks compare methods fairly; surveys need careful questions and enough responses (about 385 for plus or minus 5 points in a large population); case studies, interviews, simulation and user studies each fit particular questions. Choose by the verb in your RQ and name your design's weaknesses. Next lesson: planning the work.
key_points: A method is a specific technique; methodology is the reasoning for how your design and methods answer your research questions.
Quantitative research measures with numbers, qualitative explores meanings, mixed methods combine both; most computing theses are mainly quantitative.
Experiments change an independent variable, measure a dependent variable and hold controlled variables fixed.
Design science builds an artifact to solve a problem and evaluates it; many projects fit this design.
Survey sample size for a proportion: n = z^2 p(1 - p) / e^2, about 385 for plus or minus 5 points at 95 percent confidence; a biased sample stays biased.
Choose the design from the RQ's verb: which is better (experiment), how to build (design science), how common (survey), why (interviews), at scale (simulation).
Every design has weaknesses; name threats to validity and reliability and reduce them.
lessons.tip: Write next to each research question the single word for its design (experiment, design science, survey, interviews, simulation, user study). If you cannot choose one word, the question may be two questions.
lessons.task: For each of your research questions, write the design you will use, the independent, dependent and controlled variables (or, for qualitative parts, the data you will collect), and one weakness of that design with how you will reduce it. If you plan a survey, compute the margin of error for the number of responses you can realistically get.

quiz.q: In an experiment comparing three CNN models on the same test set, what is the independent variable?
quiz.explain: You deliberately change the model; accuracy is the dependent variable; the test set is controlled.

quiz.q: Which research question best fits a survey?
options: Which of two algorithms is faster on our dataset?
How can we build an offline Bangla voice assistant?
How long do students at our university usually wait for the campus bus?
Why do pharmacy owners resist digital stock systems?
quiz.explain: A survey suits measuring self-reported habits or opinions across many people.

quiz.q: Using n = 1.96^2 x 0.25 / e^2, roughly how many responses do you need for a margin of error of 0.10?
What is design science research?
options: Building an artifact to solve a problem and evaluating how well it works
quiz.explain: The contribution is the artifact plus evidence and design lessons.

quiz.q: A team asks users 'Do you like the new interface?' to show it is faster. What is wrong?
options: The measure does not match the question; speed needs timed tasks in a controlled comparison
Surveys are never allowed in theses
quiz.explain: This is a validity problem: the design must measure what the RQ asks.

lessons.title: Planning the Work
lessons.content:
Think about how a family plans a wedding in Bangladesh. Nobody says 'let us do the wedding' and starts randomly. They list everything: book the community centre, print cards, order the food, buy clothes, arrange the holud, hire decorators. They know some things must happen before others: cards cannot be printed until the date and venue are fixed. They estimate how long each takes, add extra days because the tailor is always late, and someone checks progress every few days. A final year project needs the same kind of plan. This lesson shows how to break the work into pieces, estimate time honestly, find the tasks that control your finish date, add buffers and keep the plan alive with weekly checks.

Why plan at all: Research has uncertainty, so some students think planning is pointless. The opposite is true. A plan does not predict the future perfectly; it gives you a baseline to notice when you are slipping, a way to see which delays matter, and something concrete to discuss with your supervisor. Without a plan, you discover in month eight that experiments, the app and the whole thesis book are all still unfinished. With a plan, you notice in month three that labelling is two weeks behind and adjust while it is cheap.

Work breakdown structure: A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the whole project into smaller and smaller pieces until each piece is a clear task that one person can finish in a few days to two weeks. For the mango thesis, level 1 might be: 1 Literature and proposal, 2 Data, 3 Models, 4 App, 5 Field evaluation, 6 Thesis writing, 7 Defence. Level 2 under Data: 2.1 design labelling guidelines, 2.2 collect images at markets, 2.3 label images, 2.4 check label agreement, 2.5 clean and split dataset. Each leaf task should have a clear output you can point to, such as 'guidelines document' or 'CSV of 3,000 labelled images'.

Milestones and deliverables: A milestone is a moment that marks completion of something important, with zero duration: 'dataset frozen', 'proposal approved', 'first full draft submitted'. A deliverable is the actual thing produced: the dataset files, the draft PDF. Milestones are the checkpoints you report to your supervisor; place one roughly every 4 to 6 weeks. Department deadlines (proposal, progress presentation, submission, defence) are fixed milestones; plan backwards from them.

Estimating time honestly: Students usually underestimate, because they imagine the task going smoothly. A useful technique is the three-point or PERT estimate. For each task, estimate an optimistic time O (everything goes well), a most likely time M, and a pessimistic time P (realistic problems, not disasters). The expected time is E = (O + 4M + P) / 6, and a rough measure of uncertainty is (P - O) / 6. This weighted average pulls your estimate towards reality when the bad case is much longer than the good case.

PERT, worked: Labelling 3,000 mango images: optimistic 3 weeks, most likely 4 weeks, pessimistic 8 weeks (if sellers stop cooperating or labels need rework). E = (3 + 4 x 4 + 8) / 6 = (3 + 16 + 8) / 6 = 27 / 6 = 4.5 weeks, with uncertainty (8 - 3) / 6, about 0.83 weeks. Training and tuning models: O = 2, M = 3, P = 6 weeks gives E = (2 + 12 + 6) / 6 = 20 / 6, about 3.3 weeks. Notice that both expected times are longer than the most likely guesses of 4 and 3 weeks, because the pessimistic side is long. Using M alone would make your plan too tight.

Dependencies: Some tasks can only start after others finish: you cannot train on the full dataset before labelling is done, and you cannot field-test the app before the model is ready. Others can run in parallel: writing the training script with dummy data while images are still being collected. Mark dependencies explicitly, because they decide the order and which delays push your end date.

The critical path, worked: Consider a simplified plan. A: collect images, 6 weeks. B: label images, 4 weeks, after A. C: write the training pipeline, 3 weeks, can start at week 0. D: run experiments, 5 weeks, after both B and C. E: build and test the app, 4 weeks, after D. Path A to B to D to E takes 6 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 19 weeks. Path C to D to E takes 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 weeks. The longest path, 19 weeks, is the critical path: any delay on A, B, D or E delays the whole project by the same amount. Task C has slack: D cannot start until B finishes at week 6 + 4 = 10, and C finishes at week 3, so C can slip by 10 - 3 = 7 weeks without hurting the end date. This tells you where to focus: protect the critical path, and use slack tasks to fill gaps. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) covers critical path methods in depth.

The Gantt chart: A Gantt chart shows tasks as horizontal bars on a timeline, with milestones as diamonds and dependencies as arrows. It is the most common planning picture in theses and proposals because anyone can read it at a glance. Keep it readable: 10 to 20 bars at the level of your WBS, not 80 tiny tasks. Spreadsheet tools, free online tools or even a hand-drawn chart photographed for the first draft are fine. Update it when plans change; an old Gantt chart that no longer matches reality is worse than none.

Buffers: Every plan needs time reserved for surprises. Two simple ways: add a project buffer at the end, for example 10 to 15 percent of the total duration before the submission deadline, or add small buffers after risky tasks on the critical path. Do not hide buffers inside every task estimate, because then they get used up by slow work rather than real surprises. In a 40-week plan, a 4 to 6 week buffer before submission is reasonable. If you never need it, you get extra time for polishing the thesis.

Two human traps: Two well-known patterns quietly destroy plans. The first is often called student syndrome: when a task has generous time, people start it late and rush at the end, so the safety margin is wasted before the work even begins. The second is Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time available, so a task given three weeks somehow takes three weeks even if it needed one. Both explain why hidden padding in every task does not help. The cure is simple: start each task as soon as its dependencies are done, set an internal finish date earlier than the real one, and hand back unused time to the shared buffer instead of spending it.

Plan the writing too: The most common planning error is a Gantt chart full of building tasks with one bar at the end called 'write thesis'. Writing a 60-page thesis well takes many weeks and several feedback rounds, each taking one or two weeks of supervisor time. Plan chapter drafts as tasks alongside the technical work: literature review after the proposal, methodology while running experiments, results as each experiment finishes, introduction and conclusion near the end. Lessons 21 and 22 cover writing the book.

Weekly planning and Kanban: The big plan shows months; the weekly plan shows what happens on Tuesday. Each week, pick the next few tasks from the critical path and the slack tasks, write them as deliverable-style goals (lesson 02), and track them on a simple Kanban board with columns To do, Doing, Done. Limit work in progress: if three tasks are in Doing, finish one before starting another. Half-finished tasks feel like progress but deliver nothing.

Tracking progress: At each weekly review, compare plan with reality.
