A simple traffic light helps: green, on track; amber, behind but recoverable within the slack or buffer; red, the end date or a department deadline is at risk. Report the colour honestly in your monthly progress note. Amber tells your supervisor early that help or a scope decision may be needed; red discovered for the first time in the last month is a crisis.

Re-planning: When reality diverges, re-plan rather than ignore. Options include: use slack or buffer; reorder tasks to work on something else while blocked; add effort temporarily; reduce scope using the must-have and could-have list from lesson 13; or, as a last resort, ask whether a deadline can move. Record the change and the reason in your minutes. A plan that changes with reasons is a living plan; a plan that never changes is usually not being looked at.

Real-life example 1, Nusrat and Rafi's plan: They built a WBS with 22 leaf tasks, estimated the risky ones with PERT, and drew a Gantt chart from June to the following March. The critical path ran through image collection, labelling, experiments and the field test. They noticed the field test depended on mango season, so they moved a small early field test into August using the first model, and kept a 5-week buffer before submission. When labelling slipped by two weeks in July, the traffic light went amber; they used part of the buffer and moved writing of the literature review chapter into the gap, so no time was wasted.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir's plan around exams: Tanvir's critical path was driver app, data collection on real trips, arrival estimation, student app and usability test. He placed the 4-week GPS data collection right after the driver app, before midterms, because data collection mostly runs automatically while drivers work. During exam weeks he scheduled only slack tasks like documentation and the server's admin page. His plan stayed green for most of the year, and he spent his buffer on polishing the thesis and rehearsing the demo.

Common mistakes: No plan at all, or a plan made once for the proposal and never opened again. Estimating only the most likely time. Ignoring dependencies. One bar called 'write thesis' at the end. No buffer, or buffers hidden everywhere. Too many tasks in progress at once. Reporting everything as green until it is suddenly red.

What boards ask: In proposal and progress presentations: 'Is this timeline realistic?', 'What is on your critical path?', 'What happens if data collection is delayed?', 'How much of the plan have you completed so far?'. A current Gantt chart with milestones met and an honest status make these questions easy.

Recap: Break the project into a WBS of clear tasks with visible outputs, set milestones every 4 to 6 weeks and plan back from department deadlines. Estimate risky tasks with PERT, E = (O + 4M + P) / 6. Mark dependencies, find the critical path and use slack. Draw a readable Gantt chart, keep a project buffer, plan writing alongside building, run weekly Kanban with limited work in progress, track with traffic lights and re-plan with recorded reasons. Next lesson: risks, scope control and research ethics.
key_points: A plan gives a baseline to notice slipping early, shows which delays matter and supports supervisor discussions.
A work breakdown structure splits the project into tasks of a few days to two weeks, each with a visible output.
Milestones mark key completions every 4 to 6 weeks; plan backwards from fixed department deadlines.
PERT estimate: E = (O + 4M + P) / 6; for 3, 4 and 8 weeks, E = 4.5 weeks, longer than the most likely 4.
The critical path is the longest dependency chain (19 weeks in the example); delays there delay everything, while other tasks have slack.
Keep a readable Gantt chart, a 10 to 15 percent project buffer and writing tasks planned alongside technical work.
Run weekly Kanban with limited work in progress, report status with traffic lights and re-plan with recorded reasons.
lessons.tip: When you estimate a task, ask 'what would make this take twice as long?' and write that as the pessimistic case. If you cannot think of anything, ask a senior who did a similar thesis.
lessons.task: Write a WBS for your project with at least 15 leaf tasks. Give PERT estimates for the three riskiest tasks, mark dependencies, find the critical path and its length, and draw a Gantt chart with milestones, writing tasks and a buffer before your submission deadline.

quiz.q: A task has O = 2, M = 5 and P = 14 days. What is the PERT expected time?
What is the critical path?
options: The longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the earliest finish date
The task the supervisor likes most
The shortest path through the plan
quiz.explain: A delay on the critical path delays the whole project.

quiz.q: Task C takes 3 weeks and can start at week 0. The next task D cannot start before week 10. How much slack does C have?
quiz.explain: C finishes at week 3 but D waits until week 10, so 10 - 3 = 7 weeks.

quiz.q: What is the most common planning mistake about writing?
options: Leaving one bar called 'write thesis' at the very end
Writing the methodology while running experiments
quiz.explain: Writing needs many weeks and feedback rounds; it must be planned throughout.

quiz.q: Your weekly review shows labelling two weeks behind but still within the buffer. What status fits?
quiz.explain: Behind but recoverable within slack or buffer is amber; report it honestly.

lessons.title: Risks, Scope Control and Research Ethics
lessons.content:
Before the monsoon, a careful farmer in Sylhet does not just hope for the best. She thinks: what could go wrong this season? A flash flood could ruin the low field, so she plants that one later. Pests could arrive, so she keeps some money for pesticide. The pump could break, so she knows a mechanic in the next village. She cannot stop the rain, but she can reduce the damage. Running a final year project is similar. Many things can go wrong: data does not arrive, a laptop dies, a teammate falls sick, the model refuses to improve. You cannot prevent every problem, but you can see the likely ones coming and prepare. This lesson covers risk management, controlling scope so the project does not balloon, and the ethics of doing research with people, data and other people's work.

What a risk is: A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, affects your project's goals: time, quality or scope. It is different from an issue, which is a problem already happening. 'The mango season may end before we collect enough images' is a risk. 'The season has ended and we have 1,200 images' is an issue. Risk management is the habit of turning likely issues into prepared-for risks.

Common risks in final year projects: Data risks: data never arrives, is smaller or messier than expected, or permission is withdrawn. Technical risks: the method does not work, libraries conflict, the model does not beat the baseline, hardware arrives late. Resource risks: free GPU quotas run out, a laptop is stolen or crashes, internet and power cuts. People risks: a teammate drops out or falls sick, the supervisor goes on leave, outside partners stop responding. Schedule risks: exams, holidays, strikes, floods. Scope risks: adding features endlessly. Ethics and legal risks: collecting personal data without consent, using code or data against its licence.

The risk register: A risk register is a simple table with columns: ID, risk description, likelihood, impact, score, owner, mitigation, contingency and status. Likelihood and impact are each rated from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The score is likelihood x impact, from 1 to 25. Sort by score and focus on the top few. Review it monthly; risks change as the project moves.

Risk scoring, worked: For the mango thesis: R1, mango season ends before enough images: likelihood 3, impact 5, score 15. R2, laptop failure loses work: likelihood 2, impact 5, score 10. R3, the model does not beat the baseline: likelihood 3, impact 3, score 9. R4, a team member is sick for weeks: likelihood 2, impact 4, score 8. R5, free GPU quota limits experiments: likelihood 4, impact 2, score 8. R6, sellers refuse to be photographed: likelihood 2, impact 3, score 6. The ranking is R1 (15), R2 (10), R3 (9), R4 and R5 (8), R6 (6). Many teams use bands such as 15 and above high, 8 to 14 medium, below 8 low. The register immediately shows where effort should go: R1 and R2 need action now.

Mitigation and contingency: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact before the risk happens. Contingency is the plan you follow if it happens anyway. For R1: mitigation, start collection in the first week of June and visit markets twice a week; contingency, use a public South Asian mango dataset plus fewer local images and state this as a limitation. For R2: mitigation, Git with a remote repository plus a cloud backup of data (the 3-2-1 rule in lesson 17), which lowers the impact from 5 to about 2. For R3: mitigation, run a baseline early; contingency, reframe as a careful comparison where a negative result is still a finding (lesson 20). Write these down; in a crisis you will not think as clearly.

Risk owners and triggers: Give each risk an owner who watches it, and a trigger that tells you it is happening: 'if we have fewer than 1,500 images by 15 July, switch to the contingency'. Triggers stop the common pattern of hoping too long. Owners prevent the situation where everybody assumed somebody else was watching.

Scope creep: Scope creep is the slow growth of what you promise to do: 'let us also add a Bangla voice feature', 'what about detecting bananas too', 'let us build a web dashboard as well'. Each addition seems small, but together they eat the buffer and threaten the core. Scope creep often comes from enthusiasm, from wanting to impress the board, or from suggestions in meetings. A bigger but half-finished project scores worse than a smaller complete one.

Scope control with MoSCoW: Sort every feature or task into four groups. Must have: without it the project fails its aim (dataset, models, comparison, basic app). Should have: important but the project still works without it (lighting analysis, offline mode). Could have: nice extras if time allows (Bangla voice output, dashboard). Won't have this time: explicitly out of scope, moved to future work (banana detection, iOS app). Write the list early, agree it with your supervisor, and when something new appears, place it in a group before anyone starts working on it. If a must-have is late, you drop could-haves first, not must-haves.

Why ethics matters in student work: Research affects people: the sellers you photograph, the students you survey, the patients whose data you use, the authors whose code you reuse. Ethics is not paperwork; it is respect and responsibility. It also protects you: a thesis built on data collected without consent, or code copied against its licence, can be rejected or cause legal trouble. Professional Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) covers laws and professional codes; here we focus on practical rules for a final year project.

Informed consent: When people take part in your research (interviews, surveys, user tests, photos of them or their property), they must agree freely, knowing what they agree to. Tell them in simple language, Bangla if appropriate: who you are, the purpose, what they will do, how long it takes, what data you collect, how it will be stored and used, that participation is voluntary, and that they can stop at any time without any penalty. Get their agreement in writing or recorded, and keep it. For the mango study, sellers agree to photographs of their fruit and stalls; faces are not needed, so the team avoids them.

Privacy and anonymisation: Collect only the personal data you really need. Remove or replace names, phone numbers, ID numbers and faces before analysis and publication; use codes like S01, S02. Store raw data with personal information securely, separately from the anonymised data, and limit who can access it. Be careful: combinations of small details (department, year, gender, home district) can identify someone even without a name. Location traces, like the GPS data in Tanvir's project, are personal data when linked to a driver; he stores them by bus ID, not driver name, and deletes raw traces after analysis.

Vulnerable groups and harm: Extra care is needed with children, patients, people in difficult financial situations and anyone who may feel unable to refuse, such as your own juniors when you are a senior or students in a teacher's class. Research with minors usually needs a parent's or guardian's consent as well as the child's agreement. Ask whether your study could cause any harm: embarrassment, loss of income, stress, exposure of private information. If yes, redesign or seek ethical review.

Ethics review: Many universities have an ethics committee or institutional review board that must approve research involving human participants or sensitive data, especially in health. Rules vary between universities, and some departments handle low-risk student work through the supervisor. Ask your supervisor early whether your project needs formal approval, and allow several weeks for it. Never start collecting data from people before the approval you need is in place.

Using other people's code and data: Open-source code and public datasets come with licences that tell you what you may do. Permissive licences such as MIT or Apache allow reuse with attribution. Copyleft licences such as GPL require derived software you distribute to be released under the same licence. Datasets often use Creative Commons licences: CC BY allows reuse with credit, CC BY-NC forbids commercial use, and some datasets are for research only. Read the licence, follow it, cite the dataset or repository properly, and state in the thesis what code you reused and what you wrote yourself. Copying code from a tutorial or a friend's thesis without saying so is plagiarism, even if it is technically allowed by a licence.

Research integrity: Ethics also covers how you treat your own results. Fabrication means inventing data or results that never existed. Falsification means changing data, results or methods so they look better, such as deleting runs that went badly or editing a screenshot. Both are serious misconduct that can lead to a failed thesis or a degree being withdrawn, even years later. Keep raw data and logs unchanged, record every exclusion with a reason, and report what really happened. Lessons 19, 20 and 24 return to honest analysis and reporting.

Real-life example 1, a risk that came true: In July, Nusrat and Rafi had only 1,300 images, below their trigger of 1,500. Because the contingency was already written, they did not panic. They added images from a public dataset with a compatible licence, cited it, and kept a separate local-only test set so their results on local mangoes remained honest. Their limitations section explained the mix. The board appreciated the transparency.

Real-life example 2, consent done right: Tanvir needed GPS traces from drivers' phones and a usability test with students. He wrote a one-page consent sheet in Bangla for drivers explaining that only bus location and time would be collected during duty hours, stored without names, used only for the thesis and deleted afterwards. For students, the online form began with a consent paragraph and a checkbox. He asked his supervisor whether ethics committee approval was needed; for this low-risk study the department required only the supervisor's sign-off, which he attached as an appendix.

Common mistakes: No risk register, or one written for the proposal and forgotten. Mitigation with no contingency. Ignoring triggers until it is too late. Saying yes to every feature idea. Collecting personal data 'just in case'. Photographing people without asking. Posting raw survey data with names online. Using datasets or code without checking licences. Starting user studies before required approval.

What boards ask: 'What were your main risks and what did you do about them?', 'How did you obtain consent?', 'Where is your data stored and who can access it?', 'Is this dataset licensed for your use?', 'Why did you not include feature X?'. Your risk register, MoSCoW list and consent documents answer these directly.

Recap: List risks across data, technical, resource, people, schedule, scope and ethics categories; score them as likelihood x impact; write mitigation, contingency, owner and trigger for the top ones; and review monthly. Control scope with MoSCoW and decide new ideas before working on them. Treat ethics as respect: informed consent, minimum data, anonymisation, extra care with vulnerable groups, ethics review when needed, and correct use and citation of others' code and data. Next lesson: collecting and preparing data.
key_points: A risk is an uncertain future event that would affect time, quality or scope; an issue is a problem already happening.
A risk register rates likelihood and impact from 1 to 5, scores them as likelihood x impact and focuses on the highest scores.
Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact beforehand; contingency is the prepared plan if the risk happens; owners and triggers stop wishful waiting.
Scope creep slowly adds features until the core is threatened; control it with MoSCoW (must, should, could, won't).
Informed consent means people agree freely knowing purpose, tasks, data use and their right to stop at any time.
Collect minimum personal data, anonymise it, store raw data securely, and take extra care with minors and vulnerable groups.
Check licences of code and datasets (MIT, Apache, GPL, CC BY, CC BY-NC), follow them, cite sources and state what you reused.
lessons.tip: For every top risk, write one trigger sentence with a number and a date, such as 'fewer than 1,500 images by 15 July'. A trigger turns worry into a decision you have already made.
lessons.task: Build a risk register for your project with at least six risks across different categories. Score each as likelihood x impact, rank them, and for the top three write mitigation, contingency, owner and trigger. Then sort your planned features into MoSCoW groups.

quiz.q: A risk has likelihood 4 and impact 3. What is its score?
quiz.explain: Score = likelihood x impact = 4 x 3 = 12.

quiz.q: What is the difference between mitigation and contingency?
options: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact beforehand; contingency is what you do if the risk happens
Contingency is done before; mitigation after
Mitigation is only for ethics risks
quiz.explain: Mitigation acts in advance; contingency is the prepared response.

quiz.q: In MoSCoW, where should a 'nice extra if time allows' feature go?
quiz.explain: Could-haves are dropped first when must-haves are at risk.

quiz.q: Which is part of informed consent?
options: Telling participants they cannot stop once started
Explaining purpose and data use and that participation is voluntary and can stop at any time
Collecting as much personal data as possible
quiz.explain: Consent must be free, informed and given before participation.

quiz.q: A dataset is licensed CC BY-NC. What does that allow?
options: Non-commercial use with credit to the source
quiz.explain: BY requires attribution; NC forbids commercial use.

lessons.title: Data Collection and Preparation
lessons.content:
A good cook knows that the best recipe cannot save rotten vegetables. If the fish is stale, the rice full of stones and the spices mislabelled, no amount of skill makes a good biryani. In most computing theses, data is the ingredients. A model trained on messy, biased or leaky data gives numbers that look impressive and mean little. Many final year projects that fail do not fail because of the algorithm; they fail because the data was too small, badly labelled or secretly overlapping between training and testing. This lesson is about getting the ingredients right: choosing between public and self-collected data, planning collection, labelling consistently, measuring label quality, cleaning, splitting without leakage, documenting and storing safely.

Why data deserves its own phase: Students are tempted to rush data to get to the 'real work' of modelling. But data decisions decide what your results can mean. If all your rotten mango photos were taken in the evening and all fresh ones in the morning, a model may learn lighting, not rot, and your 95 percent accuracy is an illusion. Experienced researchers often spend more time on data than on models. Plan for data to take a large share of your building time.

Public datasets versus your own data: Public datasets (from repositories like Kaggle, university dataset pages, government open data portals, or dataset papers) are fast to start with, often well documented and let you compare with published results. But they may not match your setting: foreign fruit varieties, English text, different cameras. Collecting your own data fits your problem exactly and is itself a contribution, especially for Bangladeshi contexts where data is scarce, but it takes time, needs consent and careful labelling. Many good theses combine both: pretrain or compare on public data, then evaluate on a smaller local dataset.

Planning a collection: Before collecting a single sample, write a short collection protocol. What exactly will you collect (images, text, sensor readings, logs, survey answers)? From where and from whom? With what device and settings? How many, and in what conditions? How will you record metadata such as date, location, device and conditions? For the mango thesis: three phone models, photos at two markets, each mango photographed from two sides on a plain cloth background and once in the crate, under the natural light of the stall, with a CSV row per photo listing image ID, market, date, time, phone and lighting tag. Consistent protocol now saves weeks of cleaning later.

Capturing variety on purpose: Real use is messy, so your data must include the variety the system will face: different lighting, angles, backgrounds, devices, speakers, accents, writing styles, times of day. If you only collect easy examples, your test results will be too optimistic. At the same time, keep a record of these variations so you can analyse performance by condition later, which is how RQ2 about lighting becomes answerable.

How much data, worked: There is no universal number, but you can reason about it. Fine-tuning a pretrained image model often works with a few hundred to a few thousand images per class, while training from scratch needs far more. If you plan 3,000 images across three classes, and you will split 70/15/15, the training set has 3,000 x 0.70 = 2,100 images and validation and test have 450 each. If the classes are fresh 1,500, semi-rotten 600 and rotten 900, the test set with stratification gets 15 percent of each: 225, 90 and 135. Ask yourself: are 90 semi-rotten test images enough to say anything reliable about that class? If not, collect more of that class, or plan cross-validation (lesson 19). Learning curves, where you train on 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the data, show whether more data would still help.

Labelling guidelines: Labels are only as good as the rules behind them. Write a labelling guide before labelling: definitions of each class in simple words, clear visual examples of each, borderline cases and how to decide them, and what to do when unsure (for example, an 'unsure' tag for later review). For mangoes: 'rotten' means any soft dark patch larger than a two-taka coin or visible mould; 'semi-rotten' means small soft spots or skin wrinkling without mould; 'fresh' means firm with no dark patches. Ask a domain expert, like an experienced fruit seller or agriculture officer, to check the definitions. Update the guide when new tricky cases appear and note the version.

Measuring label agreement: How do you know the labels are reliable? Have two people label the same sample independently and measure how often they agree. Raw agreement can be misleading because some agreement happens by chance, so researchers use Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance: kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe), where po is the observed agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance from each labeller's class proportions.

Cohen's kappa, worked: Two labellers each label the same 200 mango images as fresh or rotten. Both say fresh for 90, both say rotten for 70, labeller A says fresh but B says rotten for 15, and A says rotten but B says fresh for 25. Observed agreement po = (90 + 70) / 200 = 0.80. Labeller A said fresh 90 + 15 = 105 times and rotten 95 times; B said fresh 90 + 25 = 115 times and rotten 85 times. Chance agreement pe = (105/200 x 115/200) + (95/200 x 85/200) = 0.525 x 0.575 + 0.475 x 0.425 = 0.301875 + 0.201875 = 0.50375. Kappa = (0.80 - 0.50375) / (1 - 0.50375) = 0.29625 / 0.49625, about 0.60. A common rough guide (Landis and Koch) calls 0.41 to 0.60 moderate and 0.61 to 0.80 substantial. So 80 percent raw agreement sounds high, but kappa reveals only moderate reliability. The fix: discuss the 40 disagreements, sharpen the guidelines, and relabel.

Cleaning data: Typical cleaning steps include removing exact and near duplicates, removing corrupted files, fixing obviously wrong labels found during review, handling missing values in tabular data, standardising formats (image size, text encoding, date formats, units), and removing personal information. Write cleaning as a script, not manual clicking, so it can be rerun and described in the methodology. Keep the raw data untouched in a separate folder; cleaning produces a new version. Record how many items each step removed, for example '3,214 photos collected, 96 duplicates and 41 blurred removed, 3,077 kept'.

Splitting data: You need separate sets for different jobs. The training set teaches the model. The validation set is used to choose settings (hyperparameters, early stopping, which model). The test set is used once, at the end, to estimate real performance. If you tune on the test set, its numbers become optimistic and no longer honest. Stratified splitting keeps class proportions similar in each set, important when classes are unequal. Fix and save the split (file lists or a random seed) so every experiment uses exactly the same sets.

Data leakage, the silent killer: Leakage happens when information from the test set sneaks into training, making results look better than reality. Common forms: the same mango photographed twice, with one photo in training and one in testing; near-duplicate frames from a video split across sets; data from the same person in both sets, when you claim the model works on new people; normalising features using statistics computed on the whole dataset before splitting; time-series data split randomly so the model sees the future. Prevention: split by group (by mango ID, by person, by market day) rather than by individual sample, split before any preprocessing that learns from data, and for time data, train on the past and test on the future.

Documenting the dataset: Write a short datasheet: why the dataset was created, who collected it and when, how and where, what each field means, class counts, labelling procedure and agreement, cleaning steps, known biases and gaps (for example, only two markets, only three varieties), licence and how to access it. This goes into your methodology chapter and appendix, and is essential if you publish the dataset. It also helps future students build on your work.

Storage and backup: Keep three things separate: raw data (never modified), processed data (produced by scripts) and the scripts themselves (in Git). Large data files usually do not belong in Git; store them in cloud storage or a university drive, with the folder structure and a checksum list recorded in the repository. Back up following the 3-2-1 rule (lesson 17). Protect any personal data with restricted access. Losing three months of collected images to a dead laptop is one of the most painful and most avoidable thesis disasters.

Bangladesh-specific data: Local data is both a challenge and an opportunity. Bangla text has its own issues: Unicode normalisation, mixed Bangla and English (Banglish written in Latin script), regional spelling variants. Speech data must include regional accents. Images should reflect local conditions: dust, crowded backgrounds, varied lighting. Government portals, local research groups and published Bangla datasets are good starting points; always check licences and cite them. A careful, documented local dataset is often the most lasting contribution of a Bangladeshi BSc thesis.

Real-life example 1, the mango dataset: Nusrat and Rafi wrote a one-page protocol and a labelling guide with photos of borderline cases checked by a wholesaler. Their first agreement check on 200 images gave kappa about 0.60. After discussing disagreements and adding a rule about the two-taka coin size, a second check reached about 0.78. They split by mango ID so the two photos of each mango stayed in the same set, created a separate local-only test set from a third market, and wrote a datasheet listing that all photos came from June and July.

Real-life example 2, Tanvir's GPS data: Tanvir collected GPS points every 5 seconds from four buses for four weeks. Cleaning removed points with poor accuracy reported by the phone and periods when the bus was parked at the depot. To evaluate arrival estimates honestly, he used the first three weeks to build segment-average travel times and the fourth week only for testing, so the model never saw the days it predicted. He documented phone models, collection hours and two days lost to a strike.

Common mistakes: Collecting without a protocol. Only easy, clean examples. No labelling guide, or one labeller with no agreement check. Cleaning by hand without recording steps. Tuning on the test set. Random splits that leak duplicates, people or time. No metadata, so conditions cannot be analysed. Data only on one laptop. Ignoring licences of public datasets.

What boards ask: 'How was your data collected and labelled?', 'How do you know the labels are reliable?', 'Is your test set truly separate?', 'Is your dataset balanced?', 'How representative is it of real use?', 'Can others access it?'. Your protocol, kappa values, split rules and datasheet answer all of these.

Recap: Data is the ingredient that decides what your results mean. Choose public, own or combined data deliberately; write a collection protocol and capture real variety with metadata; reason about quantity per class and in the test set; write labelling guidelines and check agreement with Cohen's kappa; clean with scripts and keep raw data untouched; split into train, validation and test with stratification and group-based splits to avoid leakage; document with a datasheet; and store with backups. Next lesson: building the system for project-style work.
key_points: Data decides what results mean; messy, biased or leaky data produces impressive but meaningless numbers.
Public datasets are fast and comparable; your own local data fits the problem and can be a contribution; many theses combine both.
Write a collection protocol, capture real-world variety on purpose and record metadata such as device, place, time and conditions.
Labelling needs written guidelines with borderline cases; check reliability with Cohen's kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe), for example 0.80 raw agreement gave kappa about 0.60.
Clean with scripts, keep raw data untouched and record how many items each step removed.
Use separate train, validation and test sets; tune only on validation; stratify; split by group or time to prevent leakage.
Document the dataset with a datasheet and store raw data, processed data and scripts separately with backups.
lessons.tip: Before any modelling, look at 50 random samples from each class yourself, slowly. You will often spot label mistakes, duplicates or a hidden shortcut (like all rotten photos having a dark background) that no metric would reveal.
lessons.task: Write a one-page data collection protocol for your project: what, where, from whom, device and settings, target count per class, metadata fields and consent. Then write a labelling guide with definitions and two borderline cases per class. If you can, label 50 items with a friend and compute Cohen's kappa.

quiz.q: Two labellers agree on 160 of 200 items, and chance agreement pe is 0.50. What is Cohen's kappa?
Which set should be used to choose hyperparameters?
options: Any set, it does not matter
quiz.explain: Tune on validation; touch the test set only once at the end.

quiz.q: Two photos of the same mango end up, one in training and one in test. What is this?
quiz.explain: Split by mango ID (group) to keep related samples together.

quiz.q: Why keep raw data untouched and clean with scripts?
options: Scripts are faster to read than data
So cleaning can be rerun, described and corrected without losing the original
Because raw data is never needed
quiz.explain: Reproducible cleaning and an untouched original protect the work.

quiz.q: A 3,000-image dataset is split 70/15/15. How many images are in the test set?

lessons.title: Building the System (Project Track)
lessons.content:
Imagine building a new house in your village. A sensible family does not start with marble floors and a rooftop garden. First comes a solid foundation, walls and a roof, so the family can move in and live. Then they add tiles, paint, a better kitchen and, if money remains, the rooftop garden. If they started with decorations, the monsoon would arrive before the roof. Building software for a final year project follows the same order: a simple version that works end to end first, then improvements in planned steps. This lesson covers turning requirements into an architecture, choosing technologies with reasons, building a minimum viable product, iterating safely with version control and tests, preparing a reliable demo and documenting the system, using Tanvir's campus bus tracker as the running example.

What changes in a final year build: You have built software in labs and assignments, so what is different now? Three things. Scale: several components (mobile apps, server, database, maybe a model) that must work together for months. Real users: people outside your class with real needs and real phones. Evaluation: you must show with evidence that the system solves the problem, not just that it runs. Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) taught the lifecycle; here we apply it with a student team's limited time.

From requirements to a short specification: Start from your interviews and survey (lesson 11). Write functional requirements as short, testable statements: 'The driver app sends the bus location every 5 seconds while a trip is active', 'The student app shows each bus on a map and the estimated arrival time at a selected stop'. Write non-functional requirements with numbers: 'Arrival estimates have median error under 2 minutes', 'The student app opens the map in under 3 seconds on a mid-range phone over 4G', 'The driver app uses less than 5 MB of mobile data per day'. Prioritise them with MoSCoW (lesson 13). Keep the full specification short, a few pages; it is a working tool, not a showpiece. The SRS ideas from deep-cse-4-4-08 apply in compact form.

Architecture first, briefly: Sketch the main components and how data flows between them before writing code. For the bus tracker: the driver app (Android) reads GPS and sends location updates to a server API; the server stores updates in a database and computes arrival estimates; the student app (Android or web) requests bus positions and estimates from the API; an admin page lets the transport office manage routes and stops. Draw this as a simple box-and-arrow diagram, and define the interfaces (API endpoints and data formats) in a short document. This diagram becomes a figure in your methodology or system design chapter.

Choosing technologies with reasons: For every major choice, write one or two reasons tied to requirements or constraints. Android over iOS: almost all drivers and most students in the study use Android phones. A cross-platform framework such as Flutter or React Native: one codebase for driver and student apps, and the team already knows it. A lightweight backend framework and a relational database: simple data, moderate volume, the team's experience. A managed hosting service with a free tier: no budget for servers. Avoid choosing technology for fashion; the board will ask 'why not X?', and 'because it was trendy' is a weak answer. 'Because our requirements are A and B and it handles them with our skills' is strong.

Estimating load and cost, worked: Simple numbers prevent surprises. Each driver phone sends one update every 5 seconds. Over a 12-hour service day that is 12 x 3,600 / 5 = 8,640 updates per bus. Four buses send 4 x 8,640 = 34,560 updates per day. If each update is about 200 bytes including overhead, each driver phone uses about 8,640 x 200 = 1,728,000 bytes, roughly 1.7 MB per day, within the 5 MB requirement, and about 52 MB over 30 days. The server receives about 6.9 MB per day in total, tiny for any database. These numbers go into your design chapter and show the board you thought about feasibility. Real overhead varies with protocol and headers, so measure it later and report the measured value.

Minimum viable product: The minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest version that works end to end for the core use case. For the bus tracker: one driver phone sends location, the server stores the latest point, and the student app shows a dot on a map. No arrival estimates, no login, no admin page. Aim to reach this within the first few weeks of building. An end-to-end MVP exposes integration problems early (network permissions, background location limits, server deployment) when they are cheap to fix, and gives you something real to show your supervisor.

Iterations: After the MVP, grow the system in short iterations of one to three weeks, each with a clear goal tied to requirements: iteration 2, arrival estimates using segment averages; iteration 3, stop selection and notifications; iteration 4, admin page for routes; iteration 5, offline handling and performance tuning. At the end of each iteration, the system should still work end to end. Show it to a few real users when possible; early feedback from five students often changes priorities more than weeks of guessing.

Version control workflow: Use Git from the first line of code, with a remote repository as backup and collaboration point. Keep the main branch always working. Develop each feature on its own branch, merge through a pull request with a quick review, and tag releases at the end of each iteration (v0.1-mvp, v0.2-eta). Tags let you go back to the exact version used in an evaluation, which matters when you write the results chapter. Never commit passwords, API keys or personal data; keep secrets in environment variables or a local configuration file listed in .gitignore.

Code quality habits: You do not need enterprise processes, but a few habits pay off quickly. Use a consistent style and an automatic formatter. Give clear names to variables and functions. Keep functions small. Write short comments explaining why, not what. Remove dead code instead of commenting it out forever. Handle errors visibly: when the network fails, the driver app should queue updates and retry rather than silently lose them. Review each other's code. These habits make the system easier to debug in month seven and easier to explain in the defence.

Testing strategy: Software Testing (deep-cse-5-8) covered testing in depth; here is a practical minimum for a final year project. Unit tests for core logic, especially anything with calculations, such as the arrival estimation function given sample segment times. Integration tests for the API: send a location update, then request the bus position and check it. A few end-to-end checks on real phones before every demo. Field testing in real conditions: ride the bus with the app open, compare predicted and actual arrival times, note where GPS is poor. Record test results; they are evidence for your evaluation chapter.

Security and privacy basics: Even a student system handles real people's data, so a few basics are expected. Use HTTPS for every API call. Require authentication for anything that changes data, such as a driver starting a trip or an admin editing routes, so a random person cannot send fake bus locations. Validate every input on the server: a latitude outside the campus area or a timestamp from next year should be rejected. Store passwords only as salted hashes using a standard library, never as plain text. Give the database the minimum permissions it needs. Computer Security (deep-cse-6-2) covered these ideas; boards often ask 'what stops someone from faking a bus?', and a one-line answer about authenticated drivers and server-side validation is enough to show you thought about it.

Deployment and the demo environment: Your system must run somewhere reliable for the field test and the defence. Deploy the server early, ideally by the MVP stage, so deployment problems do not surprise you at the end. Keep a written deployment checklist: environment variables, database migration, how to restart. For the defence, prepare a stable demo: a frozen release, test accounts, sample data, and a backup recorded video of the full flow in case the internet or the venue's projector fails. Lesson 23 discusses demo preparation further.

Documentation: At minimum: a README explaining what the system does, how to install and run each component, and how to configure it; an architecture diagram; API documentation listing endpoints, parameters and examples; a short user guide for drivers and students, in Bangla if they prefer; and a list of known limitations. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-15, -16) covered READMEs and API docs. Good documentation also lets your department or a future student continue the project, which boards appreciate.

Evaluating a built system: A project must show that the system meets its requirements and solves the problem. Map each important requirement to a measurement: arrival error measured on 50 trips against a naive baseline, app load time measured on three phone models, data usage measured over a week, usability measured with SUS and task success rates. Lessons 18 to 20 show how to compute and present these. A project that only shows screenshots, without measured evidence, usually scores lower.

Real-life example 1, Tanvir's build: Tanvir reached the MVP in week 4: one bus dot moving on a map. Integration problems appeared immediately: Android killed the driver app in the background after a few minutes, so he switched to a foreground service with a visible notification, which drivers also preferred because they could see tracking was active. Iteration 2 added segment-average arrival estimates; unit tests with recorded trips caught a bug where estimates went negative near stops. He tagged v0.5 for the field test and kept that exact version running for the four evaluation weeks.

Real-life example 2, the mango app as a build: Even in the research-style mango thesis, Nusrat and Rafi had a build part: the offline Android app. They defined its requirements (classify a photo in under one second on a low-cost phone, work without internet, show the result in Bangla and English), built an MVP that ran the model on one stored image, then added the camera, result screen and a simple history. Measuring on-device inference time on three phones became part of their results for RQ3.

Common mistakes: Starting with the fanciest features. Choosing technology because it is trendy. No architecture sketch, so components do not fit. Building everything before testing any of it together. No version control, or committing secrets. Deploying for the first time the night before the defence. No tests for core calculations. Screenshots instead of measured evaluation. No README, so even the team cannot set it up again in six months.

Recap: Turn requirements into short testable statements with numbers, sketch the architecture and interfaces, choose technologies with reasons, and estimate load and cost with simple arithmetic (8,640 updates per bus per day, about 1.7 MB per driver phone). Build an end-to-end MVP early, grow it in short iterations, use Git with branches, reviews and release tags, keep code quality habits, test core logic and the API and in the field, deploy early, prepare a frozen demo with a backup video, document the system, and evaluate it against its requirements. Next lesson: running experiments for thesis-style work.
key_points: A final year build differs from lab work in scale, real users and the need for evidence that it solves the problem.
Write short, testable functional and non-functional requirements with numbers, prioritised with MoSCoW.
Sketch the architecture and define interfaces before coding; choose each technology with reasons tied to requirements.
Simple load and cost estimates (8,640 updates per bus per day, about 1.7 MB per phone) show feasibility; measure the real values later.
Build an end-to-end MVP early, then grow it in short iterations that keep the system working.
Use Git with feature branches, reviews and release tags; never commit secrets; test core logic, the API and in the field.
Deploy early, freeze a demo version with a backup video, write a README and docs, and evaluate the system against its requirements.
lessons.tip: Write the defence answer to 'why did you choose this technology?' in one sentence for each major choice now. If the only reason you can write is popularity, reconsider the choice while it is still cheap.
lessons.task: For your project (or the bus tracker), write five functional and three non-functional requirements with numbers, draw a box-and-arrow architecture diagram, define one API endpoint with its request and response, and describe your MVP in three sentences. Estimate one load or cost number with simple arithmetic.

quiz.q: What is a minimum viable product in a final year project?
options: The smallest version that works end to end for the core use case
A version with every planned feature
quiz.explain: An end-to-end MVP exposes integration problems early.

quiz.q: A phone sends one update every 10 seconds for 10 hours. How many updates is that?
Which is the strongest reason for choosing a technology?
options: It meets our requirements and matches the team's skills
It has the most stars online
quiz.explain: Choices should be justified by requirements and constraints.

quiz.q: Why tag releases in Git at the end of each iteration?
options: To return to the exact version used in an evaluation or demo
quiz.explain: Tags tie results to the precise code that produced them.

quiz.q: What is the best demo preparation for the defence?
options: Deploy for the first time on the morning of the defence
A frozen release with test accounts, sample data and a backup video
quiz.explain: A stable version plus a backup video protects against failures.

lessons.title: Running Experiments (Thesis Track)
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to know whether a new fertiliser really makes rice grow better. You put it on one field and get a bigger harvest. Proof? Not yet. Maybe that field had better soil, more sun or less pest damage that season. A careful farmer tests both fertilisers on similar plots, side by side, in the same season, several times, and compares the average. That is an experiment, and the same logic applies to computing theses. Claiming 'our model achieved 91 percent accuracy' means little unless you compare it fairly with a baseline, change one thing at a time, repeat runs and record everything. This lesson covers how to run experiments that a board will trust.

What an experiment is in a thesis: An experiment is a planned test that changes something on purpose (the independent variable, such as the model, a feature or a setting) and measures the effect on an outcome (the dependent variable, such as F1 score, latency or error) while keeping everything else the same (controlled variables). Lesson 11 introduced these terms. In machine learning and systems theses, experiments usually compare methods, configurations or conditions on fixed data with fixed metrics.

Baseline first: Before running your fancy method, run something simple. A baseline is a reference point that tells you whether your method adds anything. Good baselines include: a trivial baseline (always predict the majority class, or predict average travel time); a classical method (colour histogram features plus an SVM, or logistic regression on TF-IDF features for text); and a well-known existing method from the literature. If your deep model gets 88 percent accuracy and the majority baseline already gets 50 percent while the SVM gets 85 percent, your real contribution is 3 points over a classical method, which is honest and still meaningful. Without baselines, numbers float in the air.

Why run the baseline early: Running baselines in the first weeks of experimentation has several benefits. It tests your whole pipeline (data loading, splits, metric code) on something simple, so bugs appear early. It tells you how hard the problem is. And if the baseline is already excellent, you learn early that the problem may be too easy, giving time to adjust your research question. Many students discover these things only in the last month.

Change one thing at a time: When comparing, change only the variable you are studying. If model B uses a bigger image size, more epochs and a different augmentation than model A, and it wins, you do not know why. Fix image size, training budget, data splits and preprocessing across all models, unless the difference is the thing being studied. Write a small table of settings for each experiment so differences are visible.

Ablation studies: When your method has several parts, an ablation study removes or turns off one part at a time to see how much each contributes. For the mango thesis, suppose the full pipeline uses a pretrained model, data augmentation and a lighting-correction step. Train four versions: full; without augmentation; without lighting correction; without pretraining. If removing lighting correction drops F1 from 0.85 to 0.78 while removing augmentation drops it only to 0.84, lighting correction is the important part. Ablations turn 'it works' into 'here is why it works', which boards value highly.

Hyperparameter tuning, honestly: Hyperparameters are settings you choose rather than learn: learning rate, batch size, number of layers, regularisation strength. Tune them using the validation set only, never the test set. Use a sensible search: a small grid or random search over a few values, with the same budget for every method. If you tune your own method for days but use default settings for the baselines, the comparison is unfair. Record every configuration tried, not just the best one.

Random seeds and repeated runs: Training involves randomness: weight initialisation, data shuffling, augmentation, dropout. Run the same experiment twice with different random seeds and you may get noticeably different results. One run is one sample. Run each important configuration several times, typically 3 to 5 seeds when compute allows, and report the mean and standard deviation. Fix and record the seeds so others can reproduce your numbers.

Mean and standard deviation, worked: Model A over five seeds gives macro F1 scores of 0.84, 0.86, 0.83, 0.87 and 0.85. The mean is (0.84 + 0.86 + 0.83 + 0.87 + 0.85) / 5 = 4.25 / 5 = 0.85. The differences from the mean are -0.01, 0.01, -0.02, 0.02 and 0. Their squares are 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0004, 0.0004 and 0, summing to 0.001. The sample standard deviation divides by n - 1 = 4: 0.001 / 4 = 0.00025, and the square root is about 0.016. So you report 0.85 plus or minus 0.016. Model B gives 0.82, 0.81, 0.84, 0.83 and 0.80, mean 0.82 with the same standard deviation, about 0.016. A's mean is 0.03 higher and the spreads are small, which suggests a real difference; lesson 19 shows how to test this properly. If B's single best run (0.84) had been compared with A's single worst run (0.83), you would have drawn the wrong conclusion.

The experiment log: Keep a log of every run: date, code version (Git commit), dataset version and split, configuration (model, hyperparameters, seed), hardware, training time, results on validation and test, and a short note ('loss exploded after epoch 12, lowered learning rate'). Use a spreadsheet, a simple CSV written automatically by your script, or an experiment tracking tool (lesson 17). The log protects you from the classic disaster of a great result you cannot reproduce, and it gives you the exact numbers and settings for the methodology and results chapters.

Compute budget, worked: Plan your compute like money. Suppose one training run takes about 40 minutes on a free cloud GPU. Final experiments: 3 models x 5 seeds = 15 runs, 15 x 40 = 600 minutes, which is 10 GPU hours. Tuning: 3 models x 8 configurations x 1 seed = 24 runs, 24 x 40 = 960 minutes, 16 GPU hours. Total about 26 GPU hours, plus ablations. Free cloud notebook services usually have session time limits and usage limits that change over time, so check the current limits, save checkpoints often, and spread runs over days. If the budget is too big, reduce image size for tuning, tune on a subset, or use fewer configurations. Your university lab or a supervisor's research machine may also be available; ask early.

Sanity checks: Before trusting results, run quick checks that catch bugs. Can the model overfit a tiny subset of 20 images to nearly 100 percent training accuracy? If not, something is broken in the pipeline. Does performance with shuffled labels drop to chance level? If not, there is leakage. Are predictions not all the same class? Does the confusion matrix make sense? Do numbers change when you change something that should matter, and stay the same when you change something that should not? These checks take an hour and can save weeks.

Pilot runs: Before launching a big batch of runs, do a pilot: one short run of each configuration for a couple of epochs on a small subset. The pilot catches crashes, wrong paths, out-of-memory errors and absurd settings in minutes instead of discovering them after ten hours of compute. It also gives you the real time per run, which you need for the compute budget. Think of it as a rehearsal before the actual performance.

Experiments with people: Some experiments compare conditions using human participants, for example two versions of the bus app interface. In a between-subjects design, each participant uses only one version; you need more people, but there is no learning effect. In a within-subjects design, each participant uses both versions; you need fewer people, but they may do better on the second version simply because they learned the task. The standard fix is counterbalancing: half the participants use version A first and B second, the other half use B first and A second. Give everyone the same tasks, the same instructions and the same device, and record time, success and errors per task. HCI (deep-cse-5-5) covered user study design in more depth.

When to stop experimenting: Experiments can go on forever: one more model, one more setting. Stop when your research questions are answered with fair comparisons, repeated runs and the analyses you promised, or when your plan's experiment window closes. Use the remaining time for analysis and writing. A thesis with three well-run, well-analysed experiments beats one with fifteen half-finished ones. Freeze the final configuration, run the final test set evaluation once, and record that date in your log.

The test set, used once: Throughout development, look only at validation results. When all choices are fixed, evaluate each final model on the test set once and report those numbers. If you look at test results, change something and test again, your test set slowly becomes a second validation set and your final numbers become optimistic. If you must revisit, say so honestly in the thesis.

Real-life example 1, the mango experiments: Nusrat and Rafi ran the majority baseline (50 percent accuracy, since fresh was half the data) and an SVM on colour histograms (macro F1 0.71) in week one of experiments. Then they compared MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0 and a small custom CNN, each with the same 224 x 224 inputs, the same augmentation, 30 epochs and 5 seeds, tuned on validation with the same 8-configuration budget. MobileNetV2 achieved 0.85 plus or minus 0.016. An ablation showed lighting correction mattered most. Their log of 64 runs let them answer every board question about settings.

Real-life example 2, a system experiment: Tanvir's experiments were about arrival estimation. His independent variable was the method: naive distance divided by average speed versus segment averages built from three weeks of data. Controlled: the same fourth-week test trips, the same stops, the same error metric. He also checked a condition variable, peak versus off-peak hours. Each method is deterministic, so instead of random seeds he repeated the analysis across 50 separate trips and reported median and 90th percentile error.

Common mistakes: No baseline, or only a weak one. Changing several things at once. Tuning only your own method. Tuning on the test set. One run per configuration, reporting the best seed. No log, so results cannot be reproduced. Ignoring sanity checks until a reviewer spots leakage. Running out of compute in the last month. Never stopping, then having no time to write.

Recap: Run baselines first, from trivial to classical to literature methods. Change one variable at a time, and use ablations to show why your method works. Tune only on validation with equal budgets. Repeat runs with recorded seeds and report mean and standard deviation (for example 0.85 plus or minus 0.016). Log every run with code and data versions. Plan the compute budget (about 26 GPU hours in the example), run sanity checks, use the test set once, and stop when the research questions are answered. Next lesson: tools and reproducibility.
key_points: An experiment changes an independent variable, measures a dependent variable and controls everything else.
Run baselines first (trivial, classical, existing methods); they test the pipeline and give results meaning.
Change one thing at a time; ablation studies remove one component at a time to show what really matters.
Tune hyperparameters on validation only and give every method the same tuning budget.
Repeat runs with recorded seeds and report mean and standard deviation, for example five runs averaging 0.85 with SD about 0.016.
Log every run with code version, data split, configuration, seed, hardware, time and results.
Plan compute in GPU hours, run sanity checks (overfit a tiny subset, shuffled labels), use the test set once and stop when RQs are answered.
lessons.tip: Make your training script append one line to a CSV log automatically at the end of every run. Manual logging is the first habit to break under deadline pressure; automatic logging never forgets.
lessons.task: Design the experiment plan for your thesis: list your baselines, the independent, dependent and controlled variables, one ablation, the number of seeds, and estimate the compute budget in GPU hours from the time of one run. Then write the column headers for your experiment log.

quiz.q: Three runs give F1 scores 0.80, 0.82 and 0.84. What is the mean?
What is an ablation study?
options: Removing or disabling one component at a time to measure its contribution
quiz.explain: Ablations show which parts of a method matter.

quiz.q: Why run several seeds per configuration?
options: Because training is random, so one run is a single noisy sample
quiz.explain: Mean and standard deviation over seeds show typical performance and variability.

quiz.q: A sanity check: your model cannot reach high training accuracy even on 20 images. What does this suggest?
options: There is probably a bug in the pipeline
The test set is too large
quiz.explain: A working pipeline should overfit a tiny subset easily.

quiz.q: 15 runs of 40 minutes plus 24 runs of 40 minutes need how many GPU hours?
quiz.explain: 39 runs x 40 minutes = 1,560 minutes = 26 hours.

lessons.title: Tools and Reproducibility
lessons.content:
Imagine your grandmother makes a perfect pitha every winter. One year she is unwell and asks you to make it. You remember it had rice flour, date molasses and coconut, but how much of each? How long did she soak the rice? Which pan? Without the exact recipe, your pitha is different, and nobody knows why. Many final year students face the same problem with their own work. In month three they get a great result, and in month eight, when writing the results chapter, they cannot reproduce it: the code changed, a library updated, the data was re-split, and nobody remembers the settings. Reproducibility means writing down the recipe so precisely that you, your teammate or an examiner can cook the same dish again. This lesson covers the tools and habits that make your work reproducible and safe.

What reproducibility means: A result is reproducible if someone can take your code, data and instructions and get the same numbers (or numbers within the expected random variation). This is a basic expectation in science and engineering. In a thesis it matters for three practical reasons: you will need to rerun experiments after fixing a bug or for a reviewer's request; your supervisor or examiner may ask to see a result produced live; and future students or readers can build on your work only if they can run it.

Version control with Git: Git records every change to your code with a message, so you can see what changed, when and why, and go back to any earlier state. Use it from day one, commit small logical changes often, write clear messages, and push to a remote repository (GitHub, GitLab or a university server) at least daily. Tag important versions: the version used for the proposal demo, the final experiment version, the version submitted with the thesis. Lesson 05 covered branches and reviews for teams; even a solo student should use Git.

What goes in Git and what does not: Put in Git: source code, configuration files, small sample data, scripts for data processing and plotting, the environment file, documentation and the thesis source if you write in LaTeX. Keep out of Git: large datasets, trained model files, personal data, passwords and API keys, temporary outputs. List them in a .gitignore file. Large files go to cloud storage or a university drive, with their location and checksums recorded in the repository so you know exactly which version you used.

A clear folder structure: Agree on a simple structure early, for example: data/raw (never edited), data/processed (made by scripts), src (code), configs (experiment settings), notebooks (exploration), results (logs, tables, figures), models (saved checkpoints, not in Git), docs, and thesis. A clear structure means anyone can find anything, and scripts can use fixed relative paths. Students who keep files named final.py, final2.py and final_new_really.py on the desktop always lose time.

Environments and pinned versions: Code that works today may break in six months because a library changed. Record the exact versions of everything you use. In Python, a requirements.txt file with pinned versions (for example numpy==1.26.4) or an environment file for conda does this; other languages have similar lock files. Use a virtual environment per project, so projects do not interfere. Record the language version, the operating system and the GPU type in your README. For the thesis, list the main versions in the experimental setup section.

Notebooks versus scripts: Jupyter notebooks and cloud notebooks are great for exploration: looking at data, trying ideas, quick plots. But they are risky for final experiments: cells can be run out of order, hidden state can make results impossible to reproduce, and they are awkward to review in Git. A good pattern is to explore in notebooks, then move the working code into scripts or modules that run from top to bottom with one command, such as python train.py --config configs/mobilenet.yaml. Before trusting any notebook result, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top.

Configuration files: Instead of editing numbers inside the code for each experiment, put settings in configuration files: model name, image size, learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, seed, data split file. Each experiment is then one configuration file plus one code version, and both can be logged. This makes it easy to see exactly how two runs differed and to rerun any of them.

Seeds and determinism: Set random seeds for every library you use (the language's random module, numerical libraries, the deep learning framework) at the start of each run, and record them. Be aware that some GPU operations are not fully deterministic even with fixed seeds, so small differences can remain. That is another reason to report mean and standard deviation over several seeds (lesson 16), rather than claiming one exact number.

Experiment tracking: An experiment log can be as simple as a CSV file that your training script appends to automatically: run ID, date, Git commit hash, config file, seed, dataset version, training time, validation metrics and test metrics if final. Dedicated experiment tracking tools exist (some free for students or open source) that also store plots and model files, but a well-kept CSV is enough for most BSc theses. What matters is that every reported number can be traced back to a specific code version and configuration.

The 3-2-1 backup rule: A widely used backup rule says: keep at least 3 copies of important data, on at least 2 different types of storage, with at least 1 copy offsite. For a thesis: copy 1 on your laptop, copy 2 on an external drive or a teammate's computer, copy 3 in cloud storage. Code is covered by Git plus the remote. Data and models need explicit backups. Test that you can restore from the backup at least once; an untested backup is only a hope.

Backup sizes, worked: Estimate what you must store. The mango team has about 3,000 raw photos at around 2.5 MB each: 3,000 x 2.5 = 7,500 MB, about 7.5 GB. The processed 224 x 224 images at about 20 KB each take 3,000 x 20 KB = 60,000 KB, about 60 MB. Each trained small model is around 10 to 20 MB; keeping the final checkpoint of 15 runs at about 14 MB each is 15 x 14 = 210 MB. Total under 8 GB, which fits on most free or cheap cloud plans and any external drive. Doing this sum early tells you whether free storage is enough or you need the department's help.

Writing tools: LaTeX and Word: Many CSE departments provide a LaTeX template for the thesis, often used through Overleaf, an online LaTeX editor that supports collaboration and version history. LaTeX handles numbering of chapters, figures, tables and equations automatically, produces consistent formatting and works smoothly with BibTeX references. Word or Google Docs are easier to start with and fine if your department accepts them; use built-in heading styles, automatic captions and cross-references rather than typing numbers by hand. Pick one tool for the whole team early and stick to it.

Reference managers and BibTeX: A reference manager such as Zotero stores your papers, notes and citation details, and can export a BibTeX file for LaTeX or insert citations directly into Word. This means your reference list is generated automatically in IEEE or APA style, and adding or removing a citation renumbers everything correctly. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-22) covered citation styles; the point here is to start the library on day one so you never retype a reference.

One command for the whole pipeline: As the project grows, the steps multiply: clean data, split, train each model, evaluate, make tables, make figures. Write a single top-level script (for example run_all.sh, a Makefile or a small Python driver) that runs these steps in order. Then the figures and tables in your thesis come straight from the logs by script, not by copying numbers by hand into Word, which is where many typos in results tables come from. If a bug is fixed in month eight, one command regenerates every table and figure consistently.

Hardware and field records: Not everything lives in code. For hardware projects, keep a wiring diagram, a parts list with model numbers and suppliers, photos of each build stage and the firmware version flashed on each device. For field work, keep dated notes of conditions: weather, lighting, which phone, which market, any problems. These records play the same role as Git and the experiment log: they let you explain and repeat what you did, and they become figures and appendix material in the thesis.

A reproducibility checklist: Before you write the results chapter, check: Is all code committed and pushed, with the final version tagged? Is the environment file complete with pinned versions? Are dataset versions, splits and their locations recorded with checksums? Does every reported number have a log entry with commit and config? Can a teammate, starting from a fresh clone, run one command to reproduce the main table? Are backups current and tested? Is there a README explaining how to run everything? If yes to all, your work is in good shape.

Real-life example 1, saved by the log: In month seven, the board at a progress presentation asked Nusrat and Rafi why their reported MobileNet F1 had changed from 0.83 to 0.85 since the last presentation. Their experiment log showed the change came from the corrected labels after the second agreement check, with the commit hash and date. They reran the old configuration on the old labels in front of their supervisor the next day and got 0.83 again. The question turned into a demonstration of careful work.

Real-life example 2, a laptop disaster avoided: In month nine, Tanvir's laptop would not start after a power surge during load-shedding. His code was on the remote repository, his GPS dataset was in cloud storage and on a pen drive, and his thesis was on Overleaf. He borrowed a computer, cloned the repository, recreated the environment from the requirements file and continued the same evening. A classmate in another group, with everything only on one laptop, lost three weeks rebuilding.

Common mistakes: No version control, or committing once a month. Datasets and secrets in Git. No environment file, so code breaks after updates. Final results produced in a notebook run out of order. Hard-coded settings edited by hand for each run. No backups, or untested backups. Different team members using different writing tools. Typing references by hand.

Recap: Reproducibility is writing the recipe precisely. Use Git with a remote, tags and a clean .gitignore; a clear folder structure; pinned environments; scripts for final runs and notebooks only for exploration; configuration files; recorded seeds; an automatic experiment log; the 3-2-1 backup rule with tested restores (about 8 GB for the mango thesis); one shared writing tool such as Overleaf or Word with styles; and a reference manager. Run the reproducibility checklist before writing results. Next lesson: choosing and computing evaluation metrics.
key_points: Reproducibility means someone can rerun your code with your data and instructions and get the same results within random variation.
Use Git from day one with a remote, small clear commits and tags for key versions; keep data, models and secrets out with .gitignore.
Keep a clear folder structure and pin library versions in an environment or requirements file.
Explore in notebooks, but run final experiments as scripts with configuration files and recorded seeds.
Log every run automatically with commit hash, config, seed, dataset version and metrics.
Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies, 2 storage types, 1 offsite; test restoring at least once.
Choose one writing tool for the team (Overleaf/LaTeX or Word with styles) and a reference manager like Zotero from day one.
lessons.tip: Once a month, ask a teammate to clone your repository on a different computer and reproduce one key number using only the README. Every question they ask is a missing line in your documentation.
lessons.task: Set up (or sketch) your project's repository: write the folder structure, a .gitignore list, a pinned requirements file with your main libraries, and the columns of your experiment log. Then estimate your total data, model and document storage in GB and write your 3-2-1 backup plan.

quiz.q: Which of these should NOT be committed to Git?
quiz.explain: Secrets must stay out of version control; use environment variables or ignored local files.

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
options: 3 copies, 2 different storage types, 1 copy offsite
Back up every 3 days, 2 times, 1 hour each
quiz.explain: Multiple copies on different media with one offsite protects against most failures.

quiz.q: Why are notebooks risky for final results?
options: Cells can be run out of order and hidden state can make results irreproducible
quiz.explain: Move final code to scripts, or at least restart and run all cells from the top.

quiz.q: 2,000 raw photos at about 3 MB each need roughly how much storage?
quiz.explain: 2,000 x 3 MB = 6,000 MB, about 6 GB.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of pinning library versions?
options: The same code keeps working the same way later and on other machines
quiz.explain: Library updates can change behaviour; pinned versions keep the environment reproducible.

lessons.title: Evaluation I: Choosing and Computing Metrics
lessons.content:
A cricket selector cannot judge a batsman with one number. Total runs favour players who batted many innings. Average hides whether the runs came against strong or weak teams. Strike rate ignores consistency. A wise selector chooses the numbers that match the role: for an opener in Test cricket, average and balls faced; for a T20 finisher, strike rate. Evaluating a final year project is the same. The metric you choose decides what 'good' means, and a poorly chosen metric can make a weak system look strong or a good system look weak. This lesson shows how to pick metrics that match your research questions and how to compute the common ones by hand: classification metrics from a confusion matrix, regression errors, system latency and throughput, and usability scores.

The metric follows the question: Go back to your research questions and requirements (lesson 09). Each should name what success means. If the mango seller cares most about not missing rotten fruit, recall of the rotten class matters more than overall accuracy. If the bus app must give useful arrival times, error in minutes matters, and large errors may matter more than small ones. If the app must feel fast, the slow cases matter more than the average. Choose one primary metric per research question, decided before you see the results, plus a few secondary ones. Choosing the metric after seeing which one makes you look best is a form of cherry-picking.

The confusion matrix: For classification, everything starts with the confusion matrix, a table of actual classes against predicted classes. For a two-class problem with a 'positive' class (say, rotten) there are four cells. True positives (TP): rotten predicted as rotten. False negatives (FN): rotten predicted as not rotten, missed. False positives (FP): not rotten predicted as rotten, false alarms. True negatives (TN): not rotten predicted as not rotten. Every classification metric is a different way of combining these four numbers.

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total, the share of all predictions that were right. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the items the model called rotten, how many really were. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the truly rotten items, how many the model caught. F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall), the harmonic mean, which is high only when both precision and recall are high. Precision matters when false alarms are costly (throwing away good fruit); recall matters when misses are costly (rotten fruit spreading mould).

Classification metrics, worked: The mango test set has 450 images; treat rotten (135 images) as positive and the rest (315) as negative. The model gets TP = 117, FN = 18, FP = 13, TN = 302. Check: 117 + 18 + 13 + 302 = 450. Accuracy = (117 + 302) / 450 = 419 / 450, about 0.931. Precision = 117 / (117 + 13) = 117 / 130 = 0.90. Recall = 117 / (117 + 18) = 117 / 135, about 0.867. F1 = 2 x 0.90 x 0.867 / (0.90 + 0.867), about 0.883. Interpretation: when the app says rotten, it is right 90 percent of the time, but it misses about 13 percent of rotten mangoes. If misses are costly for sellers, the team might lower the decision threshold to raise recall, accepting more false alarms.

The class imbalance trap: Accuracy can lie when classes are unequal. If 95 percent of samples are negative, a model that always says negative gets 95 percent accuracy and catches nothing. That is why imbalanced problems (fraud, disease, defects, rare events) must report precision, recall and F1 for the minority class, or metrics designed for imbalance. Always report the majority-class baseline next to your accuracy so the reader sees how much better than doing nothing you are.

More than two classes: With several classes, compute precision, recall and F1 for each class, treating it as positive and all others as negative. Then combine. Macro average takes the simple mean of the per-class scores, so every class counts equally, which is good when small classes matter, like semi-rotten. Weighted average weights each class by its number of samples, so large classes dominate. Report per-class results in a table as well; an overall number can hide a class the model almost never gets right.

Thresholds and curves: Many classifiers output a probability, and you choose a threshold (often 0.5) to decide the class. Changing the threshold trades precision against recall. A precision-recall curve or ROC curve shows performance across all thresholds, and the area under the curve summarises it. These are useful in the results chapter, but always also report the metrics at the threshold you actually use in the app, because that is what users experience.

Regression errors: When the output is a number, like arrival time in minutes, use error metrics. Mean absolute error (MAE) is the average of absolute errors: easy to explain, in the same unit as the output. Root mean squared error (RMSE) squares the errors, averages, then takes the square root, so big errors count more. Worked: five trips have errors (predicted minus actual) of 1, -2, 0.5, 3 and -1.5 minutes. MAE = (1 + 2 + 0.5 + 3 + 1.5) / 5 = 8 / 5 = 1.6 minutes. RMSE = square root of ((1 + 4 + 0.25 + 9 + 2.25) / 5) = square root of (16.5 / 5) = square root of 3.3, about 1.82 minutes. RMSE is higher than MAE because the 3-minute error is penalised more. Reporting the median and the 90th percentile of absolute error also tells users how bad the typical and the bad cases are.

System performance metrics: For systems, common metrics are latency (time to respond to one request), throughput (requests handled per second), resource use (memory, CPU, battery, mobile data) and availability (share of time the system works). Measure under realistic conditions: real phones, real networks, realistic load.
