Report the measurement setup, because a latency measured on a lab Wi-Fi with a fast laptop says little about a student on 4G in a bus.

Mean versus median versus p95, worked: Ten requests to the bus API took 120, 130, 125, 140, 135, 128, 132, 900, 126 and 131 milliseconds. The mean is 2,067 / 10 = 206.7 ms, but that is misleading: nine requests took around 120 to 140 ms and one took 900 ms. The median, the middle of the sorted values, is (130 + 131) / 2 = 130.5 ms, a better picture of the typical request. For user experience, engineers also report a high percentile such as p95, the value below which 95 percent of requests fall. With 200 measured requests, sort them and take roughly the 190th value. A p95 of 900 ms means one in twenty users waits almost a second, which matters even if the median is fast. Ten measurements are far too few for reliable percentiles; measure hundreds.

Usability and the SUS score: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a widely used 10-item questionnaire. Each item is answered on a 1 to 5 scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree; odd-numbered items are positive statements and even-numbered items are negative. Scoring: for odd items subtract 1 from the response; for even items subtract the response from 5; add the ten results and multiply by 2.5 to get a score from 0 to 100. Worked: a student answers 4, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 5, 1. Odd items give 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 17; even items give 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 17; total 34 x 2.5 = 85. Average the scores across participants. A score of about 68 is often cited as average across many studies, so 85 suggests good usability. SUS is not a percentage, so do not say '85 percent usable'.

Task-based user metrics: Beyond questionnaires, measure what users actually do on realistic tasks: task success rate (how many completed the task), time on task, number of errors, and how often they needed help. For the bus app: 'find when the next bus reaches the library stop'. Combine these with a few open comments to explain the numbers. User studies need consent (lesson 13) and a fixed task script so every participant gets the same instructions.

Metrics in other kinds of work: Different tasks have their own standard metrics, and boards expect you to use the ones your field uses so results can be compared with the literature. Object detection often uses intersection over union (IoU), the overlap area of the predicted and true boxes divided by the area they cover together, and mean average precision built on it. Machine translation and text generation often report overlap with reference texts using scores such as BLEU, alongside human judgements because overlap scores miss meaning. Search and recommendation use ranking metrics such as precision at k. Energy and IoT projects report battery life, power draw and sensor error against a calibrated reference. Find the standard metrics in your closest related papers (your extraction matrix from lesson 07 already lists them) and explain each in one sentence in your thesis.

Real-life example 1, choosing the mango metrics: For RQ1 Nusrat and Rafi chose macro F1 as primary, because the semi-rotten class was small but important, with per-class precision and recall and model size in MB as secondary metrics. For RQ3 they reported field accuracy on 200 mangoes, the rotten-class recall, on-device inference time (median and p95 over 300 photos on each phone) and a short SUS questionnaire with the five sellers, noting that five participants give only an indication.

Real-life example 2, choosing the bus metrics: Tanvir's primary metric was median absolute arrival error per stop, with MAE, RMSE and the 90th percentile as secondary, because students care about the bad cases. For the system he measured API latency (median and p95 over 1,000 requests from 4G phones) and daily mobile data per driver phone (1.6 MB measured against the 1.7 MB estimate). Usability came from SUS with 15 students (mean 78) and task success on three tasks.

Common mistakes: Reporting only accuracy on imbalanced data. Choosing metrics after seeing results. Mixing up precision and recall. Reporting averages that hide one terrible class. Using the mean latency when a few slow requests dominate. Measuring latency on the developer's laptop. Calling SUS a percentage. Reporting numbers with no baseline or no measurement setup.

Recap: Choose a primary metric per research question before seeing results. Build the confusion matrix and compute accuracy, precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN) and F1 (worked example: 0.931, 0.90, 0.867, 0.883); beware imbalance and report per-class and macro averages. For numeric outputs use MAE and RMSE (1.6 and 1.82 minutes in the example), plus percentiles. For systems report median and p95 latency, throughput and resource use under realistic conditions. For usability compute SUS (85 in the example) and task metrics. Next lesson: comparing fairly and using statistics to judge whether differences are real.
key_points: Choose one primary metric per research question before seeing results; the metric defines what 'good' means.
The confusion matrix has TP, FN, FP and TN; every classification metric combines these four numbers.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 is their harmonic mean; with TP 117, FN 18, FP 13 they are 0.90, 0.867 and 0.883.
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data; report minority-class metrics, per-class tables, macro averages and the majority baseline.
For numeric outputs use MAE and RMSE; RMSE punishes large errors more (1.6 versus 1.82 minutes in the example).
For systems report median and high percentiles such as p95 latency, measured with many requests under realistic conditions.
SUS scores 10 items to give 0 to 100 (85 in the example); about 68 is often cited as average, and it is not a percentage.
lessons.tip: Write your primary metric for each research question in your proposal or in a dated note before running final experiments. It protects you from the temptation, and the accusation, of choosing the metric that flatters your results.
lessons.task: From a confusion matrix of your own (or invent one with 200 test items), compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 by hand and check with a calculator. Then compute MAE and RMSE for five prediction errors of your choice, and score one SUS questionnaire you fill in yourself for an app you use.

quiz.q: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20. What is precision?
Using the same numbers (TP = 40, FN = 20), what is recall?
Errors of 2, -2 and 4 minutes. What is the MAE?
Why report p95 latency in addition to the median?
options: It is always smaller than the median
It replaces the need for many measurements
It shows how slow the worst few percent of requests are, which users notice
quiz.explain: A fast median can hide a slow tail that affects many users.

quiz.q: On a dataset where 95 percent of samples are negative, a model has 95 percent accuracy. What should you check?
options: Recall and precision for the positive class and the majority baseline
quiz.explain: Always predicting negative already gives 95 percent; minority-class metrics reveal the truth.

lessons.title: Evaluation II: Fair Comparison and Statistics
lessons.content:
Two friends argue about who is the better bowler. One took 5 wickets in a match last week; the other took 3. Case closed? Not really. Maybe the first bowled on a cracked pitch against a weak team, while the second bowled on a flat pitch against a strong one. And one match is a tiny sample; next week the numbers could flip. To compare fairly, you would want both to bowl in similar conditions, over many matches, and then ask whether the difference is bigger than normal match-to-match variation. That is exactly what this lesson is about. Lesson 18 showed how to compute metrics. Here we ask: when method A scores 0.85 and method B scores 0.82, is A really better, or is that difference just luck? We cover fair setups, cross-validation, spread and confidence intervals, significance tests, effect size, multiple comparisons and threats to validity.

Why one number is not enough: Every measured result contains noise. A different random seed, a different test split, a different group of users or a different day of traffic gives a slightly different number. If you report one run of A and one run of B, the difference you see mixes the real difference with this noise. Boards increasingly ask 'Is the difference significant?' or 'How stable is this?'. Answering needs repeated measurements and simple statistics. Probability and Statistics (deep-cse-2-6) taught the foundations; here we apply them to thesis evaluation.

Fair comparison first: Statistics cannot fix an unfair setup. Before any test, make sure all methods use exactly the same training data, the same validation and test splits, the same preprocessing, the same metric code, and a similar tuning budget (lesson 16). Report published numbers from other papers only as context, not as direct comparisons, unless the data, splits and protocol are identical. The most common unfair comparison in student theses is a heavily tuned new method against an untuned baseline.

k-fold cross-validation: When data is limited, one fixed test set may be too small or unlucky. k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k equal parts (folds). Each fold takes a turn as the test set while the other k - 1 folds are used for training, so you get k results. With 3,000 images and k = 5, each fold has 3,000 / 5 = 600 test images and 2,400 training images, and every image is tested exactly once. Report the mean and standard deviation over the 5 folds. Use stratified folds to keep class balance and group-based folds (by mango, person or day) to avoid leakage (lesson 14). If you also tune hyperparameters, tune inside the training part of each fold, not on the fold's test part; this is called nested cross-validation when done formally.

Spread: standard deviation and standard error: The standard deviation (SD) describes how much individual runs vary around the mean. The standard error of the mean (SE) = SD / square root of n describes how precisely you know the mean itself, and it shrinks as you add runs. Using the five seeds from lesson 16, mean F1 = 0.85 and SD is about 0.0158, so SE = 0.0158 / square root of 5, about 0.0071.

Confidence intervals, worked: A 95 percent confidence interval (CI) gives a range that, under the method's assumptions, would contain the true mean in 95 percent of repeated studies. For a small number of runs, use the t distribution: CI = mean plus or minus t x SE, where t for 95 percent and n - 1 = 4 degrees of freedom is about 2.776. Margin = 2.776 x 0.0071, about 0.020. So the 95 percent CI is roughly 0.83 to 0.87. If another method's interval lies clearly above or below, the difference is likely real; if intervals overlap a lot, be cautious. Showing error bars or intervals in result tables and charts tells the board you understand uncertainty.

Significance testing in plain words: A significance test asks: if there were really no difference between A and B (the null hypothesis, lesson 09), how surprising would our observed difference be? The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large just by chance, assuming no real difference. A small p-value (commonly below 0.05) means the data would be unusual if H0 were true, so we reject H0. A p-value is not the probability that your method is better, and a large p-value does not prove there is no difference; it may just mean you had too little data.

The paired t-test, worked: When A and B are evaluated on the same folds, compare them fold by fold; this pairing removes the variation caused by easy or hard folds. Per-fold F1 for A: 0.85, 0.83, 0.86, 0.84, 0.87. For B: 0.82, 0.81, 0.84, 0.82, 0.83. Differences: 0.03, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.04. Mean difference = 0.13 / 5 = 0.026. SD of differences is about 0.0089. t = mean difference / (SD / square root of n) = 0.026 / (0.0089 / 2.236), about 6.5, with 4 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is about 0.003, well below 0.05, so the data give strong evidence that A beats B on this dataset. With so few folds, also mention that the test assumes roughly normal differences; non-parametric alternatives such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test exist, and McNemar's test compares two classifiers on the same single test set.

Effect size: practical versus statistical significance: With enough data, even a tiny difference becomes statistically significant. So also report how big the difference is, in the original unit and as an effect size. Here A is 0.026 F1 higher on average, about 2.6 points. A standardised effect size for paired data is the mean difference divided by the SD of differences: 0.026 / 0.0089, about 2.9, which is very large in standardised terms because the folds are so consistent. Then ask the practical question: does 2.6 F1 points matter for the seller? Perhaps it means catching several more rotten mangoes per hundred. Practical significance is a judgement you must argue, not a number the test gives you.

Multiple comparisons: If you compare many pairs or many settings and test each at 0.05, some will look significant by chance. With 10 independent tests and no real differences, the chance of at least one false 'significant' result is 1 - 0.95^10, about 0.40, or 40 percent. Simple remedies: decide your main comparisons in advance, report all comparisons you ran, and use a correction such as Bonferroni, which divides the threshold by the number of tests (0.05 / 10 = 0.005). Testing everything and reporting only the significant ones is p-hacking, a form of misconduct.

A single test set: bootstrap intervals: Sometimes you cannot retrain many times, for example when one training run takes a whole day. You can still show uncertainty for a fixed test set with the bootstrap. Draw a new 'test set' of the same size from your test predictions, sampling with replacement, so some items appear twice and some not at all, and compute the metric. Repeat this 1,000 times, sort the 1,000 values, and take the 25th and 975th values as an approximate 95 percent interval. A few lines of code do this, and it needs no new training. Remember it only captures the uncertainty from which test items you happened to have, not the randomness of training.

How much data is enough: Students often ask how many runs, folds or participants they need. There is no single magic number, but the logic is simple: the smaller the difference you want to detect and the noisier your measurements, the more data you need. Five seeds or five folds are common in BSc theses for model comparisons. For user studies, a small usability study with five to fifteen people can find many problems, but comparing two designs with statistics usually needs more participants. If your data is small, say so, call your findings preliminary, and avoid strong claims. A planned power analysis, covered in Research Methodology, gives a proper number.

Threats to validity: Good theses end their evaluation with an honest section on threats to validity, commonly in four groups. Internal validity: could something other than your method explain the result, such as leakage, a bug, or tuning only your method? Construct validity: do your metrics really measure what you claim, such as using SUS to claim 'speed'? External validity: will results hold for other data, places, devices or users, for example other markets, other mango varieties, other campuses? Conclusion validity: are the statistics sound, with enough data, correct tests and no fishing? For each threat, say what you did to reduce it and what remains.

Reading statistics without overclaiming: Use careful language that matches the evidence. 'On our dataset, MobileNetV2 achieved a higher macro F1 than the custom CNN (0.85 vs 0.82, paired t-test over 5 folds, p about 0.003)' is good. 'Our method is better than all CNNs' is overclaiming. If the difference was not significant, say 'we found no significant difference with 5 folds; a larger study may be needed', not 'the methods are equal'.

Real-life example 1, the mango comparison: The board at Nusrat and Rafi's progress presentation asked whether MobileNetV2 was really better than EfficientNet-B0, since their scores were 0.85 and 0.84. The team ran 5-fold cross-validation with the same folds for both, did a paired t-test and found p about 0.4, not significant. They honestly reported that the two were statistically similar on their data and chose MobileNetV2 for the app because it was smaller and faster on the phone, a practical argument. The board appreciated the honesty more than a forced claim.

Real-life example 2, the bus arrival comparison: Tanvir compared the naive method with segment averages on the same 50 test trips. For each trip he computed the absolute error of both methods at each stop and took the per-trip mean, giving 50 paired differences. Because errors were skewed by a few traffic jams, he used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test instead of a t-test, reported the median improvement of 1.4 minutes with its p-value, and listed threats: only one campus, only four weeks, no rainy-season data.

Common mistakes: Comparing single runs. Comparing to numbers copied from papers with different setups. Tuning on test folds. Reporting only significant results. Treating p below 0.05 as proof of large, important effects. Treating p above 0.05 as proof of no difference. No error bars. No threats to validity section, which boards often ask about directly.

Recap: Make the setup fair first: same data, splits, preprocessing, metric code and tuning budget. Use k-fold cross-validation (5 folds of 600 test images for 3,000 images) or repeated seeds, and report mean, SD and confidence intervals (about 0.83 to 0.87 in the example). Use paired tests on paired results (t about 6.5, p about 0.003 in the example), report effect sizes and practical meaning, control multiple comparisons (10 tests give about a 40 percent chance of a false alarm), discuss threats to internal, construct, external and conclusion validity, and phrase claims to match the evidence. Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7) goes deeper. Next lesson: analysing and presenting results.
key_points: Every result contains noise; one run per method cannot show whether a difference is real.
Fair comparison first: same data, splits, preprocessing, metric code and tuning budget for all methods.
k-fold cross-validation tests every sample once (3,000 images, 5 folds: 600 test each); use stratified, group-based folds.
Report mean, standard deviation and confidence intervals; five runs with mean 0.85 and SD 0.016 give a 95 percent CI of about 0.83 to 0.87.
A p-value is the chance of a difference this large if there were no real difference; it is not the chance your method is better.
Use paired tests for paired results (fold differences 0.03, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.04 give t about 6.5, p about 0.003) and report effect size and practical meaning.
Control multiple comparisons (10 tests at 0.05 give about a 40 percent false-alarm chance) and discuss internal, construct, external and conclusion validity.
lessons.tip: For every comparison sentence in your results chapter, check that it states the data, the metric, the size of the difference and the evidence (runs, test, p-value or interval). If any piece is missing, the sentence is a claim, not a result.
lessons.task: Take two sets of five scores (from your own experiments, or invent them for two methods on the same five folds). Compute each method's mean and SD, the 95 percent CI for one method using t = 2.776, and the paired t statistic for the differences. Then write one honest results sentence and list one threat to each of the four validity types.

quiz.q: With 2,000 samples and 5-fold cross-validation, how many test samples are in each fold?
quiz.explain: 2,000 / 5 = 400 test samples per fold.

quiz.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean?
options: If there were no real difference, a difference this large would appear about 3 percent of the time by chance
There is a 97 percent chance your method is better
The experiment has a 3 percent error
quiz.explain: The p-value is computed assuming H0 is true; it is not the probability that H1 is true.

quiz.q: Why use a paired test when two methods are evaluated on the same folds?
options: It removes the need for a baseline
It compares fold by fold, removing variation due to easy or hard folds
It is the only test that exists
quiz.explain: Pairing focuses the test on the differences between methods.

quiz.q: You run 10 independent tests at the 0.05 level with no real effects. Roughly how likely is at least one false 'significant' result?
Your results hold on two Rajshahi markets but may not hold in Sylhet with other varieties. Which validity threat is this?
quiz.explain: External validity concerns generalising beyond the studied setting.

lessons.title: Analysing and Presenting Results
lessons.content:
A doctor gets your blood test report: twenty numbers in a table. A bad doctor reads them out and sends you home. A good doctor looks for the numbers outside the normal range, connects them ('your iron is low and you feel tired, so these fit together'), checks whether a strange value might be a lab mistake, and finally tells you clearly what it means and what to do. Your results chapter needs the same doctor. Numbers from lesson 18 and comparisons from lesson 19 are the raw report. Analysis turns them into understanding: what happened, why it happened, where the system fails, what it means for your research questions, and what it does not mean. This lesson covers how to analyse results deeply and present them honestly and clearly.

Results versus discussion: Many theses separate two jobs. Results report what you found, factually: tables, figures, numbers, test outcomes, without much interpretation. Discussion interprets: why the results look like this, how they compare with related work, what they mean for the problem, and their limitations. Some departments combine them into one chapter called 'Results and Discussion', which is fine, but keep the two kinds of sentences clear in your mind. 'MobileNetV2 achieved a macro F1 of 0.85' is a result. 'This is probably because pretraining on large image collections helps with small datasets' is discussion, and should be signalled with words like 'probably' or 'suggests'.

Organise results by research question: The clearest structure follows your research questions in order. Section 5.1 answers RQ1, section 5.2 answers RQ2, and so on. Each section starts with one sentence reminding the reader of the question, then the experiment setup in brief (pointing to the methodology chapter for details), then the main table or figure, then a few sentences reading the key numbers, then a direct answer. This alignment, planned back in lesson 09, makes it easy for examiners to see that every question was answered.

Tables and figures recap: Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-10) covered how to make good tables and figures; here is the short version for results. Use tables when readers need exact numbers, such as the main comparison of methods with mean and standard deviation. Use figures for patterns: training curves, error distributions, a confusion matrix heat map, latency over load. Number and caption every table and figure so it can be understood alone, label axes with units, mark the best result clearly but honestly, and refer to each one in the text before it appears. Every figure should make one point; say that point in the caption or the first sentence about it.

Read the numbers for the reader: Never drop a table and move on. Tell the reader what to notice. A good paragraph after the main table says: which method was best and by how much, whether the difference was significant, which result was surprising, and how this answers the question. For example: 'Table 5.2 shows that MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0 performed similarly (macro F1 0.85 and 0.84, p about 0.4), both clearly above the SVM baseline (0.71). The custom CNN was lowest among deep models (0.82).' The reader should never have to guess what you want them to see.

Per-class and per-condition breakdown: Averages hide the interesting parts. Break results down by class, by condition and by subgroup. For the mango detector, per-class F1 was fresh 0.92, semi-rotten 0.74 and rotten 0.88; the macro average is (0.92 + 0.74 + 0.88) / 3, about 0.85. The breakdown immediately shows that the middle class is the hard one, which is where the discussion and future work should focus. For the bus tracker, breaking errors down by peak versus off-peak hours and by route showed that most large errors came from one route during the evening rush.

Error analysis: Error analysis means looking at actual failures, not just counting them. Collect the wrong predictions (or the worst cases), look at each one, and sort them into categories by cause. This is slow, but it is often the most insightful part of a thesis, and examiners love it because it proves you understand your system. Show a few example failures as images, logs or screenshots, with short explanations.

Error analysis, worked: The model missed 18 rotten mangoes on the test set (the false negatives from lesson 18). Nusrat and Rafi looked at all 18 photos and grouped them: 8 were photographed in dim light, 5 were at a very early stage of rotting with only a small spot, 3 were blurry, and 2 turned out to be labelling mistakes where the mango was not really rotten. As shares: 8 / 18 is about 44 percent, 5 / 18 about 28 percent, 3 / 18 about 17 percent, and 2 / 18 about 11 percent. This gave three concrete lessons: lighting matters most (matching the ablation in lesson 16), early rot is genuinely hard and may need a different camera angle or closer photos, and a quick blur check in the app could ask the user to retake a photo. The 2 label errors were also reported honestly.

Explaining why: After describing what happened, offer explanations, carefully. Good explanations connect to evidence: the ablation, the error categories, the data distribution, known properties of the methods from the literature. 'The custom CNN likely underperformed because it was trained from scratch on only 2,100 images, while the pretrained models start from features learned on large image collections; this is consistent with findings in [12] and [15].' If you cannot test an explanation, present it as a possibility, and if you can test it quickly, do so.

Negative and unexpected results: Sometimes your method does not beat the baseline, or a result goes the opposite way from your hypothesis. This is not automatically a failure of the thesis. A clearly reported negative result, with a fair setup and a thoughtful analysis of why, is a real contribution, because it tells others what does not work and under which conditions. What fails a thesis is hiding or twisting such results. Report them, investigate them (is there a bug? did the data differ?), and explain them. Many good theses include a sentence like 'Contrary to our hypothesis, data augmentation did not improve results; error analysis suggests that...'.

Comparing with related work: In the discussion, place your results among the papers from your literature review. Be careful: direct number comparison is only fair if the data and protocol match (lesson 19). Otherwise compare qualitatively: 'Unlike [8], which used lab photos with a white background, our images come from real markets; our lower accuracy partly reflects this harder setting, but the model works on phones offline.' This shows the examiner that you understand where your work fits.

Presenting system and user results: Project-track theses need results too, not only screenshots. Report what you measured against each requirement: a table with each non-functional requirement, its target, the measured value and pass or fail (for example 'ETA response under 1 second: target p95 under 1,000 ms, measured p95 620 ms, pass'). Summarise test results from your testing work (number of test cases, how many passed, defects found and fixed). For user studies, report the number of participants and who they were, task success rates, times, SUS mean and spread, and a few short quotes that explain the numbers. Keep personal details out; refer to participants as P1, P2 and so on.

Keep a results notebook while writing: As you analyse, keep a simple document listing every number that will appear in the thesis, where it came from (log entry or script) and the date. When a number changes because you fixed a bug, update it once there and regenerate the tables with your pipeline script (lesson 17). This prevents the classic problem of the abstract, results chapter and slides showing three different versions of the same number.

Honest limitations: Every study has limits; listing them honestly is a sign of maturity, not weakness. Common limitations: small or local data, a short time window, few participants, one device type, simulated rather than real conditions, untested parts of the system. For each, say how it might affect the conclusions and what would address it. Keep this connected to the threats to validity from lesson 19. Examiners often ask 'What are the limitations of your work?' in the viva; a good limitations section has already answered it.

Avoiding overclaiming: Match the strength of every claim to the strength of the evidence. Say 'on our dataset' and 'in our test conditions'. Use 'suggests' for discussion, 'shows' for direct results. Avoid words like 'proves', 'perfect', 'always', 'state of the art' unless truly justified. Do not generalise from five sellers to all of Bangladesh, or from one campus to all universities. Overclaiming is one of the fastest ways to lose an examiner's trust; careful language earns it.

Answering the research questions explicitly: End each results section, and then the conclusion chapter, with direct answers. 'RQ1: Among the tested lightweight models, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0 gave the best macro F1 (0.85 and 0.84), with no significant difference between them; both clearly outperformed the classical baseline. RQ2: ... RQ3: ...' A table with each research question, the short answer and the section where the evidence lives is a neat way to close the chapter.

Real-life example 1, the mango results chapter: Nusrat and Rafi's chapter 5 had three sections for RQ1 to RQ3. RQ1 had the main comparison table with mean and SD over five folds, the significance test results, the per-class table and the ablation table. Error analysis showed the 18 missed rotten mangoes in four categories with example photos. RQ3 reported the field test: 172 of 200 mangoes classified correctly (86 percent), lower than the lab test set, which they discussed honestly as the effect of harsher market lighting. The chapter ended with a table answering each research question.

Real-life example 2, the bus tracker discussion: Tanvir found that segment averages cut the median arrival error by 1.4 minutes, but during the evening rush on one route errors were still often above 5 minutes. Rather than hiding this, he showed a figure of error by hour, explained that a single traffic jam at a market crossing was not captured by three-week averages, and proposed live speed updates as future work. The board's main question in the viva was about this figure, and he was ready.

Common mistakes: Tables with no explanation. Only averages, no breakdown. No error analysis. Explanations stated as facts without evidence. Hiding negative results. Comparing directly with numbers from papers using different data. A limitations section with one vague sentence. Overclaiming words. Results that never clearly answer the research questions.

Recap: Separate what you found (results) from what it means (discussion). Organise by research question. Use clear tables and figures and always read them for the reader. Break results down by class and condition (per-class F1 0.92, 0.74, 0.88 averaging about 0.85). Do real error analysis (18 misses: 44, 28, 17 and 11 percent by cause). Explain carefully with evidence, report negative results honestly, compare with related work fairly, list real limitations, avoid overclaiming, and answer each research question explicitly. Next lesson: the structure of the thesis book.
key_points: Results report what you found; discussion explains what it means, with careful words like 'suggests'.
Organise results by research question: reminder, setup, main table or figure, reading of key numbers, direct answer.
Never leave a table unexplained; tell the reader what to notice and what it means.
Break results down by class, condition and subgroup; per-class F1 of 0.92, 0.74 and 0.88 shows the middle class is hard.
Error analysis looks at actual failures and groups them by cause, for example 18 misses split 8, 5, 3 and 2 (44, 28, 17, 11 percent).
Report negative and unexpected results honestly, investigate them and explain them; hiding them is what fails a thesis.
Compare with related work fairly, list real limitations, avoid overclaiming and answer every research question explicitly.
lessons.tip: Before writing the results chapter, print your main tables and figures and, for each one, write in one sentence the single point it makes. If you cannot, the table or figure needs changing or removing.
lessons.task: Take 20 errors from your own system (or 20 invented ones for a project idea) and sort them into 3 to 5 cause categories. Compute each category's share, write one paragraph of error analysis, and write one honest limitation and one research-question answer sentence based on it.

quiz.q: Which sentence belongs in the discussion rather than the results?
options: The model achieved a macro F1 of 0.85.
Table 5.1 lists the scores of four methods.
This is probably because pretraining helps with small datasets.
quiz.explain: Interpretation and explanation belong in the discussion.

quiz.q: Per-class F1 scores are 0.90, 0.70 and 0.86. What is the macro F1?
What is error analysis?
options: Looking at actual failures and grouping them by cause
Removing wrong predictions from the test set
quiz.explain: It shows where and why the system fails.

quiz.q: Your method did not beat the baseline. What is the best response?
options: Remove the baseline from the thesis
Change the metric until it wins
Report it honestly, check for bugs, analyse why and discuss it
quiz.explain: A fair, well-analysed negative result is a contribution; hiding it is misconduct.

quiz.q: Which phrasing avoids overclaiming?
options: Our app is perfect for all mango sellers
On our dataset from two Rajshahi markets, the model reached 0.85 macro F1
Our method is state of the art
This proves CNNs always beat SVMs
quiz.explain: It states the result with its conditions.

lessons.title: The Thesis Book I: Structure
lessons.content:
Think of a well-built house. Before anyone chooses curtains, the builder decides the rooms: where the entrance is, which room connects to which, how big each one should be. A house with a beautiful sofa but no clear way from the door to the kitchen is still a bad house. Your thesis book, the bound report you submit at the end, is the same. Before writing nice sentences, you need the rooms: which chapters, in what order, how long each, and what goes in the front and the back. Examiners read many theses each year; a familiar, well-organised structure lets them find what they need and trust that nothing is missing. This lesson describes the standard parts of a CSE thesis or project book, how project-style and research-style books differ, and how to plan the length of each part. Exact rules differ between universities, so always follow your own department's guidelines and template.

Why structure matters: The thesis book is the permanent record of your work. It is read by your supervisor, your examiners and the defence board, kept in the department library or repository, and later read by future students. A clear structure makes evaluation fair and quick, shows that you can organise a large technical document, and connects naturally to the slides for your defence. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-21) introduced the structure of papers and theses; this lesson goes deeper into the full book.

The three big parts: Almost every thesis has front matter (pages before chapter 1, usually numbered with Roman numerals i, ii, iii), the main body (the chapters, numbered 1, 2, 3 in Arabic numerals), and back matter (references and appendices). Front matter helps the reader and records formal approvals; the body tells the story; back matter holds evidence and details.

Front matter, part 1: The title page gives the thesis title, your names and student IDs, the degree (for example Bachelor of Science in Computer Science and Engineering), the department and university, the supervisor's name, and the month and year of submission. The declaration is a signed statement that the work is your own, that sources are acknowledged, and that it has not been submitted elsewhere for a degree. The certificate or approval page carries signatures of the supervisor and often the head of department or board members, confirming the thesis was accepted. Many universities also ask for a plagiarism or similarity report page. Use your department's exact wording for these formal pages.

Front matter, part 2: The acknowledgements thank your supervisor, people who helped (data providers, participants as a group, lab staff), and family, in a short and sincere page. The abstract (covered in the next lesson) summarises the whole work in about 200 to 300 words, or whatever your department asks. Then come the table of contents, the list of figures, the list of tables and often a list of abbreviations (CNN, ETA, GPS, SUS). Generate the contents and lists automatically with LaTeX or Word styles, so page numbers are always right.

The chapter plan: Most CSE theses use a version of this chapter plan. Chapter 1, Introduction: background and motivation, problem statement, research questions or objectives, scope, contributions, and the organisation of the book. Chapter 2, Background and Literature Review: key concepts the reader needs, then the review of related work organised by theme, ending with the gap (lesson 08). Chapter 3, Methodology or System Design: how you answered the questions, data, methods, architecture, experiment design and evaluation plan. Chapter 4, Implementation: tools, important components, algorithms and engineering decisions. Chapter 5, Results and Discussion: as in lesson 20. Chapter 6, Conclusion and Future Work: summary, answers to research questions, contributions, limitations and next steps.

What goes in the introduction: The introduction is a short version of the whole thesis. It moves from the wide context to your specific problem, states why it matters, gives the research questions or objectives, lists your contributions as a numbered list, and ends with a paragraph explaining what each following chapter contains. A reader who stops after chapter 1 should know what you did and why. It is usually written or rewritten last, once you know exactly what you achieved.

What goes in the methodology or design chapter: This chapter must contain enough detail that another student could repeat your work: data sources and sizes, collection and labelling procedure, splits, preprocessing, models or algorithms with their settings, system architecture diagrams, evaluation metrics and statistical tests, hardware and software versions, and ethics steps such as consent. Much of this comes straight from your proposal, your data documentation (lesson 14) and your experiment log (lesson 16).

What goes in the conclusion: The conclusion does not introduce new results. It briefly restates the problem and approach, answers each research question in a sentence or two, lists the contributions again in light of the results, notes the main limitations, and suggests specific future work ('collect photos in the rainy season', 'add live traffic speed'), not vague wishes ('improve accuracy'). Keep it short; two to four pages is common.

References: All sources cited in the text, and only those, appear in the reference list, in the style your department requires, often IEEE (numbered) or APA (author-year). Use your reference manager to generate it (lesson 17). Check that every entry has authors, title, venue, year and pages or a link, and that every citation number in the text matches.

Appendices: Appendices hold material that supports the thesis but would interrupt the main story: full questionnaires and consent forms, extra result tables, detailed hardware schematics, user manuals, important code excerpts, and the data dictionary. Do not dump hundreds of pages of source code; give a link to the repository and include only short, important excerpts. Each appendix is referenced from the main text ('the full questionnaire is in Appendix B').

Project-style versus research-style books: A project (system-building) book usually has a requirements chapter (stakeholders, functional and non-functional requirements, use cases, often based on SRS style from deep-cse-4-4), a design chapter (architecture, database design, UI design), an implementation chapter, and a testing and evaluation chapter (test cases, performance, user study), then the conclusion. A research book follows the introduction, literature review, methodology, experiments, results and discussion pattern more closely. Many CSE theses are a mix: an artifact built and then evaluated in experiments, which is design science (lesson 11). Choose the plan that fits your work and agree it with your supervisor early.

Formatting and templates: Departments usually specify paper size (often A4), margins (often wider on the binding side), font and size, line spacing, heading styles, page numbering and how to show figure and table captions. Many provide a LaTeX template or a Word template. Start writing in the official template from day one; reformatting a finished book a week before submission is painful and error-prone. Be consistent: same caption style, same tense rules, same way of writing numbers and units throughout.

Page budget, worked: Planning lengths stops the common problem of a 25-page literature review and a 6-page results chapter. Suppose your department expects about 60 pages of main text. A reasonable budget: introduction 6 pages (10 percent), background and literature review 12 (20 percent), methodology 12 (20 percent), implementation 9 (15 percent), results and discussion 18 (30 percent), conclusion 3 (5 percent). Total 6 + 12 + 12 + 9 + 18 + 3 = 60. At roughly 300 words of text per page, that is about 18,000 words, less in practice because figures and tables take space. The biggest chunk goes to results, because that is your contribution. Adjust for a project-style book, and treat the budget as a guide, not a law.

The story line through the chapters: A good thesis reads like one argument, not six separate essays. The introduction raises a problem and questions; the literature review shows that existing work leaves a gap; the methodology explains how you will close it; implementation shows you built it; results show what happened; the conclusion says what was learned. Each chapter should open with a short paragraph saying what it covers and how it connects to the previous one, and close with a short summary leading to the next. Examiners notice immediately when a literature review discusses topics that never appear again, or when results answer questions that were never asked. A simple check: every research question in chapter 1 should have a section in chapter 5 and a sentence in chapter 6.

Numbering and cross-references: Number chapters, sections and subsections consistently (3, 3.2, 3.2.1), but avoid going deeper than three levels; if you need a fourth level, the section is probably too long. Number figures and tables by chapter (Figure 4.3 is the third figure in chapter 4) and equations likewise. Always refer to them with automatic cross-references, so that adding a new figure renumbers everything correctly. Write 'as shown in Table 5.2' rather than 'the table below', because page breaks may move the table.

The skeleton first: Before writing paragraphs, create the full skeleton in the template: all chapter and section headings, with two or three bullet-like notes (as short sentences) under each saying what will go there, which figures and tables, and which references. Share this skeleton with your supervisor. It is far easier to move a section in the skeleton than to rewrite chapters later. The skeleton also becomes your to-do list for writing.

Real-life example 1, the mango book: Nusrat and Rafi's book had front matter of 12 pages, six chapters of 64 pages in total, 41 references and three appendices (consent form and questionnaire in Bengali and English, extra per-fold result tables, the app's user guide). Their supervisor moved a long section on CNN basics out of the literature review into a short background section, which made chapter 2 focus on related work and the gap.

Real-life example 2, the bus tracker book: Tanvir's project-style book had chapters for introduction, background, requirements analysis (with use case diagrams), system design (architecture, database schema, API design), implementation, testing and evaluation (unit and integration tests, field test of 50 trips, SUS with 15 students) and conclusion. Appendix A held the API documentation, written as in Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-16).

Common mistakes: Not using the department template. Missing formal pages or wrong wording. Manual tables of contents with wrong page numbers. A literature review longer than the results. Methodology without enough detail to repeat. New results in the conclusion. Pages of raw source code in the appendix. Inconsistent formatting between chapters written by different teammates.

Recap: A thesis book has front matter (title page, declaration, certificate, acknowledgements, abstract, contents and lists), a body of usually six chapters (introduction, background and literature, methodology or design, implementation, results and discussion, conclusion) and back matter (references and appendices). Project-style books add requirements, design and testing chapters. Use the official template, plan a page budget (for example 6, 12, 12, 9, 18 and 3 pages for 60), and build the full skeleton first. Next lesson: actually writing the thesis.
key_points: A thesis book has front matter (Roman page numbers), a main body of chapters and back matter (references and appendices).
Front matter: title page, declaration, certificate or approval, acknowledgements, abstract, contents, lists of figures, tables and abbreviations.
A common chapter plan: introduction, background and literature review, methodology or design, implementation, results and discussion, conclusion and future work.
The methodology must allow someone to repeat your work; the conclusion answers the research questions and adds no new results.
Project-style books add requirements, design and testing chapters; research-style books follow methods, experiments and results.
Use your department's template from day one; exact rules differ between universities.
Plan a page budget (for example 60 pages: 6, 12, 12, 9, 18, 3) and build the full skeleton before writing paragraphs.
lessons.tip: Put your page budget as a comment at the top of each chapter file, and check the actual page count every two weeks. If one chapter grows far past its budget, decide on purpose whether that is right, rather than discovering it at the end.
lessons.task: Create the skeleton of your thesis book: list all front matter pages, all chapter and section headings with one sentence each about their content, the planned figures and tables, and the appendices. Then write a page budget that adds up to your department's expected length.

quiz.q: Which page is part of the front matter?
quiz.explain: The declaration, title page, certificate, abstract and contents come before chapter 1.

quiz.q: What should the conclusion chapter NOT do?
quiz.explain: The conclusion summarises; new results belong in the results chapter.

quiz.q: A 60-page body gives 30 percent to results. How many pages is that?
What usually belongs in an appendix?
options: The full questionnaire and consent form
quiz.explain: Supporting details that would interrupt the main story go in appendices.

quiz.q: What extra chapters does a project-style (system-building) book usually include?
quiz.explain: System projects document requirements, design, implementation and testing.

lessons.title: The Thesis Book II: Writing It
lessons.content:
Imagine two students preparing for a 10 km run. One runs 2 km every morning for three months. The other does nothing until the last week, then tries to run 10 km every day, and ends up injured and exhausted. Writing a thesis is similar. Students who write a little steadily, from the first month, finish calm with a polished book. Students who start writing in the last four weeks produce rushed chapters full of mistakes, fight with formatting at 3 a.m., and often miss deadlines. The last lesson gave the book its rooms. This lesson is about actually filling them: when to write, in what order, how much per day, how to work with your supervisor's feedback, how to write the abstract, how to use similarity checks and AI tools honestly, and how to get the book printed, bound and submitted. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8) already taught clear sentences, citation and figures; here we apply them to the thesis.

Write as you go: The most important habit is writing during the project, not after it. When you finish the literature review, draft chapter 2. When the proposal is approved, turn it into first drafts of chapters 1 and 3. When you finish building a component, write its implementation section that week while the details are fresh. When an experiment finishes, put its table and a paragraph into chapter 5. By the time experiments end, you should already have a rough draft of most of the book, and the final months are for improving, not starting.

The writing process, briefly: Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-03) described the process: plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread. For a thesis this means: plan each chapter with the skeleton; draft fast without polishing, to get ideas down; revise for structure and argument (is the order right, is anything missing?); edit for clarity, consistency and style; finally proofread for typos, numbering and references. Do not try to write perfect sentences in the first draft; it makes writing slow and painful.

Chapter order: You do not write chapters in reading order. A good order is: methodology and implementation first (you know them best, and they come straight from your work), then results as experiments finish, then the literature review (updated from your earlier review notes), then discussion and conclusion, and finally the introduction and abstract, because they summarise everything and can only be written well once you know the final results. Front matter like acknowledgements comes at the very end.

Daily word targets, worked: Suppose your book needs about 18,000 words of text (lesson 21). You already have about 6,000 words in usable form from the proposal, literature notes and progress reports, so 12,000 words remain. You plan 8 weeks of drafting with 5 writing days a week, which is 40 writing days. 12,000 / 40 = 300 words per day. That is about one focused hour. Then you reserve 3 more weeks for revision, supervisor feedback and formatting, so the writing phase is 11 weeks in total. Seen this way, a thesis book is not a mountain but a small daily habit. Track words in a simple sheet; seeing the total grow is motivating.

Making daily writing work: Write at the same time each day, ideally when your mind is fresh, before coding or social media. Set a timer for 45 to 60 minutes and only write: no searching, no formatting. Leave notes like [CITE] or [CHECK NUMBER] and move on instead of stopping. End each session in the middle of a paragraph you know how to continue, so starting next day is easy. In a team, split chapters clearly and meet weekly to read each other's drafts.

LaTeX, Overleaf or Word in practice: If you use LaTeX on Overleaf, keep one file per chapter, use labels and references for every figure, table and equation, and compile often so errors stay small. Keep figures in a figures folder and generate them from scripts (lesson 17). If you use Word, use the department template, built-in heading styles, automatic captions, cross-references and the citation plugin of your reference manager; never type numbers by hand. Either way, keep the source in version control or use the tool's version history, and back it up.

Figures and citations, recap: Every figure and table needs a number, a caption that explains it on its own, and a mention in the text. Draw diagrams with a proper tool rather than screenshots of whiteboards, and export charts at high resolution. Cite every idea, method, dataset, tool and figure that you did not create, as taught in deep-cse-6-8-22; if you reuse or adapt someone else's figure, say so in the caption and cite it. Use one citation style throughout.

Style choices to fix early: Agree as a team on a short style sheet and stick to it: 'we' or passive voice (many CSE theses use 'we' even for one author, but follow your department); past tense for what you did and found ('we collected 3,000 photos'), present tense for what the thesis contains and for general facts ('Chapter 4 describes...', 'CNNs learn features'); British or American spelling; how to write numbers (words for one to nine, digits for 10 and above, always digits with units, such as 5 ms); and the exact names of your system, datasets and classes. Use the same term for the same thing everywhere; if chapter 3 says 'semi-rotten', chapter 5 should not switch to 'partly spoiled'.

Revising your own draft: When a chapter draft is done, let it rest for a day or two, then read it as an examiner would. Read the first sentence of every paragraph in order; together they should tell the chapter's story. Cut repetition and filler phrases. Check that every claim has a citation or a result behind it. Reading aloud catches clumsy sentences that silent reading misses.

Working with supervisor feedback: Send chapters to your supervisor one at a time, not the whole book at the end. Ask what kind of feedback you need ('Is the structure of chapter 3 right?' rather than 'Please check'). Give them reasonable time, often one to two weeks per chapter. When comments come back, keep a simple table: comment, your action, status. Address every comment, either by changing the text or by politely explaining why you kept it. Plan at least two feedback rounds for the main chapters. Supervisors are busy, so a thesis that arrives chapter by chapter gets much better feedback than one that arrives all at once.

Writing the abstract: The abstract is the most read part of the thesis, and often the only part people read in a library search. In about 200 to 300 words (follow your department's limit), it should state the context and problem in one or two sentences, what you did (method or system), how you evaluated it, the key results with real numbers, and the main conclusion or contribution. For example: 'Mango sellers in Bangladesh lose income to fruit that rots unnoticed. We built an offline Android app that classifies mangoes as fresh, semi-rotten or rotten using a lightweight CNN. On 3,000 market photos, MobileNetV2 reached a macro F1 of 0.85, and in a field test with five sellers it classified 172 of 200 mangoes correctly...' No citations, no undefined abbreviations, no vague promises. Write it last and make sure its numbers match the results chapter.

Similarity checks and honest AI use: Most universities run the thesis through a similarity-checking tool and set a maximum similarity percentage, which varies by institution. The report shows text that matches other sources. Matches from properly quoted and cited text, the reference list or standard phrases are usually acceptable; copied paragraphs without citation are plagiarism. Write in your own words from the start, and check your own draft before submission if your department allows. For AI writing tools, follow your university's policy and the advice in Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-23): you are responsible for every sentence and fact; never let a tool invent references or results; disclose AI use where required; and use such tools, if allowed, for light editing rather than writing your thinking for you. Examiners can usually tell when a student does not understand a chapter they 'wrote'.

Final checks before submission: Run through a checklist. Do all chapters follow the template and formatting rules? Are all figures, tables and equations numbered, captioned and referenced? Does every citation appear in the references and vice versa? Do the numbers in the abstract, results, conclusion and slides match? Are research questions answered explicitly? Are all formal pages present and signed? Has a teammate or friend proofread each chapter? Has the similarity report been generated and checked? Is the code repository tagged and linked?

Printing, binding and submission: Find out early what your department requires: how many printed copies, which paper, colour or black and white, the cover colour and text, the binding type (often hard binding for the final copy), and whether a soft copy (PDF, sometimes source code on a disc or link) must be submitted. Printing and binding shops near campus get very busy before deadlines, so plan at least a few days. Print one test copy first and check page numbers, figures, margins on the binding side and colour charts in black and white. Budget for printing; for several hard-bound copies it can be a noticeable cost.

Real-life example 1, writing as they went: Nusrat and Rafi turned their proposal into chapter 1 and 3 drafts in month four, wrote implementation sections as they built the app, and added each results table to chapter 5 the week the experiment finished. In the final two months they wrote 300 words a day each, sent chapters to their supervisor one at a time, and had two feedback rounds per chapter. They finished the abstract last, checked every number against the results notebook, and submitted a week early.

Real-life example 2, a late start rescued: Tanvir had built his system but written almost nothing by week 34 of 40. With his supervisor he made an emergency plan: reuse the proposal and progress reports as raw material, write 600 words a day for 4 weeks, which is 600 x 5 x 4 = 12,000 words, and accept a shorter literature review. He worked from the skeleton, wrote methodology and implementation first, and asked a friend to proofread each chapter. He submitted on time, but admitted in his acknowledgements that starting earlier would have produced a better book.

Common mistakes: Starting to write after all experiments. Trying to write perfect first drafts. Writing chapters in reading order, so the introduction promises things the results do not deliver. Sending the whole book to the supervisor in the last week. Ignoring feedback. An abstract without numbers. Inconsistent numbers between chapters. Copying text without citation, or letting AI tools invent content. Leaving printing to the last day.

Recap: Write as you go, follow the process (plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread), and write chapters in a smart order: methods and implementation first, introduction and abstract last. Turn the book into a daily habit (12,000 words over 40 days is 300 words a day), use your tool's automatic features, send chapters to your supervisor one at a time with a feedback table, write a specific abstract with real numbers, use similarity checks and AI tools honestly, run final checks, and plan printing and binding early. Next lesson: the defence presentation, demo and viva.
key_points: Write during the project, not after it: draft each chapter when its part of the work is done.
Follow plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread; do not polish while drafting.
Write methodology, implementation and results first; write the introduction and abstract last.
Turn writing into a daily habit: 12,000 remaining words over 40 writing days is 300 words a day, about one focused hour.
Send chapters to your supervisor one at a time, ask specific questions, and track every comment in a feedback table.
The abstract states problem, method, evaluation, key numeric results and contribution in about 200 to 300 words, with numbers matching the results chapter.
Use similarity checks and AI tools honestly and within policy, run a final checklist, and plan printing and binding early.
lessons.tip: Keep a file called 'parking lot' next to your thesis. Whenever you think of something to add, check or fix while writing, put it there instead of stopping. Clear the parking lot once a week. Your daily writing time stays for writing.
lessons.task: Make your writing plan: estimate the total words your book needs, subtract what you already have, choose the number of writing days, and compute your daily word target. Then draft a 200-word abstract for your project with placeholder numbers marked as [X], following the problem, method, evaluation, results, contribution order.

quiz.q: Which chapters are usually best written last?
quiz.explain: They summarise everything, so they are written once results are final.

quiz.q: You need 9,000 more words and have 30 writing days. What is your daily target?
quiz.explain: 9,000 / 30 = 300 words per day.

quiz.q: What should a good abstract include?
options: Problem, method, evaluation, key numeric results and contribution
A long literature review with citations
quiz.explain: An abstract summarises the whole work concisely, including real numbers.

quiz.q: What is the best way to work with supervisor feedback?
options: Send the whole book in the last week
Send chapters one at a time and track every comment and your action
Only ask for a final signature
quiz.explain: Chapter-by-chapter feedback with a tracking table gives better results.

quiz.q: When using AI writing tools on your thesis, which is correct?
options: Follow university policy, verify everything and never let a tool invent references or results
Let the tool write chapters you do not understand
AI use never needs to be disclosed
quiz.explain: You remain responsible for every sentence and fact in the thesis.

lessons.title: Presentation, Demo and Defence (Viva)
lessons.content:
A good cook does not just make a great biryani; at a wedding, they also serve it well: hot, on time, the right amount on each plate, and if a guest asks what spices are in it, they answer calmly. Your thesis defence is the serving. Months of work are judged partly in twenty to forty minutes in front of a board: a presentation, often a demo, and questions. Students who know their work well still lose marks when slides are crowded, the demo crashes, or a hard question makes them panic. The good news: defence skills can be prepared like any other part of the project. This lesson covers what boards look for, how to plan slides and timing, how to prepare a demo that does not fail, how to rehearse, the questions you will probably face, how to answer them, and what happens after. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-24) covered presentation basics; here we focus on the thesis defence.

What a defence or viva is: The defence (also called viva voce, or viva, or final presentation) is an oral examination of your thesis. Formats vary: some departments hold a public presentation followed by questions, others a closed session with the board, and many have both a pre-defence or progress presentation and a final defence. Typically you present for a fixed time, perhaps demonstrate the system, and then answer questions. The board then decides a grade or result, sometimes with required corrections. Find out your department's exact format, time limits and marking scheme early.

Who is on the board: Board make-up differs between universities, but commonly includes your supervisor, one or more internal teachers from the department, and sometimes an external examiner from another university or industry. Some members will have read your thesis closely; others will only skim it or see it for the first time in your talk. So your presentation must make sense to a smart CSE teacher who is not an expert in your exact topic.

What boards look for: Across universities, boards usually judge similar things: Do you understand the problem and why it matters? Is the method sound and fairly evaluated? Did you do the work yourself, and does every team member understand it? Are the results real and honestly reported? Do you know the limitations? Can you explain and defend your choices clearly? The best defences show understanding and honesty, not just impressive numbers.

Slide plan and timing, worked: Suppose you have 15 minutes to present. A rough rule is one main slide per minute, so about 15 slides. A typical plan: title 0.5 minutes; problem and motivation 2; research questions or objectives 1; related work and gap 1.5; method or system design 3; implementation highlights 1.5; results 4; conclusion and contributions 1; future work 0.5. Check: 0.5 + 2 + 1 + 1.5 + 3 + 1.5 + 4 + 1 + 0.5 = 15 minutes. Results get the most time because they are your contribution. For a two-person team, split roughly in half with a clean handover point, such as one person from problem to method and the other from implementation to conclusion. Keep backup slides after the final slide for likely questions: extra results, ablation details, dataset examples.

Making good slides: One message per slide, written as the slide title ('Lighting correction gives the largest gain', not 'Results 2'). Few words, large fonts, high-contrast colours. Use diagrams, photos and charts rather than paragraphs. Show your main result table with only the needed rows and columns and the best values highlighted. Number your slides so board members can refer to them ('On slide 9, why...'). Make sure every number matches the thesis book.

Demo preparation: A live demo is powerful but risky. Make it short (two to five minutes) and scripted: decide the exact steps, the inputs and what the audience should notice. Prepare for failure: bring the system working offline if possible (the mango app classifies on the phone; the bus tracker can replay recorded GPS data), have a recorded backup video of the demo, carry chargers, cables and an adapter for the projector, keep test data ready on the device, and arrive early to test the room's projector and internet. If something fails, say calmly 'Let me show the recorded version', and continue. Boards care far more about how you handle it than about the glitch itself.

Rehearsal: Rehearse the full presentation aloud at least three times, timed. First alone, then for teammates or friends, then a mock defence with classmates asking hard questions, ideally including one person outside your topic. Record one rehearsal on your phone and watch it: you will notice filler words, speaking too fast and looking at the screen instead of the audience. Practise the handover between teammates and the demo exactly as it will run.

Typical questions: Prepare answers to the questions boards ask again and again. Why did you choose this problem? What is your exact contribution, what is new? Why this method and not another (for example, why not a bigger model, why not a simple rule)? How did you collect and label the data, and how do you know the labels are right? How did you prevent data leakage? Why these metrics? Is the difference with the baseline significant? What are the limitations? How would it work in a different setting, such as another city or season? What did each team member do? What would you do with six more months? If you had to start again, what would you change? Write short answers and practise saying them.

Questions that test understanding: Boards often ask about basics behind your work to check that you understand it, not just used it. For a CNN thesis: what does a convolution layer do, what is transfer learning, what is overfitting and how did you control it? For a system thesis: why this database, how does your API handle many users, what happens if the network drops? For statistics: what does your p-value mean? Be ready to draw a quick diagram on the board or paper. Revise the core concepts of your topic in the last week.

Answering technique: Use a simple four-step method. Pause: take a breath and make sure you understood the question; if not, ask politely for clarification. Repeat or rephrase briefly: 'You are asking why we used macro F1 rather than accuracy.' Answer directly in one or two sentences first. Then give evidence: a number, a slide, a section of the thesis ('Table 5.3 in the backup slides shows...'). Stop when you have answered; long wandering answers invite more doubts.

Saying 'I don't know' honestly: You will not know every answer. Making something up is much worse than admitting it, because examiners usually know when an answer is invented. A good honest answer: 'I have not tested that, so I can't say for sure. My expectation would be... because..., and it would be good future work.' This shows maturity and reasoning. Similarly, if an examiner points out a real mistake, accept it calmly: 'You are right, that is a limitation; we should have...'.

Team answers: In team defences, boards often direct questions to a specific member to check that everyone understands the whole work. Every member must be able to explain the problem, the method, the main results and the limitations, not only their own part. Agree who answers which kind of question by default, but do not interrupt or correct a teammate harshly in front of the board; if needed, add politely after they finish: 'If I may add one point...'.

Body language and nerves: Nervousness is normal; even experienced researchers feel it. Practical steps: sleep well the night before, eat something light, arrive early, dress neatly as your department expects, stand facing the audience, speak a little slower than normal, and look at board members rather than the screen. Use a pointer or mouse to show what you are talking about on slides. A glass of water nearby helps when your mouth goes dry.

Progress presentations and pre-defence: Many departments hold one or more progress presentations or a pre-defence before the final defence. Treat them as practice with real examiners. Use the same slide style, write down every comment, and show at the next presentation how you acted on each one; boards remember earlier comments and are pleased to see them addressed. Some departments also hold a project showcase or poster session; a clear poster with the problem, a system diagram, one key results chart and a QR code to a demo video works well there.

The day before and the morning of: Freeze the slides the day before; last-minute edits introduce mistakes. Copy the final slides as PDF and the original file to your laptop, a pen drive and cloud storage. Charge every device fully. Test the demo once more from start to finish on the exact device you will use. On the morning, read your question bank, check the room and projector, and open the slides and demo before the board arrives.

After the defence: The board may accept the thesis as it is, accept it with minor corrections, ask for major corrections, or, rarely, ask for resubmission. Write down every comment during or right after the session, ideally with a teammate taking notes during questions. Make the corrections promptly, keep a list of each comment and how you addressed it, get your supervisor's approval, and then submit the final bound copies and soft copy as the department requires. Also thank your supervisor and board; you may need their recommendation letters later.

Real-life example 1, the mango defence: Nusrat and Rafi had 15 minutes plus a 3-minute demo. Nusrat presented problem to method, Rafi results to conclusion. The live demo ran offline on the phone with five real mangoes they brought, and a backup video was ready. The external examiner asked how they knew the semi-rotten labels were reliable; Rafi showed the backup slide with the agreement check (kappa about 0.6, then corrected labels). Another member asked if the app would work for Langra and Himsagar varieties equally; Nusrat answered that their data had both but not other varieties, and listed it as a limitation.

Real-life example 2, a demo that failed well: During Tanvir's defence the campus Wi-Fi dropped and his live map would not load. He said calmly, 'The network is down, so I will use the replay mode with recorded GPS data from last Tuesday,' and switched within thirty seconds. The board then asked how the real app handles network loss, which he could answer well because he had just demonstrated it. The failure became a strength.

Common mistakes: Too many slides and too much text. Running over time. No backup for the demo. Reading slides aloud. Not knowing basics behind the method. Inventing answers. Teammates who know only their part. Arguing defensively with examiners. Losing the list of corrections.

Recap: Learn your department's format and board make-up. Plan slides by time (15 minutes: about 15 slides, with 4 minutes on results), one message per slide, plus backup slides. Make the demo short, scripted, offline-capable and backed by a video. Rehearse aloud at least three times including a mock defence. Prepare typical and basic questions. Answer with pause, rephrase, direct answer and evidence; say 'I don't know' honestly with reasoning. Make sure every teammate understands the whole work. After the defence, record and complete corrections promptly. Next lesson: common pitfalls and how to recover from them.
key_points: The defence or viva tests whether you understand, did and can honestly defend your work; formats differ, so learn your department's rules.
Boards commonly include your supervisor, internal teachers and sometimes an external examiner; present for a smart non-specialist.
Plan slides by time: for 15 minutes about 15 slides, giving results the most time (about 4 minutes), plus backup slides.
Keep demos short and scripted, make them work offline if possible, and always have a recorded backup video.
Rehearse aloud at least three times, including a mock defence, and prepare answers to typical and basic-concept questions.
Answer by pausing, rephrasing, answering directly and giving evidence; say 'I don't know' honestly with your reasoning.
Every teammate must understand the whole work; after the defence, record all comments and complete corrections promptly.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page 'question bank' with the 20 questions you fear most and a two-sentence answer for each, plus the slide or section that supports it. Read it the morning of the defence; most questions will be on it.
lessons.task: Draft the slide plan for your defence: slide titles written as messages, minutes per slide adding up to your time limit, and three backup slides. Then write your question bank with at least ten likely questions and short answers, and plan your demo backup.

quiz.q: You have 12 minutes. Using roughly one main slide per minute, about how many main slides should you prepare?
quiz.explain: About one slide per minute gives roughly 12 main slides.

quiz.q: Your live demo fails because the internet is down. What is the best response?
options: Calmly switch to offline mode or the recorded backup video and continue
Apologise repeatedly and stop the presentation
Blame the department's network at length
Skip the rest of the talk
quiz.explain: Preparation and a calm switch to the backup show professionalism.

quiz.q: An examiner asks something you do not know. What should you do?
options: Say the question is not relevant
Admit it honestly, give your best reasoning and mention it as future work
quiz.explain: Honest reasoning is valued; invented answers are usually spotted.

quiz.q: Which slide title is best?
options: Lighting correction gives the largest gain
quiz.explain: A title that states the message tells the board what to notice.

quiz.q: In a team defence, what should every member be able to explain?
options: The problem, method, main results and limitations of the whole work
quiz.explain: Boards often question each member about the whole thesis.

lessons.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Recover
lessons.content:
Rivers in Bangladesh flood almost every year. Families who have lived beside them for generations do not panic each time. They know the warning signs: the water colour changes, the level rises at the ghat, the upstream news. They raise the plinth of the house, keep seeds and documents high, and have a plan for where to go. Problems still come, but they are smaller and recovery is faster. Final year projects have their own floods. Almost every team meets at least one serious problem: the data does not arrive, a teammate disappears, the model will not improve, the laptop dies. What separates a good thesis from a disaster is rarely luck; it is noticing the warning signs early and having a recovery plan. This lesson collects the most common pitfalls, their early signs, how to prevent them, and how to recover, with two full rescue stories at the end.

Why talk about failure: Students often hide problems from their supervisor and even from their teammates, hoping things will fix themselves. Usually they get worse, and by the time they are visible, there is little time left to fix them. Supervisors have seen these problems many times and can help much more when told early. A thesis is also a lesson in managing real projects, where problems are normal. Lessons 12 and 13 covered planning and risk; this lesson is the practical survival guide.

Pitfall 1, the late start: Sign: in month two you still have no clear topic, have read few papers and have no weekly routine. Prevention: treat the thesis as a course with fixed weekly hours from week one (lesson 02), set early mini deadlines with your supervisor. Recovery: pick a topic with existing data and a known baseline, narrow the scope sharply, and make an honest week-by-week plan with your supervisor to the deadline.

Pitfall 2, scope creep: Sign: the feature list keeps growing, new 'small' ideas appear every week, and the core is still unfinished. Prevention: fix must-have, should-have and could-have features in the proposal, and keep a 'later' list (lesson 13). Recovery: cut to the minimum that answers the research questions. Worked: you have 25 working days left and six planned features estimated at 10, 8, 7, 6, 5 and 4 days, total 40 days, which is 15 days too many. The must-haves are the 10, 8 and 5-day features: 10 + 8 + 5 = 23 days, leaving a 2-day buffer. The 7, 6 and 4-day features go to future work. Cutting is not failure; finishing the core well is success.

Pitfall 3, coding before reading: Sign: you have built a lot, but cannot name three closely related papers or explain why your approach is better than existing ones. Prevention: do the literature search and reading before heavy building (lessons 06 to 08). Recovery: spend one focused week on the closest related work, add at least one proper baseline from it, and be honest in the thesis about what is new and what is not.

Pitfall 4, no baseline or an unfair one: Sign: your results table has only your method, or the baseline uses default settings while yours is heavily tuned. Prevention: run baselines first (lesson 16).
