Recovery: add a simple baseline and a classical one with equal tuning budgets now, even if your improvement looks smaller afterwards; examiners trust smaller honest gains more than large unfair ones.

Pitfall 5, data that never arrives: Sign: you are waiting for a company, hospital or office to share data, and weeks pass with promises. Prevention: confirm data access in writing before the proposal, and have a plan B dataset (lesson 13). Recovery: switch to a public dataset in the same domain, or collect a smaller dataset yourself, and rephrase the research questions to match. Set a firm date, for example two weeks, after which you switch regardless.

Pitfall 6, lost work: Sign: code only on one laptop, no Git, no backup of data. Prevention: Git with a remote from day one and the 3-2-1 backup rule (lesson 17). Recovery: gather every fragment (emails, old pen drives, chat attachments, cloud notebooks), rebuild the most important parts first, and tell your supervisor immediately so the plan can be adjusted.

Pitfall 7, results that do not improve: Sign: weeks of trying new settings, but performance is stuck or worse than the baseline. Prevention: sanity checks, pilot runs and error analysis early (lessons 16 and 20). Recovery: check for bugs and leakage first; look at failure cases to understand why; try one well-reasoned change at a time rather than random ones; and if the method truly does not beat the baseline, write a careful negative-result thesis with strong analysis, which is acceptable at many departments when done honestly. Discuss the change of framing with your supervisor.

Pitfall 8, p-hacking and cherry-picking: Sign: you are tempted to report only the best seed, quietly drop a bad dataset, tune on the test set, or choose the metric that flatters you. Prevention: decide metrics and comparisons in advance and log everything (lessons 16, 18, 19). Recovery: stop, rerun properly, and report all results honestly. Data manipulation and fabricated results are serious academic misconduct, and can lead to a failed thesis or worse; no deadline is worth that.

Pitfall 9, the teammate who disappears: Sign: a teammate misses meetings, does not push code, gives vague updates. Prevention: a written team agreement, clear task ownership and weekly visible progress (lesson 05). Recovery: talk to them privately and kindly first; there may be health or family problems. If nothing changes, document contributions factually (commits, task board, meeting notes) and inform your supervisor early, not at the defence. Re-plan the work so the thesis can succeed even with less help.

Pitfall 10, the unreachable supervisor: Sign: emails unanswered for weeks, meetings cancelled. Prevention: agree on a meeting schedule and communication channel at the start (lesson 04); send short, specific updates. Recovery: send a polite written summary with specific questions and decisions you plan to take unless advised otherwise, ask for a short meeting, ask a co-supervisor or senior lab member for interim help, and if the problem continues for a long time, consult the thesis coordinator politely.

Pitfall 11, last-week writing: Sign: one month before submission, chapters exist only as headings. Prevention: write as you go (lesson 22). Recovery: freeze all new experiments today; write methodology and implementation first from your logs; reuse proposal and progress reports; set a daily word target and protect writing time; reduce the literature review to the essential; ask friends to proofread chapter by chapter.

Pitfall 12, plagiarism and AI misuse: Sign: copied paragraphs 'to rewrite later', references you have never opened, chapters you cannot explain, or text generated by tools that you did not check. Prevention: write in your own words from notes, cite as you write, follow your university's AI policy (deep-cse-6-8-23). Recovery: before submission, rewrite any copied text, verify every reference exists and supports your claim, and remove anything you cannot defend. The similarity check and the viva will find these problems if you do not.

Pitfall 13, the shiny new tool: Sign: you switch frameworks, languages or model types every few weeks because a new one looks better, and nothing is finished. Prevention: choose a stack you or your team already know reasonably well, unless learning the new tool is itself part of the research. Recovery: freeze the stack now, finish the core with what works, and mention the alternative as future work.

Pitfall 14, burnout and health: Sign: weeks of very late nights, skipped meals, constant anxiety, falling behind in other courses, or conflict with family about time. Prevention: a realistic plan with buffers, fixed rest days, sleep, and exercise as simple as a daily walk. Recovery: talk to your supervisor, a trusted teacher or the university counselling service if one exists; adjust the plan; remember that a slightly smaller thesis finished in good health is far better than a collapse in the final month. Your health matters more than any grade.

Warning signs dashboard: Once a month, ask yourself honestly: Are we on schedule against our milestones? Has the supervisor seen progress in the last two weeks? Is all code and data backed up? Do we have a baseline result? Is every team member active? Is the thesis draft growing? Any 'no' is a yellow flag to discuss at the next meeting; two or more are a red flag that needs a recovery plan now.

Making a recovery plan: A recovery plan has five steps. First, describe the problem honestly in writing, with facts. Second, estimate the time and resources left. Third, list options (cut scope, change data, change method, ask for help, request an extension where rules allow). Fourth, choose with your supervisor and write down the new plan, with weekly milestones. Fifth, track it weekly and adjust. Many successful theses had a recovery plan at some point.

Rescue story 1, the hospital data that never came: A team in Chattogram planned to detect pneumonia from chest X-rays using images from a local hospital. By month five, the data had not arrived despite repeated promises. Their supervisor set a two-week deadline; when it passed, they switched to a well-known public chest X-ray dataset, rewrote RQ1 to compare lightweight models on that data, and kept a small RQ3 on how the model behaved on 40 local images that the hospital eventually provided late, with consent and anonymisation. They clearly explained the change in the thesis and finished on time.

Rescue story 2, the vanished teammate and the stuck model: In a three-person team building a Bengali fake-news classifier, one member stopped coming in month six, and the model was stuck at the same score as a TF-IDF baseline. The remaining two documented contributions and informed the supervisor, who agreed to adjust the scope. They did a careful error analysis, found that many 'fake' examples were satire mislabelled during collection, cleaned the labels with a second annotator, and saw a modest real improvement. They wrote an honest thesis whose main contribution was the cleaned dataset and analysis, and it was well received.

Common mistakes in recovery: Hiding the problem until the defence. Changing many things at once in panic. Working all night for weeks and burning out. Blaming teammates in front of the board. Faking or polishing results to cover the gap. Waiting for perfect conditions instead of choosing a good-enough option and moving.

Recap: Most theses meet at least one serious problem. Learn the common pitfalls: late start, scope creep, coding before reading, no fair baseline, missing data, lost work, stuck results, p-hacking, disappearing teammates, unreachable supervisors, last-week writing, plagiarism and AI misuse, shiny new tools and burnout. Watch the warning signs monthly, prevent what you can, tell your supervisor early, and use a five-step recovery plan. Cut scope with numbers (40 days of features into 25 available: keep 23 days of must-haves). Next lesson: what comes after the thesis.
key_points: Almost every thesis meets a serious problem; noticing warning signs early and having a recovery plan matter more than luck.
Tell your supervisor about problems early; hidden problems grow and leave little time to fix.
Cut scope with numbers: with 25 days and 40 days of features, keep the 23 days of must-haves and move the rest to future work.
If data does not arrive by a firm date, switch to a public or self-collected dataset and adjust the research questions.
When results are stuck, check bugs and leakage, do error analysis, change one thing at a time, or write an honest negative-result thesis.
Never p-hack, cherry-pick or fabricate; it is academic misconduct, and no deadline is worth it.
Use a monthly warning-signs check and a five-step recovery plan: describe, estimate, list options, decide with the supervisor, track weekly.
lessons.tip: Put a 15-minute 'risk check' at the end of every monthly supervisor meeting: go through the warning signs dashboard together. Problems discussed in month four are solvable; the same problems discovered in month ten often are not.
lessons.task: Run the warning signs dashboard for your own project (or a project idea) and mark each item yes or no. For the riskiest item, write a five-step recovery plan. Then list your features with day estimates and check that the must-haves fit your remaining time with a buffer.

quiz.q: You have 30 working days left and features estimated at 12, 9, 8, 6 and 5 days. The must-haves are 12, 8 and 6 days. Do they fit with a buffer?
options: Yes, they need 26 days, leaving 4 days of buffer
quiz.explain: 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 days, leaving 30 - 26 = 4 days of buffer.

quiz.q: The company promised data three months ago but nothing has arrived. What is the best action?
options: Keep waiting until the last month
Set a firm date, then switch to a public or self-collected dataset and adjust the research questions
quiz.explain: A firm deadline and a plan B keep the thesis on track honestly.

quiz.q: Your teammate has stopped contributing. What should you do first?
options: Talk to them privately and kindly to understand what is happening
Complain to the board during the defence
quiz.explain: Start with a private conversation; then document and inform the supervisor early if needed.

quiz.q: Which is academic misconduct?
options: Switching to a public dataset and explaining why
Reporting only the best seed and hiding worse runs
quiz.explain: Cherry-picking results misrepresents the evidence.

quiz.q: One month before submission, your chapters are only headings. What is the best first step?
options: Rewrite the literature review in full detail
Freeze new experiments and write methodology and implementation first from your logs
quiz.explain: Writing what you know best first, from existing logs, makes fast progress.

lessons.title: After the Thesis and Capstone
lessons.content:
When a farmer harvests rice, the work does not end at cutting. Some grain is sold, some is kept to eat, and the best is saved as seed for next season. A farmer who sells everything has nothing to plant. Your thesis is a harvest of a year's work, and many students 'sell' it once, for a grade, then forget it in a cupboard. But the same work can become a published paper, the strongest project in your portfolio, the story that gets you a job, the evidence in a scholarship application, an open-source tool others use, or even a product. This final lesson shows how to get more from your thesis after the defence, then walks once through the whole mango detector project from start to finish as a capstone, and closes the course with a recap and where to go next.

Why the thesis matters after graduation: For many CSE graduates the thesis is the largest piece of independent work they have done. Employers ask about it in interviews because it shows how you handle a long, uncertain project. Universities abroad read about it in applications because it shows research potential. A published paper based on it is a lasting, checkable record. And the code, data and skills you built can keep being useful. A little extra effort in the weeks after the defence multiplies the value of the year.

Publishing: is it worth it?: Not every thesis needs to become a paper, but many good ones can. A paper is worth trying if your work has a clear contribution (a new dataset, a fair comparison in a new setting, a working system with real evaluation, a useful negative result), if your evaluation is solid, and if your supervisor agrees and will be a co-author. Publishing helps most if you plan higher studies or research jobs; for industry jobs, a strong GitHub project and a good interview story may matter as much.

Choosing a venue: Papers go to journals (longer review, often months, revisions possible) or conferences (fixed deadlines, a few months to decision, presentation at the event). For a first paper from a BSc thesis, a reputable conference is often the practical choice. Check that the topic fits the venue's call for papers, that the proceedings are published by a known publisher, that past papers are similar in quality to yours, and how your department and future universities view the venue. Your supervisor's experience here is invaluable.

Conferences in Bangladesh and abroad: Bangladesh hosts several established computing and engineering conferences, often organised by universities, for example ICCIT (International Conference on Computer and Information Technology) and ICECE (International Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering, held at BUET), with proceedings commonly published through IEEE. Abroad there are many regional and international conferences and workshops in every area; workshops attached to larger conferences can be a good first step for student work. Registration fees and travel can be expensive; some conferences allow online presentation, and some offer student discounts. Ask your department about any support for publication or travel.

Predatory venues, recap: Technical Writing and lesson 06 warned about predatory journals and conferences, which take money and publish almost anything with little or no real review. Warning signs: unsolicited flattering emails inviting you to publish, promises of very fast acceptance, very broad scope ('all fields of science and engineering'), unclear editorial board, fees hidden until acceptance, and indexing claims you cannot verify. Publishing there can harm your record. When in doubt, ask your supervisor and check the venue's past papers and publisher.

Turning a thesis into a paper: A thesis is long and explains everything; a paper is short and focused. Conference papers often have a page limit, commonly somewhere around 4 to 8 pages depending on the venue, so a 64-page thesis must shrink by roughly ten times. Steps: choose one main contribution and the research questions that support it; follow the paper structure from Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8-21): abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, results, conclusion; cut background that experts already know; keep the main comparison table, one or two key figures and the most insightful error analysis; rewrite rather than copy-paste, and follow the venue's template exactly. Your thesis can be cited or noted according to the venue's rules; ask your supervisor how to handle overlap.

The review process: After submission, reviewers score and comment. You may get acceptance, acceptance with changes, or rejection. Rejection is normal, even for experienced researchers. Read the comments calmly, improve the paper, and submit elsewhere. If accepted, address every reviewer comment in the camera-ready version, register, and present well; lesson 23's skills apply directly.

Portfolio and GitHub: Whether or not you publish, make the work visible. Clean up the repository: a clear README with the problem, a screenshot or demo GIF, how to install and run, results summary, and a link to the thesis or paper (lesson 17 and deep-cse-6-8-15). Remove secrets and personal data, add a licence, and pin the repository on your GitHub profile. Record a two-minute demo video. A recruiter who can see a working, documented project in thirty seconds remembers you.

CV and interviews: On your CV, describe the thesis in one or two lines with your role, the technology and a concrete result: 'Built an offline Android app that classifies mango freshness with a lightweight CNN (macro F1 0.85 on 3,000 market images; field-tested with five sellers).' In interviews, be ready to tell the story in about two minutes using a simple structure: situation (the problem), task (your goal), action (what you did, especially your part in a team), result (numbers), and what you learned. Prepare to discuss a hard problem you faced and how you solved it; lesson 24's recovery stories are excellent interview material.

Higher studies: For MS or PhD applications, the thesis is central. Your statement of purpose (SOP) should explain what you researched, what you found, what you learned about doing research, and how it connects to what you want to study next and with which faculty. Recommendation letters from your supervisor and board members carry weight, especially if they can describe your independence and honesty; ask early, at least a month before deadlines, and send them your CV, transcript, thesis abstract and a list of deadlines. A paper, even in a modest venue, and a public repository strengthen the application.

Open-sourcing code and data: Releasing your code and, where allowed, your data helps others build on your work and is increasingly expected. Before releasing data, check consent, privacy and ownership (lesson 13 and Professional Ethics, deep-cse-6-6): remove personal information, get permission from data providers, and document the dataset with a data card describing collection, labels, splits and limitations. Choose a licence for code (for example MIT or Apache 2.0) and for data (for example a Creative Commons licence) that fits your goals and any restrictions.

Turning it into a product: Some projects solve a real problem that people would use. Turning a thesis prototype into a product needs more: reliability, support for many devices, a business model, legal and privacy compliance, and real user feedback. Start small: a pilot with a few real users, measure whether they keep using it, and learn. University innovation centres, startup competitions and incubators in Bangladesh can provide mentoring. Even if it never becomes a business, a pilot with real users is a strong story.

Capstone: the mango detector, end to end: Here is the whole journey in one place. Months 1 to 2: Nusrat and Rafi explored ideas, scored topics with a weighted matrix (lesson 03), chose mango freshness detection, and agreed weekly meetings with their supervisor. Month 3: literature search and reading, an extraction matrix and a review that found a gap: few studies used real market photos or offline phone deployment. Month 4: problem statement, three research questions, a proposal with timeline and budget, and an approved proposal defence. Months 4 to 5: consent forms, photos at two Rajshahi markets, 3,000 labelled images, an agreement check (kappa about 0.6) and label corrections, grouped splits to avoid leakage. Months 6 to 7: baselines first (majority 50 percent accuracy, SVM 0.71 macro F1), three lightweight CNNs with equal tuning budgets and five seeds, ablations showing lighting correction mattered most, everything logged and backed up. Month 8: 5-fold cross-validation and paired tests (MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0 statistically similar; both well above the baseline), error analysis of 18 missed rotten mangoes, and the offline Android app. Month 9: field test with five sellers and 200 mangoes (172 correct). Months 9 to 10: writing chapter by chapter with supervisor feedback, abstract last. Month 11: defence with a live offline demo and backup video, minor corrections. Month 12: final bound copies, an open repository with a data card, and a 6-page paper submitted to a conference with their supervisor.

What made it work: Looking back, the mango project succeeded not because of a brilliant model but because of habits taught in this course: a narrow, useful problem; reading before building; a clear plan with buffers; honest data work; baselines and fair comparisons; logging and backups; careful statistics; deep error analysis; writing as they went; and honest, prepared defence answers. Tanvir's bus tracker, a system-style project, followed the same habits with requirements, design, testing and a field study in place of model experiments.

Course recap: Across 25 lessons you have learned to run a final year project or thesis end to end: understand what it is and plan your time (lessons 01 to 02); choose a topic, supervisor and team (03 to 05); find, read and review literature (06 to 08); define the problem, research questions and proposal (09 to 10); design the method, plan and manage risk and ethics (11 to 13); collect data, build systems and run experiments reproducibly (14 to 17); evaluate with the right metrics and statistics and analyse results honestly (18 to 20); write the thesis book (21 to 22); present and defend it (23); recover from problems (24); and use the work afterwards (25).

What next: If research excites you, Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7) goes deeper into research design, statistics, qualitative methods and the research process. Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8) remains your guide for clear writing at every stage. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) deepens planning and risk for larger projects. Most importantly, start: choose a problem you care about, talk to a possible supervisor this week, and open a notebook for ideas.

Common mistakes after the thesis: Leaving the repository private and messy. Never trying to publish good work, or publishing in predatory venues. Describing the thesis vaguely on the CV. Not being able to explain your own part in interviews. Asking for recommendation letters a few days before deadlines. Releasing data without consent or anonymisation.

Recap: Treat the thesis as a harvest with seed for the future. Publish good work in reputable venues (for example ICCIT or ICECE in Bangladesh, or international conferences and workshops), avoid predatory ones, and shrink a 64-page thesis into a focused paper of a few pages. Clean up the GitHub repository with a README and demo, describe the work with concrete numbers on your CV, tell it as a story in interviews, use it in SOPs with early recommendation requests, open-source code and data responsibly, and consider a pilot if it could be a product. The capstone shows how habits, not luck, carried a project from idea to paper. Next step: Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7), and your own thesis.
key_points: After the defence, a thesis can become a paper, a portfolio project, an interview story, evidence for higher studies, open-source work or a product.
Publish if there is a clear contribution and solid evaluation; choose reputable venues with your supervisor, such as established conferences in Bangladesh or abroad.
Avoid predatory venues: flattering invitations, very fast acceptance, very broad scope, hidden fees, unverifiable indexing.
Turning a thesis into a paper means focusing on one contribution and shrinking roughly ten times, from about 64 pages to a few pages, in the venue's template.
Make the work visible: a clean GitHub repository with README and demo, a concrete CV line with numbers, and a two-minute interview story.
For higher studies, connect the thesis to your SOP and ask supervisors for recommendation letters at least a month early; release data only with consent and anonymisation.
The mango capstone shows that good habits (narrow problem, reading first, baselines, logging, honest evaluation, writing as you go) carry a project from idea to paper.
lessons.tip: Within two weeks of your defence, while everything is fresh, spend one day cleaning the repository, writing the README, recording a demo video and adding a CV line. Students who wait 'until later' rarely do it at all.
lessons.task: Write a one-line CV description of your project (or a planned one) with a concrete number, a two-minute STAR-style interview story, and a short plan for after the defence: whether to publish and where, what to open-source, and who to ask for recommendation letters.

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign of a predatory venue?
options: It is organised by a university and published by a known publisher
Past papers are easy to find
An unsolicited flattering email promising acceptance within days for a fee
quiz.explain: Fast guaranteed acceptance for money is a classic predatory sign.

quiz.q: A 60-page thesis must become a 6-page paper. Roughly how much must it shrink?
quiz.explain: 60 / 6 = 10, so the paper keeps only the most important content.

quiz.q: What is the best CV line for a thesis?
options: Did a thesis on machine learning
Built an offline Android app classifying mango freshness with a lightweight CNN (macro F1 0.85 on 3,000 market images)
quiz.explain: It states what you built, the technology and a concrete result.

quiz.q: Before releasing your dataset publicly, what must you check?
options: Whether it has more than 1,000 items
Nothing, data should always be public
quiz.explain: Ethical and legal checks come first, then documentation and a licence.

quiz.q: When should you ask your supervisor for a recommendation letter?
options: At least a month before, with your CV, transcript, abstract and deadlines
quiz.explain: Early requests with materials help the supervisor write a strong letter.
